entry.title: Diagnosing Slow Requests and Excessive Network Usage

link.title: Diagnosing Slow Requests and Excessive Network Usage

entry.content:
Two complaints reach every app team eventually: “the screen takes forever to load” and “the app uses a lot of data.” Both sound like server problems, and both are usually client problems: requests that wait for each other when they could run together, the same resource fetched three times by three components, payloads sent uncompressed, a poll every 30 seconds that nobody remembers adding. None of them shows up in a profile of the app’s CPU usage, and none of them shows up in the server’s latency dashboards, which report each request as fast.

The way out is to measure the network behavior of a screen, not of individual requests, and to keep measuring it in tests so that a regression fails a build instead of a review. This article builds a small audit from URLSessionTaskMetrics, uses it on a deliberately wasteful screen against a local server, and fixes each problem it finds: a waterfall, duplicate and N+1 requests, queueing behind the connection limit, uncompressed responses, and polling. Each fix is measured, and the end result is locked in with a network budget test.

The examples use Swift 6 language mode and were compiled and run with the Swift 6.4 toolchain from Xcode 27.1 on macOS 26. They send requests to LocalServer, the loopback HTTP server from the appendix of the first article; paste that code first, then the blocks below in order, into one main.swift. The metrics fields used here are explained in Reading URLSessionTaskMetrics.

A method, not a tool

Network performance problems are found the same way every time:

  1. Measure a user-visible unit of work, such as opening a screen, from the first request to the last. Record every request: when it started and ended, how many bytes it moved, whether it was a duplicate.
  2. Look for shape, not speed. Total time is a symptom. The diagnosis is in the shape of the requests over time: a staircase means a waterfall, a pile-up at the start means queueing, two identical bars mean a duplicate.
  3. Fix one pattern, measure again.
  4. Write the result down as a budget that a test enforces: at most so many requests, so many bytes, so many sequential round trips.

The first step needs a recorder. The audit below is a session delegate that turns each task’s metrics into an entry, and summarizes the entries:

import Foundation
import Synchronization

struct AuditEntry: Sendable {
    let path: String
    let start: Date
    let end: Date
    let queued: Double          // ms between the task starting and its request being sent
    let wireBytes: Int64        // response body bytes as received
    let decodedBytes: Int64     // after Content-Encoding was undone
    let reused: Bool
}

final class NetworkAudit: NSObject, URLSessionTaskDelegate, Sendable {
    private let entries = Mutex<[AuditEntry]>([])

    func urlSession(_ session: URLSession, task: URLSessionTask, didFinishCollecting metrics: URLSessionTaskMetrics) {
        guard let last = metrics.transactionMetrics.last, let url = last.request.url else { return }
        let queued = last.requestStartDate.map { $0.timeIntervalSince(metrics.taskInterval.start) * 1000 } ?? 0
        let entry = AuditEntry(path: url.path() + (url.query().map { "?" + $0 } ?? ""),
                               start: metrics.taskInterval.start, end: metrics.taskInterval.end, queued: queued,
                               wireBytes: metrics.transactionMetrics.reduce(0) { $0 + $1.countOfResponseBodyBytesReceived },
                               decodedBytes: last.countOfResponseBodyBytesAfterDecoding, reused: last.isReusedConnection)
        entries.withLock { $0.append(entry) }
    }

    func reset() { entries.withLock { $0.removeAll() } }

    struct Report: CustomStringConvertible {
        let requests: Int
        let duplicates: [String]
        let wall: Double          // ms from first start to last end
        let busy: Double          // ms summed over all requests
        let wireBytes: Int64
        let decodedBytes: Int64
        let worstQueued: Double

        /// Average number of requests in flight while the screen loaded.
        var parallelism: Double { wall > 0 ? busy / wall : 0 }

        var description: String {
            String(format: "%d requests, %d duplicates, %.0f ms wall, parallelism %.2f, %lld B on the wire (%lld decoded), worst queue %.0f ms",
                   requests, duplicates.count, wall, parallelism, wireBytes, decodedBytes, worstQueued)
        }
    }

    var report: Report {
        let all = entries.withLock { $0 }
        let start = all.map(\.start).min() ?? .now
        let end = all.map(\.end).max() ?? .now
        let counts = Dictionary(all.map { ($0.path, 1) }, uniquingKeysWith: +)
        return Report(requests: all.count,
                      duplicates: counts.filter { $0.value > 1 }.keys.sorted(),
                      wall: end.timeIntervalSince(start) * 1000,
                      busy: all.reduce(0) { $0 + $1.end.timeIntervalSince($1.start) * 1000 },
                      wireBytes: all.reduce(0) { $0 + $1.wireBytes },
                      decodedBytes: all.reduce(0) { $0 + $1.decodedBytes },
                      worstQueued: all.map(\.queued).max() ?? 0)
    }
}

Parallelism is the one derived number worth explaining. If the requests’ durations add up to \(B\) (the busy time) and the screen took \(W\) from first request to last, then \(B/W\) is the average number of requests in flight, Little’s law again. A value near 1 with several requests means they ran one after another.

The server and a wasteful screen

The server below is a small library API. Every route answers after 60 ms, standing in for a mobile round trip, and book responses are about 2 KB of JSON. It compresses responses with gzip when the client accepts it and the server has compression switched on, which the test toggles:

func crc32(_ data: Data) -> UInt32 {
    var table = [UInt32](repeating: 0, count: 256)
    for index in 0..<256 {
        var value = UInt32(index)
        for _ in 0..<8 { value = value & 1 != 0 ? 0xEDB8_8320 ^ (value >> 1) : value >> 1 }
        table[index] = value
    }
    var crc: UInt32 = 0xFFFF_FFFF
    for byte in data { crc = table[Int((crc ^ UInt32(byte)) & 0xFF)] ^ (crc >> 8) }
    return crc ^ 0xFFFF_FFFF
}

/// RFC 1952 framing around the raw DEFLATE stream that Foundation's `.zlib` algorithm produces.
func gzip(_ data: Data) throws -> Data {
    var output = Data([0x1F, 0x8B, 0x08, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0xFF])
    output.append(try (data as NSData).compressed(using: .zlib) as Data)
    for value in [crc32(data), UInt32(truncatingIfNeeded: data.count)] {
        withUnsafeBytes(of: value.littleEndian) { output.append(contentsOf: $0) }
    }
    return output
}

let compressionEnabled = Mutex(false)

func book(_ id: String) -> String {
    let synopsis = String(repeating: "A desert planet, a noble family, and a prophecy. ", count: 36)
    return #"{"id":"\#(id)","title":"Book \#(id)","author":"Frank Herbert","synopsis":"\#(synopsis)"}"#
}

let server = try await LocalServer.start { request in
    let body: String
    switch request.path {
    case "/me": body = #"{"id":"u-1","branch":"central"}"#
    case "/me/loans": body = "[" + (1...5).map { #"{"bookID":"b-\#($0)"}"# }.joined(separator: ",") + "]"
    case "/books": body = "[" + (request.query["ids"] ?? "").split(separator: ",").map { book(String($0)) }.joined(separator: ",") + "]"
    case let path where path.hasPrefix("/books/"): body = book(String(path.dropFirst(7)))
    case "/branches/central/hours": body = #"{"open":"09:00","close":"18:00"}"#
    default: return .text("not found", status: 404)
    }
    let data = Data(body.utf8)
    var headers: [(name: String, value: String)] = [("Content-Type", "application/json")]
    var payload = data
    if compressionEnabled.withLock({ $0 }), request.header("Accept-Encoding")?.contains("gzip") == true {
        payload = try! gzip(data)
        headers.append(("Content-Encoding", "gzip"))
    }
    return HTTPResponse(status: 200, headers: headers, body: [.bytes(payload)], delay: .milliseconds(60))
}

let audit = NetworkAudit()
let session = URLSession(configuration: .ephemeral, delegate: audit, delegateQueue: nil)

func get<T: Decodable>(_ path: String, as type: T.Type) async throws -> T {
    let (data, _) = try await session.data(from: URL(string: server.baseURL.absoluteString + path)!)
    return try JSONDecoder().decode(T.self, from: data)
}

struct Me: Decodable { let id: String; let branch: String }
struct Loan: Decodable { let bookID: String }
struct BookDTO: Decodable { let id: String; let title: String }
struct Hours: Decodable { let open: String; let close: String }

The “My loans” screen shows the user’s loans with each book’s title, and the opening hours of their branch. This first version is written the way screens often grow: each component loads what it needs, one await after another, and a header component loads the current user again on its own:

struct LoansScreen { let titles: [String]; let hours: Hours }

func loadNaively() async throws -> LoansScreen {
    let me = try await get("/me", as: Me.self)
    let loans = try await get("/me/loans", as: [Loan].self)
    var titles: [String] = []
    for loan in loans {
        titles.append(try await get("/books/\(loan.bookID)", as: BookDTO.self).title)  // N+1
    }
    let hours = try await get("/branches/\(me.branch)/hours", as: Hours.self)
    _ = try await get("/me", as: Me.self)  // the header view loads the user too
    return LoansScreen(titles: titles, hours: hours)
}

let naive = try await loadNaively()
let before = audit.report
print("naive:", before)
assert(naive.titles.count == 5)
assert(before.requests == 9 && before.duplicates == ["/me"])
assert(before.parallelism < 1.1)   // a waterfall: one request at a time

The audit’s report for the naive screen:

naive: 9 requests, 1 duplicates, 632 ms wall, parallelism 1.00, 9350 B on the wire (9350 decoded), worst queue 6 ms

Nine requests, one of them a duplicate, each waiting for the previous one: a parallelism of 1.00 is the numeric signature of a waterfall. The server answered every request in 60 ms, so its dashboards show nothing wrong, and the user waited more than half a second.

The waterfall and its critical path

A screen’s minimum load time is set by its critical path: the longest chain of requests where each one needs the previous one’s result. Requests that do not depend on each other can overlap, so with a round-trip time of \(R\):

\[T_{\text{screen}} \;\ge\; R \times (\text{length of the longest dependency chain})\]

In the naive version every request waits for the one before it, so the chain has nine links. The real dependencies are fewer. The loans do not need the user’s profile, since the server identifies the user by their credentials; the books need the loans; the hours need the profile’s branch. The longest true chain is two requests long: loans, then books. Everything else can run alongside.

gantt
    accTitle: The naive loans screen as a waterfall of nine requests, compared with the fixed version in two rounds
    dateFormat x
    axisFormat %L ms
    section Naive
    /me :0, 70
    /me/loans :70, 140
    /books/b-1 :140, 210
    /books/b-2 :210, 280
    /books/b-3 :280, 350
    /books/b-4 :350, 420
    /books/b-5 :420, 490
    /branches/central/hours :490, 560
    /me (duplicate) :560, 630
    section Fixed
    /me :0, 75
    /me/loans :0, 75
    /books?ids=b-1..b-5 :75, 150
    /branches/central/hours :75, 150

The fix applies three changes, one per pattern:

  • Overlap independent requests with async let, so the user and the loans load together, and the books and the hours load together.
  • Batch the N+1 into one request for all five books, through the server’s ids parameter. Designing an API Client Around Consumer Needs measured the three strategies for this.
  • Load shared data once. The header gets the Me value that the screen already loaded. In a larger app, the coalescer from Coalescing Duplicate Requests does this across components that cannot easily share.
func loadEfficiently() async throws -> LoansScreen {
    async let me = get("/me", as: Me.self)
    async let loans = get("/me/loans", as: [Loan].self)
    let (profile, loanList) = try await (me, loans)                 // round 1
    let ids = loanList.map(\.bookID).joined(separator: ",")
    async let books = get("/books?ids=\(ids)", as: [BookDTO].self)  // round 2, together
    async let hours = get("/branches/\(profile.branch)/hours", as: Hours.self)
    return LoansScreen(titles: try await books.map(\.title), hours: try await hours)
}

audit.reset()
let efficient = try await loadEfficiently()
let after = audit.report
print("fixed:", after)
assert(efficient.titles == naive.titles)
assert(after.requests == 4 && after.duplicates.isEmpty)
assert(after.wall < 200 && after.parallelism > 1.7)

fixed: 4 requests, 0 duplicates, 151 ms wall, parallelism 1.99, 9325 B on the wire (9325 decoded), worst queue 3 ms

Four requests in two rounds, 151 ms instead of 632, and the same data on screen. The critical path predicted two round trips, about 120 ms plus overhead, and that is what the measurement shows.

Bytes on the wire: compression

The fixed screen still moved about 9 KB, almost all of it the books’ synopses as plain JSON. JSON compresses well, because it repeats key names and, in most APIs, much of the data. URLSession advertises Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate on every request and decompresses responses transparently, as the first article showed, so compression costs the client nothing to accept. Whether it happens is up to the server, and servers often skip it for API responses because nobody turned it on:

compressionEnabled.withLock { $0 = true }
audit.reset()
let compressed = try await loadEfficiently()
let gzipped = audit.report
print("gzip:", gzipped)
assert(compressed.titles == efficient.titles)
assert(gzipped.decodedBytes == after.decodedBytes)        // the same JSON after decoding
assert(gzipped.wireBytes * 5 < gzipped.decodedBytes)      // a fraction of it on the wire

gzip: 4 requests, 0 duplicates, 142 ms wall, parallelism 1.98, 357 B on the wire (9325 decoded), worst queue 2 ms

The same 9.3 KB of JSON crossed the network as 357 bytes. The synopsis text in this example is unusually repetitive, which flatters the ratio; for more realistic data, a list of 500 varied book records encoded as 67 KB of JSON compressed to 4.9 KB with the same DEFLATE algorithm, a factor of 13.6. countOfResponseBodyBytesReceived and countOfResponseBodyBytesAfterDecoding in the metrics are exactly the pair that reveals whether compression is happening; if they are equal for JSON responses, it is not.

Compression is one of three byte-level fixes, in order of how much they usually save:

Fix Saves Where it is covered
Don’t download it again: freshness and ETag validation The whole body on repeat visits HTTP Caching
Compress it: Content-Encoding: gzip or br 70–95% of JSON This section
Send less: fields the screen needs, images at the size displayed Varies, often the most for images Designing an API Client

Queueing behind the connection limit

The audit’s worstQueued column has stayed at 1 ms so far. It grows when a screen starts more requests to one host than the session allows in flight. A grid of 40 thumbnails is the classic case:

func thumbnails(limit: Int) async throws -> NetworkAudit.Report {
    let configuration = URLSessionConfiguration.ephemeral
    configuration.httpMaximumConnectionsPerHost = limit
    let thumbnailAudit = NetworkAudit()
    let grid = URLSession(configuration: configuration, delegate: thumbnailAudit, delegateQueue: nil)
    try await withThrowingTaskGroup(of: Void.self) { group in
        for index in 1...40 {
            group.addTask { _ = try await grid.data(from: server.baseURL.appending(path: "books/t-\(index)")) }
        }
        try await group.waitForAll()
    }
    grid.finishTasksAndInvalidate()
    return thumbnailAudit.report
}

let sixConnections = try await thumbnails(limit: 6)
let twentyConnections = try await thumbnails(limit: 20)
print("6 connections:", sixConnections, "\n20 connections:", twentyConnections)
assert(sixConnections.worstQueued > 300)
assert(twentyConnections.worstQueued < sixConnections.worstQueued / 2)

6 connections: 40 requests, 0 duplicates, 512 ms wall, parallelism 21.96, 5368 B on the wire (73422 decoded), worst queue 439 ms
20 connections: 40 requests, 0 duplicates, 161 ms wall, parallelism 30.61, 5368 B on the wire (73422 decoded), worst queue 88 ms

The parallelism column here counts tasks that are waiting in the session’s queue as well as those on the wire, which is what the user experiences as “loading.” With six connections, the last thumbnails waited 439 ms in the session’s queue before their requests were sent, about \(\lceil 40/6 \rceil - 1 = 6\) rounds of 60 ms, while the server had nothing to do. That waiting is invisible on the server and appears in the metrics only as the gap between the task starting and its request being sent. The fixes are, in order of preference: request fewer, larger things, such as a sprite or a smaller first page; serve the host over HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, where one connection carries many concurrent streams; or raise httpMaximumConnectionsPerHost for a session dedicated to that host, as Choosing a URLSession Configuration suggested for media.

Data usage over a day: polling

Excessive data usage is rarely one large request. It is usually a small request made very often. A poll every \(\tau\) seconds makes \(86\,400/\tau\) requests a day, each costing its headers \(h\) plus, when the data changed, a body \(b\). With conditional requests, an unchanged response costs only headers, so if the data changes in a fraction \(p\) of polls:

\[\text{bytes per day} \approx \frac{86\,400}{\tau}\,\big(h + p\,b\big)\]

For a 30-second poll of a 20 KB response with about 600 bytes of request and response headers, an app that refetches unconditionally (\(p = 1\)) moves about 59 MB a day, and keeps the radio waking up 2,880 times. With ETag validation and data that changes in 5% of polls, the same poll moves about 4.6 MB. With a push notification or a server-sent event when the data actually changes, as in Streaming Responses and Incremental Parsing, the polling cost disappears.

func dailyBytes(interval: Double, headers: Double, body: Double, changeRate: Double) -> Double {
    86_400 / interval * (headers + changeRate * body)
}
let unconditional = dailyBytes(interval: 30, headers: 600, body: 20_000, changeRate: 1)
let conditional = dailyBytes(interval: 30, headers: 600, body: 20_000, changeRate: 0.05)
assert(Int(unconditional / 1_000_000) == 59 && Int(conditional / 100_000) == 46)

The wake-ups matter as much as the bytes. Each request from an idle radio forces it into a high-power state that it leaves only after a delay of its own, so 2,880 small requests cost far more energy than the same bytes in a few large ones. Batch background work, respect isConstrained (Low Data Mode) and isExpensive as described in Offline Behavior and Reachability Assumptions, and stop polling when the screen is not visible.

Budgets that fail builds

The fixes above are only as durable as the next change to the screen. A network budget turns the measurements into a test: it loads the screen against the local server and fails if the screen makes more requests, moves more bytes, or needs more sequential round trips than agreed. The round trips are measured as wall time in units of the server’s fixed latency:

struct NetworkBudget {
    var maxRequests: Int
    var maxRoundTrips: Int
    var maxWireBytes: Int64
    var latency: Double = 60

    func violations(of report: NetworkAudit.Report) -> [String] {
        var problems: [String] = []
        if report.requests > maxRequests { problems.append("\(report.requests) requests > \(maxRequests)") }
        if !report.duplicates.isEmpty { problems.append("duplicates: \(report.duplicates)") }
        let roundTrips = Int((report.wall / latency).rounded())
        if roundTrips > maxRoundTrips { problems.append("\(roundTrips) sequential round trips > \(maxRoundTrips)") }
        if report.wireBytes > maxWireBytes { problems.append("\(report.wireBytes) bytes > \(maxWireBytes)") }
        return problems
    }
}

let loansBudget = NetworkBudget(maxRequests: 4, maxRoundTrips: 2, maxWireBytes: 2_000)

audit.reset()
_ = try await loadEfficiently()
assert(loansBudget.violations(of: audit.report).isEmpty)

audit.reset()
_ = try await loadNaively()
let regressions = loansBudget.violations(of: audit.report)
print(regressions)
assert(regressions.count == 3)   // requests, duplicates, and round trips are over budget
print(audit.report.wireBytes)       // bytes are within budget: compression is still on

The naive version fails three of the four checks, with messages that say which number is over budget and by how much: 9 requests > 4, duplicates: ["/me"], and 10 sequential round trips > 2. It passes the byte budget, at 863 bytes, only because the server is now compressing: five separately compressed book responses still fit under 2 KB. That is a useful reminder that each budget line guards a different failure, and that the request and round-trip limits are what catch structural regressions. A budget like this belongs in the test suite for every screen that matters, and in code review the conversation becomes “this change adds a request to the loans screen; is it worth it?” rather than a discovery months later.

Tools for the field

The local audit finds structural problems. Problems that depend on real networks, devices, and users need other tools:

Tool What it shows
Instruments, Network template Connections and HTTP traffic per process on a device, with timings for every request
Network Link Conditioner (Xcode Additional Tools) The app on simulated 3G, high-latency, or lossy links, which makes waterfalls painfully visible
networkQuality (macOS) The capacity and responsiveness of the current network, so a slow test run can be told apart from a slow link
URLSessionTaskMetrics aggregated in the app Percentiles per route and network type from real users, as built in Reading URLSessionTaskMetrics
MetricKit, MXNetworkTransferMetric Daily cellular and Wi-Fi upload and download totals per app version, reported by the system
os_signpost intervals around screen loads The network audit’s timeline next to CPU and main-thread activity in Instruments

The combination that catches most problems is the local audit and budget in tests, for structure, and aggregated metrics in production, for the network conditions no test reproduces.

Summary

  • Measure a screen’s requests as a whole: count, duplicates, bytes, wall time, and parallelism, busy time divided by wall time.
  • A parallelism near 1 with several requests is a waterfall. The screen’s load time is bounded by \(R\) times its longest true dependency chain, not by its request count.
  • Measured on the example screen: overlapping independent requests, batching an N+1, and loading shared data once took nine requests in 632 ms to four in 151 ms.
  • Compare countOfResponseBodyBytesReceived with the decoded count to see whether compression happens; gzip cut the screen’s 9.3 KB to 357 bytes, and realistic JSON compresses by a factor of about 13.
  • Queueing behind the connection limit shows up as the gap between task start and request start; 40 requests on six connections queued for up to 439 ms.
  • Polling costs \(\frac{86\,400}{\tau}(h + p\,b)\) bytes a day and as many radio wake-ups; validate, batch, or replace it with push.
  • Lock improvements in with a network budget test that fails on extra requests, duplicates, round trips, or bytes.

Exercise

Add the thumbnail grid to the loans screen, loading a 3 KB image per book, and give the screen a budget that includes it. Then make the images load lazily, only for the first six visible rows, and the rest as the user scrolls, using the prefetch formula from Pagination. Measure the screen’s initial and total bytes with the audit, and write two budgets: one for the first frame and one for a full scroll. Finally, run the screen with Network Link Conditioner’s “3G” profile on a device and compare the measured wall time with \(R\) times the critical path.

Further reading

  • Ilya Grigorik, High Performance Browser Networking, especially the chapters on latency, TCP, and mobile networks; the principles apply directly to apps.
  • Analyze HTTP traffic in Instruments, WWDC21.
  • Apple’s MXNetworkTransferMetric documentation, for field data on transfer volumes.

entry.title: Reading URLSessionTaskMetrics
entry.content:
“The request is slow” is not a diagnosis. A request can be slow because the name took long to resolve, because the connection needed a TCP and TLS handshake to a distant server, because the server took long to think, because the response was large, or because the request waited in the session’s own queue before any of that started. Each cause has a different fix, and guessing between them is how teams spend a week optimizing a server that was never the bottleneck.

URLSessionTaskMetrics answers the question for every request, from inside the app, on the user’s real network. For each task it reports a timeline of the phases of every HTTP transaction, whether a connection was reused, which protocol was negotiated, whether the response came from the cache, and how many bytes went each way. This article reads those fields against the local server, where every number can be checked, and against real HTTPS endpoints, where they show what a phone actually pays for. It ends with a recorder that turns per-request metrics into the percentiles that matter.

The examples use Swift 6 language mode and were compiled and run with the Swift 6.4 toolchain from Xcode 27.1 on macOS 26. They send requests to LocalServer, the loopback HTTP server from the appendix of the first article; paste that code first, then the blocks below in order, into one main.swift. The TLS section uses the test certificate authority and server identity generated in App Transport Security and TLS Trust; the files must be in the working directory.

Collecting metrics

Metrics arrive through one delegate method, urlSession(_:task:didFinishCollecting:), called once per task after it completes. A session delegate receives it for every task; the delegate: parameter of the async methods receives it for one task. The collector below stores each task’s metrics by task identifier, behind a lock, because the session calls it on its own delegate queue:

import Foundation
import Network
import Security
import Synchronization

final class MetricsCollector: NSObject, URLSessionTaskDelegate, Sendable {
    private let collected = Mutex<[URLSessionTaskMetrics]>([])

    func urlSession(_ session: URLSession, task: URLSessionTask, didFinishCollecting metrics: URLSessionTaskMetrics) {
        collected.withLock { $0.append(metrics) }
    }

    var all: [URLSessionTaskMetrics] { collected.withLock { $0 } }
    var last: URLSessionTaskMetrics? { all.last }
}

func milliseconds(_ start: Date?, _ end: Date?) -> Double? {
    guard let start, let end else { return nil }
    return end.timeIntervalSince(start) * 1000
}

A URLSessionTaskMetrics value has three parts: taskInterval, the task’s whole life from creation to completion; redirectCount; and transactionMetrics, one URLSessionTaskTransactionMetrics for each request-response pair the task made, including redirects and cache lookups.

The phases of a transaction

Each transaction carries timestamps for the phases of loading a resource, defined in the same terms as the W3C’s Resource Timing for browsers:

gantt
    accTitle: The phases of a cold HTTPS request to www.apple.com, measured with URLSessionTaskMetrics
    dateFormat x
    axisFormat %L ms
    section DNS
    domainLookup (cached) :0, 1
    section Connection
    TCP handshake :1, 17
    TLS handshake :17, 32
    section Exchange
    request sent :32, 33
    waiting for first byte :33, 42
    response body :42, 45
Phase Timestamps What it costs
Queueing fetchStartDate → domainLookupStartDate Waiting for a connection slot or the cache
DNS domainLookupStartDate → domainLookupEndDate Name resolution, often cached
Connect connectStartDate → connectEndDate TCP or QUIC handshake, including TLS
TLS secureConnectionStartDate → secureConnectionEndDate The TLS part of the connect phase
Request requestStartDate → requestEndDate Sending headers and body
Waiting requestEndDate → responseStartDate Network round trip plus server processing
Download responseStartDate → responseEndDate Receiving the body

The connect phase contains the TLS phase; they are not consecutive. A reused connection has no DNS, connect, or TLS timestamps at all, which is the most direct way to see that reuse happened. The “waiting” phase is often called time to first byte, and it is the only phase that includes the server’s own work.

The timeline above comes from a real request. Three requests to public HTTPS endpoints from the Mac used for this series, over Wi-Fi, produced:

let collector = MetricsCollector()
let session = URLSession(configuration: .ephemeral, delegate: collector, delegateQueue: nil)
for url in ["https://www.apple.com/library/test/success.html",
            "https://www.apple.com/library/test/success.html",
            "https://www.google.com/generate_204"] {
    _ = try await session.data(from: URL(string: url)!)
}
// Printed for each network transaction: protocol, reuse, phase durations, TLS version, header bytes sent

www.apple.com   h2  reused=false  dns 1.0  connect 31.0 (tls 15.0)  ttfb 9.2   total 45.1   TLS 1.3  header bytes sent 142
www.apple.com   h2  reused=true   dns -    connect -                ttfb 7.9   total 8.1    TLS 1.3  header bytes sent 48
www.google.com  h3  reused=false  dns 1.0  connect 170.0 (tls 167.0) ttfb 53.9 total 242.8  TLS 1.3  header bytes sent 113

Several lessons are in those three lines:

  • The first request to www.apple.com spent 31 ms of its 45 ms connecting. The second, on the reused HTTP/2 connection, took 8 ms in total. Connection reuse, not server speed, was the difference.
  • The second request sent 48 header bytes instead of 142, because HTTP/2’s HPACK compression (RFC 7541) sends repeated headers as references to an earlier request’s.
  • The Google endpoint was reached over HTTP/3, on QUIC. Its connect and TLS phases nearly coincide, 170 and 167 ms, because QUIC performs the transport and TLS 1.3 handshakes together.

Round trips set the floor

The phases explain why latency, not bandwidth, dominates small requests. If the round-trip time to the server is \(R\) and the server needs \(S\) to produce the response, a request on a new HTTPS connection over TCP needs one round trip for the TCP handshake, one for the TLS 1.3 handshake, and one for the request itself:

\[T_{\text{cold, TCP+TLS 1.3}} \;\ge\; 3R + S, \qquad T_{\text{cold, QUIC}} \;\ge\; 2R + S, \qquad T_{\text{reused}} \;\ge\; R + S\]

TLS 1.2 adds another round trip, and QUIC can even send the request in its first flight on reconnection with 0-RTT, at the cost of replay protection. The TCP part of the connect phase, secureConnectionStartDate − connectStartDate, is itself one round trip, so the metrics provide an estimate of \(R\) for free: about 16 ms in the apple.com measurement, which also bounds the server’s think time in the 9 ms “waiting” phase to almost nothing. On a cellular network where \(R\) is 80 ms, the same cold request costs at least 240 ms before the server does anything, which is why connection reuse and fewer, larger requests matter more on phones than any server optimization.

Reading the fields against a known server

The local server makes every field checkable. It serves a fast route, a slow route that waits 150 ms before answering, a redirect, and a cacheable route:

let server = try await LocalServer.start { request in
    switch request.path {
    case "/fast": .json(#"{"ok":true}"#)
    case "/slow": HTTPResponse(status: 200, headers: [("Content-Type", "application/json")],
                               body: [.bytes(Data(repeating: 65, count: 5_000))], delay: .milliseconds(150))
    case "/moved": HTTPResponse(status: 302, headers: [("Location", "/landing")])
    case "/landing": .json(#"{"moved":true}"#)
    case "/cached": .json(#"{"ok":true}"#, headers: [("Cache-Control", "max-age=60")])
    default: .text("not found", status: 404)
    }
}

let collector = MetricsCollector()
let configuration = URLSessionConfiguration.default
configuration.urlCache = URLCache(memoryCapacity: 1_000_000, diskCapacity: 0)
let session = URLSession(configuration: configuration, delegate: collector, delegateQueue: nil)

_ = try await session.data(from: server.baseURL.appending(path: "fast"))
let cold = collector.last!.transactionMetrics.last!
_ = try await session.data(from: server.baseURL.appending(path: "slow"))
let warm = collector.last!.transactionMetrics.last!

assert(cold.networkProtocolName == "http/1.1" && cold.resourceFetchType == .networkLoad)
assert(!cold.isReusedConnection && cold.connectStartDate != nil)
assert(warm.isReusedConnection && warm.connectStartDate == nil && warm.domainLookupStartDate == nil)
assert(cold.remoteAddress == "127.0.0.1" && cold.remotePort == server.port)
assert(cold.localPort == warm.localPort)   // the same TCP connection, seen from the client side

let waiting = milliseconds(warm.requestEndDate, warm.responseStartDate)!
assert(waiting >= 150 && waiting < 250)    // the server's 150 ms shows up as time to first byte
assert(warm.countOfResponseBodyBytesReceived == 5_000)
assert(warm.countOfRequestHeaderBytesSent > 100 && warm.countOfRequestBodyBytesSent == 0)
assert(!warm.isCellular && !warm.isExpensive && !warm.isConstrained)

The server’s 150 ms delay appeared, as it should, in the waiting phase, between the end of the request and the first byte of the response. The second request reused the first one’s TCP connection: no DNS or connect timestamps, and the same local port.

Redirects and the cache add transactions

A task’s transactionMetrics is an array because one task can make several exchanges. A redirect makes two:

_ = try await session.data(from: server.baseURL.appending(path: "moved"))
let redirected = collector.last!
assert(redirected.redirectCount == 1 && redirected.transactionMetrics.count == 2)
assert((redirected.transactionMetrics[0].response as? HTTPURLResponse)?.statusCode == 302)
assert((redirected.transactionMetrics[1].response as? HTTPURLResponse)?.statusCode == 200)

The cache adds transactions of its own. A fresh cached response produces one transaction with resourceFetchType == .localCache and no network timestamps. A response that was stored without freshness information, like the /fast route’s, which has no Cache-Control, produces two on its next use: a cache transaction for the stored candidate, then the network transaction that replaced it:

_ = try await session.data(from: server.baseURL.appending(path: "cached"))
_ = try await session.data(from: server.baseURL.appending(path: "cached"))
let hit = collector.last!
assert(hit.transactionMetrics.count == 1 && hit.transactionMetrics[0].resourceFetchType == .localCache)
assert(hit.transactionMetrics[0].networkProtocolName == nil && hit.transactionMetrics[0].remoteAddress == nil)

_ = try await session.data(from: server.baseURL.appending(path: "fast"))
let revalidated = collector.last!.transactionMetrics.map(\.resourceFetchType)
assert(revalidated == [.localCache, .networkLoad])

This is the reliable way to answer “was this served from the cache?” The response itself cannot tell you: as HTTP Caching showed, even a revalidated 304 is delivered as a 200.

Cache lookups also combine with redirects. Had /moved pointed at /slow, which this session had already stored without freshness information, the task would have had three transactions, the 302, a cache candidate for /slow, and the network load that replaced it. Code that reads transactionMetrics.last for the final exchange, as the recorder below does, is unaffected; code that assumes transactionMetrics.count == redirectCount + 1 is not.

TLS details

Over HTTPS, the transaction also reports the negotiated TLS version and cipher suite. Against the TLS-enabled LocalServer from the ATS article, with the test CA trusted by a delegate:

func identity() throws -> sec_identity_t {
    let p12 = try Data(contentsOf: URL(fileURLWithPath: "server.p12"))
    var items: CFArray?
    let options: [String: Any] = [kSecImportExportPassphrase as String: "test", kSecImportToMemoryOnly as String: true]
    guard SecPKCS12Import(p12 as CFData, options as CFDictionary, &items) == errSecSuccess,
          let first = (items as? [[String: Any]])?.first else { throw URLError(.clientCertificateRejected) }
    return sec_identity_create(first[kSecImportItemIdentity as String] as! SecIdentity)!
}

final class TrustTestCA: NSObject, URLSessionTaskDelegate, Sendable {
    let collector = MetricsCollector()
    func urlSession(_ session: URLSession, task: URLSessionTask, didReceive challenge: URLAuthenticationChallenge)
        async -> (URLSession.AuthChallengeDisposition, URLCredential?) {
        guard let trust = challenge.protectionSpace.serverTrust,
              let ca = try? Data(contentsOf: URL(fileURLWithPath: "ca.der")),
              let anchor = SecCertificateCreateWithData(nil, ca as CFData) else { return (.performDefaultHandling, nil) }
        SecTrustSetAnchorCertificates(trust, [anchor] as CFArray)
        return SecTrustEvaluateWithError(trust, nil) ? (.useCredential, URLCredential(trust: trust)) : (.cancelAuthenticationChallenge, nil)
    }
    func urlSession(_ session: URLSession, task: URLSessionTask, didFinishCollecting metrics: URLSessionTaskMetrics) {
        collector.urlSession(session, task: task, didFinishCollecting: metrics)
    }
}

let tlsOptions = NWProtocolTLS.Options()
sec_protocol_options_set_local_identity(tlsOptions.securityProtocolOptions, try identity())
let secure = try await LocalServer.start(tls: tlsOptions) { _ in .json(#"{"secure":true}"#) }
let trustDelegate = TrustTestCA()
_ = try await URLSession(configuration: .ephemeral).data(from: secure.baseURL, delegate: trustDelegate)
let tls = trustDelegate.collector.last!.transactionMetrics.last!
assert(tls.negotiatedTLSProtocolVersion == .TLSv13)
assert(tls.secureConnectionStartDate != nil && tls.secureConnectionEndDate != nil)
assert(tls.connectStartDate! <= tls.secureConnectionStartDate! && tls.secureConnectionEndDate! <= tls.connectEndDate!)
print("TLS 1.3, cipher suite 0x\(String(tls.negotiatedTLSCipherSuite!.rawValue, radix: 16))")

The assertion on the timestamps confirms the table: the TLS phase lies inside the connect phase. The cipher suite printed 0x1302, TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, the same suite the public servers above negotiated; it is a TLS 1.3 suite and satisfies App Transport Security.

From single requests to percentiles

One request’s metrics explain one request. Decisions need distributions: “the 95th-percentile time to first byte for the catalog endpoint is 800 ms on cellular.” The recorder below reduces each transaction to a few numbers, keyed by a route template so that /books/7 and /books/8 aggregate together, and computes percentiles with the nearest-rank method:

\[P_p = x_{(\lceil p\,n \rceil)}\]

where \(x_{(k)}\) is the \(k\)-th smallest of the \(n\) samples. The mean is a poor summary for latency, because latency distributions are skewed: a few very slow requests pull the mean up while saying nothing about the typical one, and the typical one says nothing about the slow requests users notice.

struct Sample: Sendable {
    let route: String
    let waiting: Double     // ms, request end to first byte
    let total: Double       // ms, fetch start to response end
    let reused: Bool
    let fromCache: Bool
}

final class MetricsRecorder: NSObject, URLSessionTaskDelegate, Sendable {
    private let samples = Mutex<[Sample]>([])
    let route: @Sendable (URL) -> String

    init(route: @escaping @Sendable (URL) -> String) { self.route = route }

    func urlSession(_ session: URLSession, task: URLSessionTask, didFinishCollecting metrics: URLSessionTaskMetrics) {
        guard let final = metrics.transactionMetrics.last, let url = final.request.url else { return }
        let sample = Sample(route: route(url),
                            waiting: milliseconds(final.requestEndDate, final.responseStartDate) ?? 0,
                            total: milliseconds(final.fetchStartDate, final.responseEndDate) ?? 0,
                            reused: final.isReusedConnection,
                            fromCache: final.resourceFetchType == .localCache)
        samples.withLock { $0.append(sample) }
    }

    func percentile(_ p: Double, of keyPath: KeyPath<Sample, Double>, route: String) -> Double? {
        let values = samples.withLock { $0 }.filter { $0.route == route && !$0.fromCache }.map { $0[keyPath: keyPath] }.sorted()
        guard !values.isEmpty else { return nil }
        return values[max(0, Int((p * Double(values.count)).rounded(.up)) - 1)]
    }

    func reuseRate(route: String) -> Double {
        let network = samples.withLock { $0 }.filter { $0.route == route && !$0.fromCache }
        return network.isEmpty ? 0 : Double(network.filter(\.reused).count) / Double(network.count)
    }
}

The test drives 200 requests at a route whose server-side delay follows a known distribution: 90% take 20 ms, 10% take 200 ms. The recorder should find that the median waiting time is near 20 ms and the 95th percentile near 200 ms, and that a mean would describe neither:

let books = try await LocalServer.start { request in
    let slow = Int(request.query["n"] ?? "0")! % 10 == 0
    return HTTPResponse(status: 200, headers: [("Content-Type", "application/json")],
                        body: [.bytes(Data("{}".utf8))], delay: .milliseconds(slow ? 200 : 20))
}
let recorder = MetricsRecorder { url in
    url.path().split(separator: "/").map { Int($0) == nil ? String($0) : ":id" }.joined(separator: "/")
}
let recordingSession = URLSession(configuration: .ephemeral, delegate: recorder, delegateQueue: nil)
try await withThrowingTaskGroup(of: Void.self) { group in
    for n in 0..<200 {
        group.addTask {
            var components = URLComponents(url: books.baseURL.appending(path: "books/\(n % 25)"), resolvingAgainstBaseURL: false)!
            components.queryItems = [URLQueryItem(name: "n", value: "\(n)")]
            _ = try await recordingSession.data(from: components.url!)
        }
    }
    try await group.waitForAll()
}

let p50 = recorder.percentile(0.50, of: \.waiting, route: "books/:id")!
let p95 = recorder.percentile(0.95, of: \.waiting, route: "books/:id")!
let p99Total = recorder.percentile(0.99, of: \.total, route: "books/:id")!
print(String(format: "waiting p50 %.0f ms, p95 %.0f ms; total p99 %.0f ms; reuse %.0f%%",
             p50, p95, p99Total, recorder.reuseRate(route: "books/:id") * 100))
assert(p50 >= 20 && p50 < 60)
assert(p95 >= 200 && p95 < 300)
assert(recorder.reuseRate(route: "books/:id") > 0.9)   // six connections served 200 requests

The run printed a median waiting time of 25 ms and a 95th percentile of 207 ms, close to the fast requests’ 20 ms and the slow requests’ 200 ms: exactly the shape the server was given, plus a few milliseconds of overhead. The mean, about 38 ms, would have suggested that every request is moderately slow, which no request was. The reuse rate, 97%, shows the session at work: with the default limit of six connections per host, nearly all of the 200 requests went over an existing connection.

total includes queueing, which here is large: the 99th percentile of total time was 1.48 seconds, for requests whose server work took at most 200 ms, because 200 concurrent requests shared six connections and most of each request’s time was spent waiting for a free one. That queueing is visible only in metrics, between fetchStartDate and the moment the request is sent, and it is the subject of Diagnosing Slow Requests and Excessive Network Usage.

Using metrics in production

Metrics are cheap to collect and easy to over-collect. A few rules keep them useful and safe:

  • Aggregate on the device. Send percentiles per route and network type at intervals, not one record per request. A dozen numbers per route per hour answer nearly every question.
  • Segment by what changes the answer. Network type (isCellular, isExpensive, isConstrained), protocol (networkProtocolName), and reuse change latency more than anything in the app’s code. A p95 across all of them hides the cellular cold-start case that users complain about.
  • Treat addresses as personal data. localAddress and remoteAddress include the device’s IP address, which can identify a user and approximate their location. Do not upload them; Redacting Sensitive Data from Network Logs applies here too.
  • Template the routes. Grouping by full URL produces one bucket per book; grouping by books/:id produces one per endpoint, and keeps identifiers out of analytics.

Summary

  • urlSession(_:task:didFinishCollecting:) delivers one URLSessionTaskMetrics per task, with a transaction for every exchange, including redirects and cache lookups.
  • Phases: queueing, DNS, connect (which contains TLS), request, waiting for the first byte (round trip plus server time), and download. Reused connections have no DNS, connect, or TLS timestamps.
  • Measured against public servers: a reused HTTP/2 connection cut a request from 45 ms to 8 ms and its header bytes from 142 to 48; HTTP/3 merged the transport and TLS handshakes.
  • Round trips set a floor: at least \(3R + S\) for a cold TCP and TLS 1.3 request, \(2R + S\) over QUIC, \(R + S\) on a reused connection.
  • resourceFetchType == .localCache is the reliable signal of a cache hit; a stale stored response produces a cache transaction followed by a network one.
  • Aggregate into percentiles per route template and network type. Measured: a 90/10 mix of 20 ms and 200 ms server times gave p50 near 20 ms and p95 near 200 ms, which a mean of about 38 ms would hide.

Exercise

Extend MetricsRecorder to keep, per route, a histogram with fixed buckets (0–25, 25–50, 50–100, 100–250, 250–500, 500–1000, over 1000 ms) instead of every sample, so it can run for days in constant memory. Compute approximate percentiles from the histogram by interpolating within the bucket that contains the rank, and compare them with the exact percentiles from the 200-request test. How large is the error at p50 and p95, and how would you choose buckets so the error is smallest where you make decisions?

Further reading

  • Apple’s URLSessionTaskMetrics and URLSessionTaskTransactionMetrics.
  • Analyze HTTP traffic in Instruments, WWDC21.
  • The W3C Resource Timing specification, which defines the same phases for browsers.
  • RFC 9000: QUIC and RFC 7541: HPACK.

Previous: Verifying Contracts Against a Controlled Server. Next: Diagnosing Slow Requests and Excessive Network Usage.

Return to the Networking roadmap.
entry.summary: “The request is slow” is not a diagnosis. A request can be slow because the name took long to resolve, because the connection needed a TCP and TLS handshake to a distant server, because the server took long to think, because the response was large, or because the request waited in the session’s own queue before any of that started. Each cause has a different fix, and guessing between them is how teams spend a week optimizing a server that was never the bottleneck. URLSessionTaskMetrics answers the question for every request, from inside the app, on the user’s real network. For each task it reports a timeline of the phases of every HTTP transaction, whether a connection was reused, which protocol was negotiated, whether the response came from the cache, and how many bytes went each way. This article reads those fields against the local server, where every number can be checked, and against real HTTPS endpoints, where they show what a phone actually pays for. It ends with a recorder that turns per-request metrics into the percentiles that matter.

entry.title: Verifying Contracts Against a Controlled Server

link.title: Verifying Contracts Against a Controlled Server

entry.content:
Unit tests with stubbed responses prove that a client handles the responses its authors wrote down. They cannot prove that the server sends those responses. The gap between the two is where integration failures live: the server renames authorName to author, starts returning prices as strings, or begins to require a header the app never sends, and every client test still passes because every fixture still says what it always said.

A contract closes that gap by making the fixtures themselves the thing both sides test against. The client’s tests record what it sends and what it relies on in the responses, as data. The server’s tests replay the same requests and check that the real responses still satisfy what the client relies on. This article builds that loop: a small contract format with type-based matching, a LocalServer that serves the contract to the client and rejects requests that do not match it, and a provider check that runs the contract against three versions of a server, one that is compatible, one that adds a field, and one that breaks the client in a way no client-side test could catch.

The examples use Swift 6 language mode and Swift Testing, and were run with swift test using the Swift 6.4 toolchain from Xcode 27.1 on macOS 26. Each block is labeled with the file it belongs to in a Swift package with a Library target and a LibraryTests test target. The tests use LocalServer, the loopback HTTP server from the appendix of the first article, placed in the test target.

What a contract records

The idea is known as consumer-driven contract testing, and Pact is its best-known implementation. The consumer, here the app, declares a set of interactions. Each one is a request the consumer sends and the minimum the consumer needs from the response:

flowchart LR
    accTitle: The consumer-driven contract testing loop
    subgraph Consumer["Consumer (app) tests"]
        C1[Client code] -->|requests| CS[Contract server<br/>serves contract responses<br/>rejects unknown requests]
    end
    CS -->|writes| K[(contract.json<br/>interactions)]
    K -->|replayed by| PV
    subgraph Provider["Provider (API) tests"]
        PV[Verifier] -->|contract requests| P[Real provider]
        P -->|responses| PV
        PV --> R{Every response satisfies<br/>what the consumer relies on?}
    end

Two properties make this different from sharing a fixture file. The contract describes what the consumer relies on, not a full example response, so the provider can add fields, reorder them, and change values freely; only changes that would break the consumer fail. And each side runs the contract in its own test suite, against its own code, so a breaking change fails the build of the side that made it, before it ships.

The client

The consumer is a client for three endpoints: a search, a book detail, and a reservation, which sends a JSON body:

import Foundation

public struct BookSummary: Decodable, Equatable, Sendable {
    public let id: String
    public let title: String
    public let authorName: String
}

public struct BookDetail: Decodable, Equatable, Sendable {
    public let id: String
    public let title: String
    public let authorName: String
    public let pages: Int
    public let subjects: [String]
}

public struct Reservation: Decodable, Equatable, Sendable {
    public let id: String
    public let bookID: String
    public let readyBy: String
}

public enum CatalogError: Error, Equatable { case status(Int), decoding(String) }

public struct CatalogAPI: Sendable {
    let baseURL: URL
    let session: URLSession
    public init(baseURL: URL, session: URLSession = .shared) { (self.baseURL, self.session) = (baseURL, session) }

    public func search(_ text: String) async throws -> [BookSummary] {
        var components = URLComponents(url: baseURL.appending(path: "books"), resolvingAgainstBaseURL: false)!
        components.queryItems = [URLQueryItem(name: "q", value: text)]
        return try await send(URLRequest(url: components.url!))
    }

    public func book(_ id: String) async throws -> BookDetail {
        try await send(URLRequest(url: baseURL.appending(components: "books", id)))
    }

    public func reserve(_ id: String, pickupBranch: String) async throws -> Reservation {
        var request = URLRequest(url: baseURL.appending(components: "books", id, "reservations"))
        request.httpMethod = "POST"
        request.setValue("application/json", forHTTPHeaderField: "Content-Type")
        request.httpBody = try JSONEncoder().encode(["pickupBranch": pickupBranch])
        return try await send(request)
    }

    private func send<Value: Decodable>(_ request: URLRequest) async throws -> Value {
        var request = request
        request.setValue("application/json", forHTTPHeaderField: "Accept")
        let (data, response) = try await session.data(for: request)
        let status = (response as? HTTPURLResponse)?.statusCode ?? 0
        guard (200..<300).contains(status) else { throw CatalogError.status(status) }
        do { return try JSONDecoder().decode(Value.self, from: data) }
        catch { throw CatalogError.decoding("\(error)") }
    }
}

A contract format with type matching

A contract must say “this field is a string” without saying which string, or every changed value would break it. The format below describes JSON by shape: strings, integers, booleans, arrays of a shape, and objects with required fields. An example value travels alongside each shape, because the consumer’s tests need concrete data to serve:

import Foundation

indirect enum Shape: Codable, Equatable, Sendable {
    case string
    case integer
    case boolean
    case array(Shape)
    case object([String: Shape])

    /// Every path where `value` does not have this shape. Extra object members are allowed.
    func mismatches(in value: Any?, at path: String = "$") -> [String] {
        switch (self, value) {
        case (.string, is String): return []
        case (.integer, let number as NSNumber) where CFGetTypeID(number) != CFBooleanGetTypeID()
                                                    && number.doubleValue == number.doubleValue.rounded():
            return []
        case (.boolean, let number as NSNumber) where CFGetTypeID(number) == CFBooleanGetTypeID(): return []
        case (.array(let element), let array as [Any]):
            return array.enumerated().flatMap { element.mismatches(in: $1, at: "\(path)[\($0)]") }
        case (.object(let fields), let object as [String: Any]):
            return fields.keys.sorted().flatMap { key in
                object[key].map { fields[key]!.mismatches(in: $0, at: "\(path).\(key)") } ?? ["\(path).\(key) is missing"]
            }
        default:
            return ["\(path) should be \(self.name), got \(Self.describe(value))"]
        }
    }

    private static func describe(_ value: Any?) -> String {
        switch value {
        case nil: "nothing"
        case is NSNull: "null"
        case is String: "a string"
        case let number as NSNumber: CFGetTypeID(number) == CFBooleanGetTypeID() ? "a boolean" : "a number \(number)"
        case is [Any]: "an array"
        case is [String: Any]: "an object"
        default: "\(type(of: value!))"
        }
    }

    private var name: String {
        switch self {
        case .string: "a string"
        case .integer: "an integer"
        case .boolean: "a boolean"
        case .array: "an array"
        case .object: "an object"
        }
    }
}

struct Interaction: Codable, Equatable, Sendable {
    struct Request: Codable, Equatable, Sendable {
        var method: String
        var path: String
        var query: [String: String] = [:]
        var headers: [String: String] = [:]
        var body: Shape?
    }
    struct Response: Codable, Equatable, Sendable {
        var status: Int
        var headers: [String: String] = ["Content-Type": "application/json"]
        var body: Shape
        var example: String  // served to the consumer; must itself match `body`
    }

    var description: String
    var request: Request
    var response: Response
}

struct Contract: Codable, Sendable {
    var consumer: String
    var provider: String
    var interactions: [Interaction]
}

Matching is deliberately one-directional, following the tolerant reader principle: a response may contain more than the contract asks for, but not less, and not different types. Integers are checked as numbers with no fractional part, and booleans separately, because JSONSerialization represents both as NSNumber, and a 1 must not satisfy a boolean field or the reverse.

The consumer’s contract for its three endpoints:

import Foundation

let summaryShape = Shape.object(["id": .string, "title": .string, "authorName": .string])

let catalogContract = Contract(consumer: "LibraryApp", provider: "CatalogAPI", interactions: [
    Interaction(
        description: "search for books by title",
        request: .init(method: "GET", path: "/books", query: ["q": "dune"], headers: ["Accept": "application/json"]),
        response: .init(status: 200, body: .array(summaryShape),
                        example: #"[{"id":"b-7","title":"Dune","authorName":"Frank Herbert"}]"#)),
    Interaction(
        description: "fetch a book's details",
        request: .init(method: "GET", path: "/books/b-7", headers: ["Accept": "application/json"]),
        response: .init(status: 200,
                        body: .object(["id": .string, "title": .string, "authorName": .string,
                                       "pages": .integer, "subjects": .array(.string)]),
                        example: #"{"id":"b-7","title":"Dune","authorName":"Frank Herbert","pages":412,"subjects":["Science fiction"]}"#)),
    Interaction(
        description: "reserve a book for pickup",
        request: .init(method: "POST", path: "/books/b-7/reservations",
                       headers: ["Content-Type": "application/json", "Accept": "application/json"],
                       body: .object(["pickupBranch": .string])),
        response: .init(status: 201, body: .object(["id": .string, "bookID": .string, "readyBy": .string]),
                        example: #"{"id":"r-1","bookID":"b-7","readyBy":"2026-10-20"}"#)),
])

The consumer side: a server that holds the client to the contract

The contract server is a LocalServer that answers each request with the example response of the matching interaction, and answers anything else with a 500 whose body says exactly why the request did not match. It also records which interactions were exercised, so a test can prove the whole contract was used. LocalServer.start takes its handler before it returns the server, so the state the handler needs lives in a separate Sendable object, the ledger, created first:

import Foundation
import Synchronization

final class ContractLedger: Sendable {
    let contract: Contract
    private let used = Mutex<Set<String>>([])
    private let rejected = Mutex<[String]>([])
    init(_ contract: Contract) { self.contract = contract }

    var exercised: Set<String> { used.withLock { $0 } }
    var mismatches: [String] { rejected.withLock { $0 } }

    func respond(to request: HTTPRequest) -> HTTPResponse {
        var reasons: [String] = []
        for interaction in contract.interactions {
            let problems = Self.problems(request, against: interaction.request)
            if problems.isEmpty {
                used.withLock { _ = $0.insert(interaction.description) }
                return HTTPResponse(status: interaction.response.status,
                                    headers: interaction.response.headers.map { ($0.key, $0.value) },
                                    body: [.bytes(Data(interaction.response.example.utf8))])
            }
            reasons.append("\(interaction.description): \(problems.joined(separator: "; "))")
        }
        let report = "No interaction matches \(request.method) \(request.target)\n" + reasons.joined(separator: "\n")
        rejected.withLock { $0.append(report) }
        return .text(report, status: 500)
    }

    static func problems(_ request: HTTPRequest, against expected: Interaction.Request) -> [String] {
        var problems: [String] = []
        if request.method != expected.method { problems.append("method \(request.method) ≠ \(expected.method)") }
        if request.path != expected.path { problems.append("path \(request.path) ≠ \(expected.path)") }
        for (name, value) in expected.query where request.query[name] != value {
            problems.append("query \(name)=\(request.query[name] ?? "nil") ≠ \(value)")
        }
        for (name, value) in expected.headers where request.header(name) != value {
            problems.append("header \(name): \(request.header(name) ?? "nil") ≠ \(value)")
        }
        if let shape = expected.body {
            let json = try? JSONSerialization.jsonObject(with: request.body, options: [.fragmentsAllowed])
            problems += shape.mismatches(in: json, at: "body")
        }
        return problems
    }
}

func startContractServer(_ contract: Contract) async throws -> (LocalServer, ContractLedger) {
    let ledger = ContractLedger(contract)
    let server = try await LocalServer.start { ledger.respond(to: $0) }
    return (server, ledger)
}

The consumer tests run the real client against the contract server. Each test is short, because the contract carries the data:

import Foundation
import Testing
@testable import Library

@Suite struct ConsumerContract {
    @Test func theClientHonorsEveryInteraction() async throws {
        let (server, ledger) = try await startContractServer(catalogContract)
        let api = CatalogAPI(baseURL: server.baseURL, session: URLSession(configuration: .ephemeral))

        let results = try await api.search("dune")
        #expect(results.first?.authorName == "Frank Herbert")
        let detail = try await api.book("b-7")
        #expect(detail.pages == 412)
        let reservation = try await api.reserve("b-7", pickupBranch: "Central")
        #expect(reservation.bookID == "b-7")

        #expect(ledger.mismatches.isEmpty)
        #expect(ledger.exercised == Set(catalogContract.interactions.map(\.description)))
    }

    @Test func examplesSatisfyTheirOwnShapes() throws {
        for interaction in catalogContract.interactions {
            let example = try JSONSerialization.jsonObject(with: Data(interaction.response.example.utf8))
            #expect(interaction.response.body.mismatches(in: example).isEmpty, "\(interaction.description)")
        }
    }

    @Test func aDriftingClientIsCaughtHere() async throws {
        let (server, ledger) = try await startContractServer(catalogContract)
        var request = URLRequest(url: server.baseURL.appending(path: "books/b-7/reservations"))
        request.httpMethod = "POST"
        request.setValue("application/json", forHTTPHeaderField: "Content-Type")
        request.setValue("application/json", forHTTPHeaderField: "Accept")
        request.httpBody = Data(#"{"branch":"Central"}"#.utf8)   // a refactor renamed the field
        let (_, response) = try await URLSession.shared.data(for: request)
        #expect((response as? HTTPURLResponse)?.statusCode == 500)
        #expect(ledger.mismatches.first?.contains("body.pickupBranch is missing") == true)
    }

    @Test func publishTheContract() throws {
        let encoder = JSONEncoder()
        encoder.outputFormatting = [.prettyPrinted, .sortedKeys]
        let file = FileManager.default.temporaryDirectory.appending(path: "LibraryApp-CatalogAPI.json")
        try encoder.encode(catalogContract).write(to: file)
        let reloaded = try JSONDecoder().decode(Contract.self, from: Data(contentsOf: file))
        #expect(reloaded.interactions == catalogContract.interactions)
    }
}

The third test is the consumer half of the contract’s value. A refactor that renames pickupBranch in the request body would pass every stubbed unit test, because stubs answer whatever they are sent. Against the contract server it fails with a message that names the field. The fourth test writes the contract to a file, which in a real project is the artifact the client’s CI publishes for the provider’s CI to verify, often through a contract broker.

The provider side: replaying the contract

The provider check sends each interaction’s request to a real server and checks the status, the content type, and the body’s shape. Here the “real” providers are three versions of the catalog API, each on its own LocalServer:

import Foundation

enum ProviderVersion: String, CaseIterable, Sendable {
    case v1          // the version the contract was written against
    case v2Additive  // adds fields and an optional header; reorders nothing the client reads
    case v3Breaking  // renames authorName to author, and returns pages as a string

    func handle(_ request: HTTPRequest) -> HTTPResponse {
        let author = self == .v3Breaking ? #""author":"Frank Herbert""# : #""authorName":"Frank Herbert""#
        let extra = self == .v2Additive ? #","coverURL":"https://covers.example/b-7.jpg","rating":4.6"# : ""
        let pages = self == .v3Breaking ? #""412""# : "412"
        switch (request.method, request.path) {
        case ("GET", "/books"):
            return .json(#"[{"id":"b-7","title":"Dune",\#(author)\#(extra)},{"id":"b-8","title":"Dune Messiah",\#(author)}]"#)
        case ("GET", "/books/b-7"):
            return .json(#"{"id":"b-7","title":"Dune",\#(author),"pages":\#(pages),"subjects":["Science fiction","Classics"]\#(extra)}"#,
                         headers: self == .v2Additive ? [("X-Catalog-Revision", "2")] : [])
        case ("POST", "/books/b-7/reservations"):
            return .json(#"{"id":"r-\#(Int.random(in: 100...999))","bookID":"b-7","readyBy":"2026-10-21"\#(extra)}"#, status: 201)
        default:
            return .text("not found", status: 404)
        }
    }
}

struct VerificationFailure: CustomStringConvertible {
    let interaction: String
    let problems: [String]
    var description: String { "\(interaction): \(problems.joined(separator: "; "))" }
}

func verify(_ contract: Contract, against baseURL: URL) async throws -> [VerificationFailure] {
    var failures: [VerificationFailure] = []
    for interaction in contract.interactions {
        var components = URLComponents(url: baseURL.appending(path: String(interaction.request.path.dropFirst())),
                                       resolvingAgainstBaseURL: false)!
        if !interaction.request.query.isEmpty {
            components.queryItems = interaction.request.query.map { URLQueryItem(name: $0.key, value: $0.value) }
        }
        var request = URLRequest(url: components.url!)
        request.httpMethod = interaction.request.method
        interaction.request.headers.forEach { request.setValue($0.value, forHTTPHeaderField: $0.key) }
        if interaction.request.body != nil {
            request.httpBody = Data(#"{"pickupBranch":"Central"}"#.utf8)  // in a real broker, an example travels with the request too
        }
        let (data, response) = try await URLSession(configuration: .ephemeral).data(for: request)
        let http = response as! HTTPURLResponse
        var problems: [String] = []
        if http.statusCode != interaction.response.status {
            problems.append("status \(http.statusCode) ≠ \(interaction.response.status)")
        }
        if let type = interaction.response.headers["Content-Type"], http.mimeType != type {
            problems.append("Content-Type \(http.mimeType ?? "nil") ≠ \(type)")
        }
        let json = try? JSONSerialization.jsonObject(with: data, options: [.fragmentsAllowed])
        problems += interaction.response.body.mismatches(in: json)
        if !problems.isEmpty { failures.append(VerificationFailure(interaction: interaction.description, problems: problems)) }
    }
    return failures
}

import Foundation
import Testing

@Suite struct ProviderVerification {
    @Test(arguments: ProviderVersion.allCases)
    func verifyProvider(_ version: ProviderVersion) async throws {
        let provider = try await LocalServer.start { version.handle($0) }
        let failures = try await verify(catalogContract, against: provider.baseURL)
        switch version {
        case .v1, .v2Additive:
            #expect(failures.isEmpty, "\(failures)")
        case .v3Breaking:
            #expect(failures.map(\.interaction) == ["search for books by title", "fetch a book's details"])
            let detail = failures.first { $0.interaction == "fetch a book's details" }
            #expect(detail?.problems == ["$.authorName is missing", "$.pages should be an integer, got a string"])
        }
    }
}
Provider change Contract result Would a client-side stub test notice?
v2: adds coverURL, rating, a response header, more subjects Passes No, and it does not need to
v3: renames authorName to author Fails: $.authorName is missing, and $[0].authorName / $[1].authorName for the search No: stubs still send authorName
v3: sends pages as "412" Fails: $.pages should be an integer No

The breaking version’s failures name the interaction, the JSON path, and the reason, which is exactly the review comment the provider’s team needs: “the app reads authorName and pages as an integer.” The additive version passed, because every field the app relies on is still there with the same type, and the extra ones are ignored, as the app’s Decodable types already ignore them.

Which changes are safe

The rules the verifier enforces generalize into the compatibility rules for JSON APIs that every client and server team should share:

Change on the provider Safe for existing clients?
Add a response field Yes, if clients ignore unknown fields
Add an optional request field or query parameter Yes
Add a new enum value in a response Only if clients have an unknown case (see Decoding JSON with Codable)
Remove or rename a response field the client reads No
Change a field’s type, including number to string No
Make an optional request field required No
Change status codes for existing outcomes No
Tighten validation of request values Usually no

Two of the “yes” rows depend on the client: they are safe only for clients written as tolerant readers. The contract encodes that assumption by allowing extra members, so a client that broke on unknown fields would be breaking its own contract.

Where contracts fit

Contracts complement the other kinds of test in this series rather than replacing any of them:

  • Stubbed unit tests (URLProtocol fixtures, failure matrices) check the client’s handling of every response, including ones a contract does not describe, such as a 503.
  • Contract tests check that the client’s requests and the provider’s responses agree on the parts that matter. They are the only fast test that fails when the other side changes.
  • End-to-end tests against a real staging environment check deployment, authentication, and data, slowly and with more flakiness, and should be few.

A contract is only as good as the interactions in it. It describes what the app relies on today, so it must be updated when the app starts relying on something new, which is easiest when the consumer tests above are the only place fixtures for these endpoints come from.

Summary

  • A consumer-driven contract records the requests a client sends and the minimum it relies on in each response, as data both sides test against.
  • Describe responses by shape, not by value, and allow extra fields: the tolerant-reader rule that lets providers evolve.
  • On the consumer side, serve the contract’s examples from a controlled server that rejects any request that does not match, with a message that names the mismatch, and check that every interaction was exercised.
  • On the provider side, replay each interaction’s request against the real service and check status, content type, and body shape.
  • Measured: an additive provider change passed; renaming authorName and sending pages as a string failed with the exact JSON paths, changes no stubbed client test would have caught.
  • Share the compatibility rules: adding fields is safe for tolerant readers; removing, renaming, retyping, and tightening are not.

Exercise

Add an optional(Shape) case to Shape, use it for a new subtitle field in the book detail interaction, and check that a provider that omits subtitle passes and one that sends "subtitle": 3 fails. Then add request-body examples to Interaction.Request so the verifier stops hard-coding the reservation body, and add a provider version that requires a new pickupDate field in the reservation request, which the verifier should report as a 400 from the provider for the reservation interaction.

Further reading

  • The Pact documentation, on consumer-driven contracts and brokers.
  • Martin Fowler, Contract Test and Tolerant Reader.
  • Ian Robinson, Consumer-Driven Contracts: A Service Evolution Pattern.

Previous: Testing Status Codes, Invalid Payloads, and Transport Errors. Next: Reading URLSessionTaskMetrics.
