entry.summary: Unit tests with stubbed responses prove that a client handles the responses its authors wrote down. They cannot prove that the server sends those responses. The gap between the two is where integration failures live: the server renames authorName to author, starts returning prices as strings, or begins to require a header the app never sends, and every client test still passes because every fixture still says what it always said. A contract closes that gap by making the fixtures themselves the thing both sides test against. The client’s tests record what it sends and what it relies on in the responses, as data. The server’s tests replay the same requests and check that the real responses still satisfy what the client relies on. This article builds that loop: a small contract format with type-based matching, a LocalServer that serves the contract to the client and rejects requests that do not match it, and a provider check that runs the contract against three versions of a server, one that is compatible, one that adds a field, and one that breaks the client in a way no client-side test could catch.

entry.title: Testing Status Codes, Invalid Payloads, and Transport Errors

link.title: Testing Status Codes, Invalid Payloads, and Transport Errors

entry.content:
The happy path of a networking client gets tested by accident: every developer runs it a hundred times a day. The failure paths get tested by users. A 429 with Retry-After arrives for the first time in production, a CDN returns an HTML error page with status 200, a server deploy starts sending "price": null, and the code that handles each case has never run.

Failure handling is also the part of a client that is easiest to test exhaustively, because every failure is a small, well-defined input: a status code, a body, an error code. This article turns the error model from Separating Transport Errors from Application Failures into a test suite with Swift Testing’s parameterized tests: a matrix of status codes, a corpus of invalid payloads, a table of transport errors, and a mutation fuzzer that feeds a thousand corrupted variants of a valid response to the decoder and checks that the client never crashes and never returns invalid data.

The examples use Swift 6 language mode and Swift Testing, and were run with swift test using the Swift 6.4 toolchain from Xcode 27.1 on macOS 26. Each block is labeled with the file it belongs to in a Swift package with a Library target and a LibraryTests test target. The tests use the parallel-safe URLProtocol fixture from Isolating HTTP Fixtures with URLProtocol; copy its StubProtocol.swift into the test target.

The client and its error model

The client fetches a book’s price and availability. Its error type is the contract under test: each case corresponds to something the UI does differently, and each carries whether retrying can help:

import Foundation

public struct Offer: Decodable, Equatable, Sendable {
    public let bookID: String
    public let priceCents: Int
    public let currency: String
    public let inStock: Bool

    public init(bookID: String, priceCents: Int, currency: String, inStock: Bool) {
        (self.bookID, self.priceCents, self.currency, self.inStock) = (bookID, priceCents, currency, inStock)
    }
}

public enum OfferError: Error, Equatable, Sendable {
    case cancelled
    case offline
    case unreachable
    case timedOut
    case insecure
    case transport(URLError.Code)
    case notFound
    case unauthorized
    case rateLimited(retryAfter: Int?)
    case rejected(status: Int, problemType: String?)
    case server(status: Int)
    case unexpectedStatus(Int)
    case unexpectedContentType(String?)
    case invalidPayload(String)

    public var isRetryable: Bool {
        switch self {
        case .offline, .unreachable, .timedOut, .transport, .rateLimited: true
        case .server(let status): [502, 503, 504].contains(status)
        default: false
        }
    }
}

public struct PriceClient: Sendable {
    let session: URLSession
    let baseURL: URL
    public init(session: URLSession, baseURL: URL) { (self.session, self.baseURL) = (session, baseURL) }

    public func offer(for bookID: String) async throws(OfferError) -> Offer {
        let data: Data
        let response: URLResponse
        do {
            (data, response) = try await session.data(from: baseURL.appending(components: "offers", bookID))
        } catch let error as URLError {
            throw Self.classify(error)
        } catch {
            throw .transport(.unknown)
        }
        guard let http = response as? HTTPURLResponse else { throw .unexpectedStatus(0) }
        try Self.check(http, data: data)
        guard http.mimeType == "application/json" else { throw .unexpectedContentType(http.mimeType) }
        let offer: Offer
        do { offer = try JSONDecoder().decode(Offer.self, from: data) }
        catch { throw .invalidPayload("undecodable") }
        try Self.validate(offer, requested: bookID)
        return offer
    }

    static func classify(_ error: URLError) -> OfferError {
        switch error.code {
        case .cancelled: .cancelled
        case .notConnectedToInternet, .dataNotAllowed, .internationalRoamingOff: .offline
        case .cannotFindHost, .cannotConnectToHost, .dnsLookupFailed: .unreachable
        case .timedOut: .timedOut
        case .secureConnectionFailed, .serverCertificateUntrusted, .serverCertificateHasBadDate,
             .serverCertificateHasUnknownRoot, .serverCertificateNotYetValid, .appTransportSecurityRequiresSecureConnection: .insecure
        default: .transport(error.code)
        }
    }

    static func check(_ http: HTTPURLResponse, data: Data) throws(OfferError) {
        switch http.statusCode {
        case 200..<300: return
        case 401: throw .unauthorized
        case 404, 410: throw .notFound
        case 429: throw .rateLimited(retryAfter: http.value(forHTTPHeaderField: "Retry-After").flatMap(Int.init))
        case 400..<500:
            let type = http.mimeType == "application/problem+json"
                ? (try? JSONDecoder().decode([String: String].self, from: data))?["type"] : nil
            throw .rejected(status: http.statusCode, problemType: type)
        case 500..<600: throw .server(status: http.statusCode)
        default: throw .unexpectedStatus(http.statusCode)
        }
    }

    static func validate(_ offer: Offer, requested bookID: String) throws(OfferError) {
        guard offer.bookID == bookID else { throw .invalidPayload("offer for another book") }
        guard (0...10_000_000).contains(offer.priceCents) else { throw .invalidPayload("price out of range") }
        guard offer.currency.count == 3, offer.currency.allSatisfy({ $0.isASCII && $0.isUppercase }) else {
            throw .invalidPayload("bad currency")
        }
    }
}

A matrix of status codes

Status handling is a function from (status, headers, body) to an outcome, so it is tested as a table. Each row is one argument to a parameterized test, and Swift Testing reports every row as its own test case, so a failure names the row:

import Foundation
import Testing
@testable import Library

let catalog = URL(string: "https://api.library.example/v1")!
let validOffer = #"{"bookID":"b-7","priceCents":1299,"currency":"EUR","inStock":true}"#

struct StatusCase: Sendable, CustomTestStringConvertible {
    let status: Int
    var headers: [String: String] = ["Content-Type": "application/json"]
    var body = "{}"
    let expected: Result<Offer, OfferError>
    var testDescription: String { "\(status) \(headers["Content-Type"] ?? "-")" }
}

let statusCases: [StatusCase] = [
    StatusCase(status: 200, body: validOffer, expected: .success(Offer(bookID: "b-7", priceCents: 1299, currency: "EUR", inStock: true))),
    StatusCase(status: 203, body: validOffer, expected: .success(Offer(bookID: "b-7", priceCents: 1299, currency: "EUR", inStock: true))),
    StatusCase(status: 204, headers: [:], body: "", expected: .failure(.unexpectedContentType("text/plain"))),
    StatusCase(status: 304, expected: .failure(.unexpectedStatus(304))),
    StatusCase(status: 400, expected: .failure(.rejected(status: 400, problemType: nil))),
    StatusCase(status: 401, expected: .failure(.unauthorized)),
    StatusCase(status: 403, headers: ["Content-Type": "application/problem+json"],
               body: #"{"type":"https://library.example/problems/region-locked","title":"Not sold here"}"#,
               expected: .failure(.rejected(status: 403, problemType: "https://library.example/problems/region-locked"))),
    StatusCase(status: 404, expected: .failure(.notFound)),
    StatusCase(status: 410, expected: .failure(.notFound)),
    StatusCase(status: 422, expected: .failure(.rejected(status: 422, problemType: nil))),
    StatusCase(status: 429, headers: ["Retry-After": "30"], expected: .failure(.rateLimited(retryAfter: 30))),
    StatusCase(status: 429, headers: ["Retry-After": "Wed, 21 Oct 2026 07:28:00 GMT"], expected: .failure(.rateLimited(retryAfter: nil))),
    StatusCase(status: 499, expected: .failure(.rejected(status: 499, problemType: nil))),
    StatusCase(status: 500, expected: .failure(.server(status: 500))),
    StatusCase(status: 502, headers: ["Content-Type": "text/html"], body: "<h1>Bad Gateway</h1>", expected: .failure(.server(status: 502))),
    StatusCase(status: 503, expected: .failure(.server(status: 503))),
    StatusCase(status: 504, expected: .failure(.server(status: 504))),
    StatusCase(status: 599, expected: .failure(.server(status: 599))),
    StatusCase(status: 200, headers: ["Content-Type": "text/html"], body: "<html>Sign in to Wi-Fi</html>",
               expected: .failure(.unexpectedContentType("text/html"))),
]

@Suite struct StatusMatrix {
    @Test(arguments: statusCases)
    func mapsStatus(_ row: StatusCase) async {
        let fixture = Fixture { _ in StubResponse(status: row.status, headers: row.headers, body: Data(row.body.utf8)) }
        let client = PriceClient(session: fixture.session(), baseURL: catalog)
        let outcome: Result<Offer, OfferError>
        do { outcome = .success(try await client.offer(for: "b-7")) } catch { outcome = .failure(error) }
        #expect(outcome == row.expected)
    }

    @Test func retryabilityFollowsTheContract() {
        #expect(OfferError.server(status: 503).isRetryable)
        #expect(!OfferError.server(status: 500).isRetryable)
        #expect(OfferError.rateLimited(retryAfter: 30).isRetryable)
        #expect(!OfferError.rejected(status: 400, problemType: nil).isRetryable)
        #expect(!OfferError.cancelled.isRetryable && !OfferError.insecure.isRetryable)
    }
}

A few rows deserve a note, because they record decisions rather than obvious facts:

  • 204 with no body and no Content-Type is reported as unexpectedContentType("text/plain"), because a GET for an offer must return one. That text/plain is the system’s default for a missing type, as the first article measured. An endpoint where 204 is valid needs its own path through the client, not a special case here.
  • 304 cannot occur on a session with a cache, which turns it into the cached 200, as the caching article showed; without a cache it is a protocol violation for this request.
  • Retry-After as an HTTP date is parsed as nil by this client, which is a known limitation recorded as a test. The retryAfter function in the retry article handles dates; changing the client means changing this row, which is the point of writing it down.
  • 499 and 599 are unregistered codes. They fall into their class, as RFC 9110 requires.

A corpus of invalid payloads

Status 200 with a body the client cannot use is the failure most likely to crash an app, because code tends to trust a successful response. The corpus below collects the shapes of broken payload that real servers produce, each with the outcome the client must report:

import Foundation
import Testing
@testable import Library

struct PayloadCase: Sendable, CustomTestStringConvertible {
    let name: String
    let body: Data
    let expected: Result<Offer, OfferError>
    var testDescription: String { name }

    init(_ name: String, _ body: String, _ expected: Result<Offer, OfferError>) {
        self.init(name, Data(body.utf8), expected)
    }
    init(_ name: String, _ body: Data, _ expected: Result<Offer, OfferError>) {
        (self.name, self.body, self.expected) = (name, body, expected)
    }
}

let dune = Offer(bookID: "b-7", priceCents: 1299, currency: "EUR", inStock: true)
let undecodable = Result<Offer, OfferError>.failure(.invalidPayload("undecodable"))

let payloadCases: [PayloadCase] = [
    PayloadCase("valid", validOffer, .success(dune)),
    PayloadCase("extra fields are ignored", #"{"bookID":"b-7","priceCents":1299,"currency":"EUR","inStock":true,"promo":{"x":1}}"#, .success(dune)),
    PayloadCase("empty body", "", undecodable),
    PayloadCase("truncated", String(validOffer.dropLast(9)), undecodable),
    PayloadCase("not JSON", "OK", undecodable),
    PayloadCase("array instead of object", "[\(validOffer)]", undecodable),
    PayloadCase("null required field", #"{"bookID":"b-7","priceCents":null,"currency":"EUR","inStock":true}"#, undecodable),
    PayloadCase("missing required field", #"{"bookID":"b-7","currency":"EUR","inStock":true}"#, undecodable),
    PayloadCase("number as string", #"{"bookID":"b-7","priceCents":"1299","currency":"EUR","inStock":true}"#, undecodable),
    PayloadCase("fractional cents", #"{"bookID":"b-7","priceCents":12.99,"currency":"EUR","inStock":true}"#, undecodable),
    PayloadCase("overflowing number", #"{"bookID":"b-7","priceCents":99999999999999999999,"currency":"EUR","inStock":true}"#, undecodable),
    PayloadCase("bool as number", #"{"bookID":"b-7","priceCents":1299,"currency":"EUR","inStock":1}"#, undecodable),
    PayloadCase("byte order mark", "\u{FEFF}" + validOffer, .success(dune)),
    PayloadCase("invalid UTF-8", Data([0x7B, 0x22, 0xFF, 0xFE, 0x22, 0x7D]), undecodable),
    PayloadCase("negative price", #"{"bookID":"b-7","priceCents":-1,"currency":"EUR","inStock":true}"#,
                .failure(.invalidPayload("price out of range"))),
    PayloadCase("lowercase currency", #"{"bookID":"b-7","priceCents":1299,"currency":"eur","inStock":true}"#,
                .failure(.invalidPayload("bad currency"))),
    PayloadCase("another book's offer", #"{"bookID":"b-8","priceCents":1299,"currency":"EUR","inStock":true}"#,
                .failure(.invalidPayload("offer for another book"))),
    PayloadCase("deeply nested", String(repeating: "[", count: 10_000) + String(repeating: "]", count: 10_000), undecodable),
]

@Suite struct PayloadCorpus {
    @Test(arguments: payloadCases)
    func handlesPayload(_ row: PayloadCase) async {
        let fixture = Fixture { _ in StubResponse(body: row.body) }
        let client = PriceClient(session: fixture.session(), baseURL: catalog)
        let outcome: Result<Offer, OfferError>
        do { outcome = .success(try await client.offer(for: "b-7")) } catch { outcome = .failure(error) }
        #expect(outcome == row.expected)
    }
}

Every row is a real failure mode. Several are covered in depth in Decoding JSON with Codable, including the byte order mark the parser accepts and the overflowing number reported as corrupted data. The last three rows decode successfully and are rejected by validation, which is the layer Validating Decoded Data adds: a response for the wrong book is valid JSON and a dangerous payload. The deeply nested row checks that 10,000 levels of nesting produce an error rather than a stack overflow, which is the kind of input a fuzzer finds and a person rarely thinks to write.

A table of transport errors

Transport failures come from the session, so the fixture produces them with didFailWithError. A table maps each URLError.Code to the case the UI needs:

import Foundation
import Testing
@testable import Library

let transportCases: [(URLError.Code, OfferError)] = [
    (.notConnectedToInternet, .offline),
    (.dataNotAllowed, .offline),
    (.cannotFindHost, .unreachable),
    (.cannotConnectToHost, .unreachable),
    (.timedOut, .timedOut),
    (.networkConnectionLost, .transport(.networkConnectionLost)),
    (.secureConnectionFailed, .insecure),
    (.serverCertificateUntrusted, .insecure),
    (.appTransportSecurityRequiresSecureConnection, .insecure),
    (.badServerResponse, .transport(.badServerResponse)),
    (.cannotParseResponse, .transport(.cannotParseResponse)),
    (.cancelled, .cancelled),
]

@Suite struct TransportTable {
    @Test(arguments: transportCases)
    func mapsTransportError(_ code: URLError.Code, _ expected: OfferError) async {
        let fixture = Fixture { _ in .failure(code) }
        let client = PriceClient(session: fixture.session(), baseURL: catalog)
        await #expect(throws: expected) { try await client.offer(for: "b-7") }
    }

    @Test func everyCaseIsCoveredOnce() {
        let codes = transportCases.map(\.0.rawValue)
        #expect(Set(codes).count == codes.count)
    }
}

The fixture fails the request with the given error, and URLSession delivers it to the client unchanged, which is exactly what makes a stub the right tool for this table: producing serverCertificateUntrusted or notConnectedToInternet for real takes a misconfigured server or an airplane. The table also guards the classification against accidental change. Moving networkConnectionLost into .offline, a tempting simplification, fails one named row, and the review that follows can discuss whether a lost connection really means the device is offline, which the transport error article argued it does not.

Exhaustive where it is cheap

The tables above choose their rows. When inputs combine, choosing gets harder: statuses times content types times bodies is a product, and the interesting failures are often at combinations nobody listed. Here the product is small enough to run whole. With \(s\) statuses, \(t\) content types, and \(b\) bodies, the full matrix has:

\[N = s \cdot t \cdot b = 19 \times 4 \times 6 = 456 \text{ cases}\]

Stubbed requests take well under a millisecond each, and the whole matrix ran in about a tenth of a second, so the suite can simply check an invariant over all of them instead of an expected value for each: the client either returns a valid offer, which only happens for a 2xx JSON response with a valid body, or throws, and it never crashes:

import Foundation
import Testing
@testable import Library

@Suite struct ExhaustiveMatrix {
    static let statuses = [200, 201, 202, 203, 204, 206, 301, 304, 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 422, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504]
    static let contentTypes = ["application/json", "application/problem+json", "text/html", "application/json; charset=utf-8"]
    static let bodies = [validOffer, "", "{}", "null", "<html>", #"{"type":"x"}"#]

    @Test func everyCombinationIsHandled() async {
        var successes = 0
        for status in Self.statuses {
            for type in Self.contentTypes {
                for body in Self.bodies {
                    let fixture = Fixture { _ in StubResponse(status: status, headers: ["Content-Type": type], body: Data(body.utf8)) }
                    let client = PriceClient(session: fixture.session(), baseURL: catalog)
                    do {
                        let offer = try await client.offer(for: "b-7")
                        successes += 1
                        #expect((200..<300).contains(status) && body == validOffer && type.hasPrefix("application/json"))
                        #expect(offer == dune)
                    } catch {
                        // Any OfferError is acceptable here; the invariant is that nothing else happens.
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        #expect(successes == 12)  // six 2xx statuses × two JSON content types, including 204: see below
    }
}

The final count is a cross-check on the invariant, and it caught something on its first run. The expectation had been ten successes: five 2xx statuses that carry a body, times two JSON content types, on the reasoning that a 204 No Content response has no body. The run produced twelve. The stub delivered the valid offer as the body of a 204, URLSession passed it through, and the client accepted it. Over a real connection that cannot happen, because HTTP/1.1 framing ends a 204 response at its headers and the bytes would never be read as its body. It is one more entry for the fidelity table in the URLProtocol article: a stub can produce responses no server can, so an invariant that fails under a stub may describe an impossible case rather than a bug. Here the count was updated, with a comment, rather than adding a 204 check to production code for an input that cannot occur.

When the product is too large to run whole, pairwise testing, which covers every pair of values across parameters with far fewer cases, is the standard compromise.

Mutation fuzzing the decoder

The corpus contains the failures someone thought of. A mutation fuzzer finds the ones nobody did: it takes a valid payload, applies random small changes such as flipping a byte, deleting a range, duplicating a range, or inserting a JSON-significant character, and feeds each variant to the client. The property is the same as in the matrix: a valid offer or an OfferError, never a crash, and never an offer that fails validation.

The generator is seeded, so a failure is reproducible from the seed printed in its message. SplitMix64 is a tiny, well-known generator suitable for tests:

import Foundation
import Testing
@testable import Library

struct SplitMix64: RandomNumberGenerator {
    var state: UInt64
    mutating func next() -> UInt64 {
        state &+= 0x9E37_79B9_7F4A_7C15
        var z = state
        z = (z ^ (z >> 30)) &* 0xBF58_476D_1CE4_E5B9
        z = (z ^ (z >> 27)) &* 0x94D0_49BB_1331_11EB
        return z ^ (z >> 31)
    }
}

func mutate(_ input: [UInt8], using random: inout SplitMix64) -> [UInt8] {
    var bytes = input
    for _ in 0..<Int.random(in: 1...4, using: &random) {
        guard !bytes.isEmpty else { break }
        let index = Int.random(in: 0..<bytes.count, using: &random)
        switch Int.random(in: 0..<5, using: &random) {
        case 0: bytes[index] ^= UInt8(1 << Int.random(in: 0..<8, using: &random))       // flip a bit
        case 1: bytes.removeSubrange(index..<min(bytes.count, index + Int.random(in: 1...8, using: &random)))
        case 2: bytes.insert(contentsOf: bytes[index..<min(bytes.count, index + 6)], at: index)   // duplicate
        case 3: bytes.insert(Array("{}[]\",:-0e.\\".utf8).randomElement(using: &random)!, at: index)
        default: bytes[index] = UInt8.random(in: 0...255, using: &random)                  // replace
        }
    }
    return bytes
}

@Suite struct DecoderFuzzing {
    @Test(arguments: [UInt64(1), 2, 3, 4])
    func mutatedOffersNeverEscapeTheErrorModel(seed: UInt64) async {
        var random = SplitMix64(state: seed)
        let original = Array(validOffer.utf8)
        var accepted = 0
        for iteration in 0..<250 {
            let body = Data(mutate(original, using: &random))
            let fixture = Fixture { _ in StubResponse(body: body) }
            let client = PriceClient(session: fixture.session(), baseURL: catalog)
            do {
                let offer = try await client.offer(for: "b-7")
                accepted += 1
                // Anything accepted must satisfy the validation rules.
                #expect(offer.bookID == "b-7" && (0...10_000_000).contains(offer.priceCents) && offer.currency.count == 3,
                        "seed \(seed) iteration \(iteration): \(String(decoding: body, as: UTF8.self))")
            } catch {
                // Every rejection is an OfferError by construction of typed throws.
            }
        }
        print("seed \(seed): \(accepted) of 250 mutants accepted")
    }
}

Four seeds of 250 mutants each, a thousand corrupted payloads, ran in about a tenth of a second, in parallel with the other suites. In the measured run, between zero and two mutants per seed were still accepted, changes such as a digit of the price that produce a different but valid offer, and every accepted one satisfied the validation rules. Typed throws make the other half of the property free: offer(for:) is declared throws(OfferError), so the compiler guarantees no other error type escapes, and the fuzzer only has to look for crashes and invalid acceptances.

Fuzzing at this scale is a smoke test, not a proof. Its value is in what it finds without being told where to look; when it finds something, the mutant goes into the payload corpus as a named row, and the fuzzer keeps looking.

Summary

  • Test failure handling as tables: one parameterized test per dimension, with each row a named test case and an expected outcome.
  • The status matrix records decisions, such as how 204, 304, unregistered codes, and date-valued Retry-After are treated, so that changing one is a visible change to a row.
  • The payload corpus covers empty, truncated, mistyped, null, overflowing, BOM-prefixed, invalid UTF-8, deeply nested, and semantically wrong bodies; the last group is caught by validation, not decoding.
  • A stub produces transport errors that are hard to produce for real; a table maps every URLError.Code the client distinguishes.
  • When the product of inputs is small, run it all and check an invariant; here 456 combinations in about a tenth of a second. The invariant’s count exposed a stub-only response, a 204 with a body.
  • A seeded mutation fuzzer feeds a thousand corrupted payloads to the client and checks that it never crashes or accepts invalid data; typed throws guarantee the error type.

Exercise

Add a currencyMinorUnits rule to validation (JPY has none, so priceCents must be a whole yen amount) and extend the payload corpus with rows that exercise it. Then run the fuzzer with a JPY offer as the seed payload and check whether any mutant slips past the new rule. Finally, add a test that records, using Swift Testing’s withKnownIssue, the current behavior for an HTTP-date Retry-After, so that the day someone implements date parsing the known issue starts failing and reminds them to update the row.

Further reading

  • Go further with Swift Testing, WWDC24, on parameterized tests and known issues.
  • Apple’s Swift Testing documentation.
  • Andreas Zeller et al., The Fuzzing Book, on mutation-based fuzzing.

Previous: Isolating HTTP Fixtures with URLProtocol. Next: Verifying Contracts Against a Controlled Server.

Return to the Networking roadmap.
entry.summary: The happy path of a networking client gets tested by accident: every developer runs it a hundred times a day. The failure paths get tested by users. A 429 with Retry-After arrives for the first time in production, a CDN returns an HTML error page with status 200, a server deploy starts sending "price": null, and the code that handles each case has never run. Failure handling is also the part of a client that is easiest to test exhaustively, because every failure is a small, well-defined input: a status code, a body, an error code. This article turns the error model from Separating Transport Errors from Application Failures into a test suite with Swift Testing’s parameterized tests: a matrix of status codes, a corpus of invalid payloads, a table of transport errors, and a mutation fuzzer that feeds a thousand corrupted variants of a valid response to the decoder and checks that the client never crashes and never returns invalid data.

entry.title: Isolating HTTP Fixtures with URLProtocol
entry.content:
A test that talks to a real server is slow, depends on the network and the server’s data, and cannot easily produce the responses that matter most: the 503, the truncated body, the timeout. The standard way to give URLSession canned responses without changing the code under test is URLProtocol, the extension point the URL Loading System uses to decide how to load a request. A test registers a protocol class on a session’s configuration, and every request through that session is answered by the test’s own code.

It is an old API with sharp edges, and two of them cut most test suites: a shared static handler that races once tests run in parallel, which Swift Testing does by default, and request bodies that are not where the code expects them. This article builds a fixture protocol that is safe under parallel tests and Swift 6 strict concurrency, uses it to test a small client’s success, failure, redirect, timeout, and cancellation paths, and then measures what a URLProtocol stub does not reproduce from the real HTTP stack, so the tests’ claims stay honest.

The examples use Swift 6 language mode and Swift Testing, and were run with swift test using the Swift 6.4 toolchain from Xcode 27.1 on macOS 26. Each block is labeled with the file it belongs to in a Swift package with a Library target and a LibraryTests test target.

How URLProtocol fits in

When a session starts a task, it asks each class in its configuration’s protocolClasses, in order, whether it can handle the request. The first class whose canInit(with:) returns true is instantiated for the request, and its startLoading() produces the response by calling methods on its client:

sequenceDiagram
    accTitle: How URLSession hands a request to a URLProtocol subclass
    participant Code as Code under test
    participant Session as URLSession
    participant Stub as StubProtocol
    Code->>Session: data(for: request)
    Session->>Stub: canInit(with: request)? → true
    Session->>Stub: init(request:cachedResponse:client:), startLoading()
    Stub-->>Session: client.urlProtocol(_, didReceive: response, cacheStoragePolicy:)
    Stub-->>Session: client.urlProtocol(_, didLoad: data)
    Stub-->>Session: client.urlProtocolDidFinishLoading(_)
    Session-->>Code: (data, response)
    Note over Session,Stub: On cancellation, the session calls stopLoading()

Registering the class on a configuration scopes it to sessions created from that configuration. URLProtocol.registerClass(_:) registers it globally, for URLSession.shared and everything else in the process, which is exactly the coupling between tests that a fixture should avoid.

The code under test

The client below is ordinary production code. It takes a session and a base URL, and maps outcomes into a small error type in the spirit of Separating Transport Errors from Application Failures:

import Foundation

public struct Book: Codable, Equatable, Sendable {
    public let id: String
    public let title: String
    public init(id: String, title: String) { (self.id, self.title) = (id, title) }
}

public enum ClientError: Error, Equatable {
    case status(Int)
    case transport(URLError.Code)
    case decoding
}

public struct BookClient: Sendable {
    let session: URLSession
    let baseURL: URL

    public init(session: URLSession, baseURL: URL) { (self.session, self.baseURL) = (session, baseURL) }

    public func book(_ id: String) async throws(ClientError) -> Book {
        try await send(URLRequest(url: baseURL.appending(components: "books", id)))
    }

    public func create(title: String) async throws(ClientError) -> Book {
        var request = URLRequest(url: baseURL.appending(path: "books"))
        request.httpMethod = "POST"
        request.setValue("application/json", forHTTPHeaderField: "Content-Type")
        request.httpBody = try? JSONEncoder().encode(["title": title])
        return try await send(request)
    }

    private func send<Value: Decodable>(_ request: URLRequest) async throws(ClientError) -> Value {
        let data: Data
        let response: URLResponse
        do {
            (data, response) = try await session.data(for: request)
        } catch let error as URLError {
            throw .transport(error.code)
        } catch {
            throw .transport(.unknown)
        }
        let status = (response as? HTTPURLResponse)?.statusCode ?? 0
        guard (200..<300).contains(status) else { throw .status(status) }
        do { return try JSONDecoder().decode(Value.self, from: data) } catch { throw .decoding }
    }
}

Nothing in it knows about tests. The seam is the URLSession it receives, which is all a URLProtocol fixture needs.

The shared-handler trap

The URLProtocol stub found in many codebases looks like this:

// Does not compile in Swift 6 language mode.
final class LegacyStub: URLProtocol {
    static var handler: ((URLRequest) -> (HTTPURLResponse, Data))?
    override class func canInit(with request: URLRequest) -> Bool { true }
    override class func canonicalRequest(for request: URLRequest) -> URLRequest { request }
    override func startLoading() { /* uses LegacyStub.handler */ }
    override func stopLoading() {}
}
// error: static property 'handler' is not concurrency-safe because it is nonisolated global shared mutable state

Swift 6 rejects it, and the error is not pedantry. Each test sets LegacyStub.handler and then makes a request; with tests running in parallel, which Swift Testing does by default, test A’s request can be answered by test B’s handler. The resulting failures are intermittent and depend on scheduling, the worst kind. Marking the property nonisolated(unsafe) silences the compiler and keeps the race. The fix is to give every test its own fixture and route each request to the right one.

A fixture registry that is safe in parallel

Each test creates a Fixture, which holds its handler and records the requests it receives. The fixture is registered under a unique ID, and the test’s session sends that ID as a header on every request, through httpAdditionalHeaders. The protocol looks up the fixture by the header, so concurrent tests never see each other’s fixtures:

import Foundation
import Synchronization

struct StubResponse: Sendable {
    var status = 200
    var headers: [String: String] = ["Content-Type": "application/json"]
    var body = Data()
    var delay: Duration = .zero
    var error: URLError.Code?
    var redirect: URL?

    static func json(_ text: String, status: Int = 200) -> StubResponse {
        StubResponse(status: status, body: Data(text.utf8))
    }
    static func failure(_ code: URLError.Code) -> StubResponse { StubResponse(error: code) }
}

struct RecordedRequest: Sendable {
    let method: String
    let url: URL
    let headers: [String: String]
    let body: Data
}

final class Fixture: Sendable {
    let id = UUID().uuidString
    private let handler: @Sendable (RecordedRequest) -> StubResponse
    private let recorded = Mutex<[RecordedRequest]>([])
    private let stops = Mutex(0)

    init(_ handler: @escaping @Sendable (RecordedRequest) -> StubResponse) { self.handler = handler }

    var requests: [RecordedRequest] { recorded.withLock { $0 } }
    var stopCount: Int { stops.withLock { $0 } }

    func respond(to request: RecordedRequest) -> StubResponse {
        recorded.withLock { $0.append(request) }
        return handler(request)
    }
    func stopped() { stops.withLock { $0 += 1 } }

    /// A session whose every request is answered by this fixture, and only this fixture.
    func session(timeout: TimeInterval = 5) -> URLSession {
        FixtureRegistry.shared.register(self)
        let configuration = URLSessionConfiguration.ephemeral
        configuration.protocolClasses = [StubProtocol.self]
        configuration.httpAdditionalHeaders = [StubProtocol.fixtureHeader: id]
        configuration.timeoutIntervalForRequest = timeout
        return URLSession(configuration: configuration)
    }
}

final class FixtureRegistry: Sendable {
    static let shared = FixtureRegistry()
    private let fixtures = Mutex<[String: Fixture]>([:])
    func register(_ fixture: Fixture) { fixtures.withLock { $0[fixture.id] = fixture } }
    func fixture(for id: String?) -> Fixture? { id.flatMap { id in fixtures.withLock { $0[id] } } }
}

The protocol itself does four things in startLoading(): find the fixture, reconstruct the request including its body, wait if the response is delayed, and deliver the response through the client. Its only stored state is the in-flight delay task, so stopLoading() can cancel it:

final class StubProtocol: URLProtocol, @unchecked Sendable {
    static let fixtureHeader = "X-Fixture-ID"
    private let pending = Mutex<Task<Void, Never>?>(nil)

    // Only sessions configured by `Fixture.session()` list this class, so it can claim every request:
    // a request without a fixture fails loudly instead of reaching the real network.
    override class func canInit(with request: URLRequest) -> Bool { true }
    override class func canonicalRequest(for request: URLRequest) -> URLRequest { request }

    override func startLoading() {
        guard let fixture = FixtureRegistry.shared.fixture(for: request.value(forHTTPHeaderField: Self.fixtureHeader)) else {
            client?.urlProtocol(self, didFailWithError: URLError(.unsupportedURL))
            return
        }
        let recorded = RecordedRequest(method: request.httpMethod ?? "GET", url: request.url!,
                                       headers: request.allHTTPHeaderFields ?? [:], body: Self.body(of: request))
        let response = fixture.respond(to: recorded)
        guard response.delay > .zero else { return deliver(response, for: recorded) }
        let protocolInstance = UncheckedSendable(self)  // see below
        let delayed = Task {
            do { try await Task.sleep(for: response.delay) } catch { return }
            protocolInstance.value.deliver(response, for: recorded)
        }
        pending.withLock { $0 = delayed }
    }

    override func stopLoading() {
        pending.withLock { $0?.cancel() }
        FixtureRegistry.shared.fixture(for: request.value(forHTTPHeaderField: Self.fixtureHeader))?.stopped()
    }

    private func deliver(_ response: StubResponse, for request: RecordedRequest) {
        if let code = response.error {
            client?.urlProtocol(self, didFailWithError: URLError(code))
            return
        }
        let http = HTTPURLResponse(url: request.url, statusCode: response.status, httpVersion: "HTTP/1.1",
                                   headerFields: response.headers)!
        if let target = response.redirect {
            var next = URLRequest(url: target)
            next.allHTTPHeaderFields = request.headers
            client?.urlProtocol(self, wasRedirectedTo: next, redirectResponse: http)
            return
        }
        client?.urlProtocol(self, didReceive: http, cacheStoragePolicy: .notAllowed)
        client?.urlProtocol(self, didLoad: response.body)
        client?.urlProtocolDidFinishLoading(self)
    }

    /// Inside a URLProtocol, a body set with `httpBody` arrives as `httpBodyStream`.
    private static func body(of request: URLRequest) -> Data {
        if let body = request.httpBody { return body }
        guard let stream = request.httpBodyStream else { return Data() }
        stream.open()
        defer { stream.close() }
        var data = Data()
        var buffer = [UInt8](repeating: 0, count: 16_384)
        while stream.hasBytesAvailable {
            let count = stream.read(&buffer, maxLength: buffer.count)
            guard count > 0 else { break }
            data.append(buffer, count: count)
        }
        return data
    }
}

/// URLProtocol inherits from a non-Sendable Objective-C class, so even an `@unchecked Sendable`
/// subclass's `self` cannot be captured by a `Task`. This wrapper makes that one hand-off explicit.
struct UncheckedSendable<Value>: @unchecked Sendable {
    let value: Value
    init(_ value: Value) { self.value = value }
}

The class is @unchecked Sendable because URLProtocol is an Objective-C class the compiler cannot reason about; its own state is behind a Mutex, and the fixture it talks to is Sendable. The body reconstruction handles the second trap from the introduction, measured below: by the time a request reaches a protocol, httpBody is nil and the body is in httpBodyStream.

Tests

With the fixture in place, tests read as a description of the exchange: what the server answers, what the client returns, and what the server received.

import Foundation
import Testing
@testable import Library

let api = URL(string: "https://api.library.example/v2")!

@Suite struct BookClientTests {
    @Test func decodesABook() async throws {
        let fixture = Fixture { _ in .json(#"{"id":"b-7","title":"Dune"}"#) }
        let client = BookClient(session: fixture.session(), baseURL: api)

        let book = try await client.book("b-7")

        #expect(book == Book(id: "b-7", title: "Dune"))
        let request = try #require(fixture.requests.first)
        #expect(request.method == "GET")
        #expect(request.url.absoluteString == "https://api.library.example/v2/books/b-7")
    }

    @Test func sendsTheBodyItCreates() async throws {
        let fixture = Fixture { request in
            let sent = try? JSONDecoder().decode([String: String].self, from: request.body)
            return .json(#"{"id":"b-9","title":"\#(sent?["title"] ?? "?")"}"#, status: 201)
        }
        let client = BookClient(session: fixture.session(), baseURL: api)

        let created = try await client.create(title: "Children of Dune")

        #expect(created.title == "Children of Dune")
        let request = try #require(fixture.requests.first)
        #expect(request.method == "POST")
        #expect(request.headers["Content-Type"] == "application/json")
        #expect(request.body == Data(#"{"title":"Children of Dune"}"#.utf8))
    }

    @Test func mapsAStatusCode() async {
        let fixture = Fixture { _ in .json(#"{"error":"not found"}"#, status: 404) }
        let client = BookClient(session: fixture.session(), baseURL: api)
        await #expect(throws: ClientError.status(404)) { try await client.book("missing") }
    }

    @Test func mapsATransportError() async {
        let fixture = Fixture { _ in .failure(.networkConnectionLost) }
        let client = BookClient(session: fixture.session(), baseURL: api)
        await #expect(throws: ClientError.transport(.networkConnectionLost)) { try await client.book("b-7") }
        #expect(fixture.requests.count == 1)
    }

    @Test func followsARedirect() async throws {
        let fixture = Fixture { request in
            request.url.path().hasSuffix("/old")
                ? StubResponse(status: 301, headers: ["Location": "/v2/books/b-7"],
                               redirect: URL(string: "https://api.library.example/v2/books/b-7"))
                : .json(#"{"id":"b-7","title":"Dune"}"#)
        }
        let client = BookClient(session: fixture.session(), baseURL: api)
        #expect(try await client.book("old").title == "Dune")
        #expect(fixture.requests.map { $0.url.lastPathComponent } == ["old", "b-7"])
    }

    @Test func timesOut() async {
        let fixture = Fixture { _ in StubResponse(body: Data("{}".utf8), delay: .seconds(10)) }
        let client = BookClient(session: fixture.session(timeout: 0.3), baseURL: api)
        let start = ContinuousClock.now
        await #expect(throws: ClientError.transport(.timedOut)) { try await client.book("slow") }
        #expect(ContinuousClock.now - start < .seconds(2))
    }

    @Test func cancellationStopsLoading() async throws {
        let fixture = Fixture { _ in StubResponse(body: Data("{}".utf8), delay: .seconds(10)) }
        let client = BookClient(session: fixture.session(), baseURL: api)
        let task = Task { try await client.book("slow") }
        try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(100))
        task.cancel()
        let result = await task.result
        #expect(throws: ClientError.transport(.cancelled)) { try result.get() }
        try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(50))
        #expect(fixture.stopCount == 1)
    }

    @Test(arguments: 0..<50)
    func parallelFixturesNeverCross(index: Int) async throws {
        let fixture = Fixture { _ in .json(#"{"id":"b-\#(index)","title":"Book \#(index)"}"#) }
        let client = BookClient(session: fixture.session(), baseURL: api)
        try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(Int.random(in: 0...20)))
        #expect(try await client.book("b-\(index)").title == "Book \(index)")
        #expect(fixture.requests.count == 1)
    }
}

All 13 tests, 62 test cases counting the parameterized ones, pass under swift test, which runs them in parallel. The 50 parameterized cases start in random order with random delays, each with its own fixture, and each receives its own response. The timeout test also documents that timeoutIntervalForRequest is enforced for protocol-backed tasks: a 0.3 s timeout against a response delayed by ten seconds failed with timedOut in well under two seconds. The cancellation test shows the other half of the contract: cancelling the Swift task made the session call stopLoading(), which cancelled the pending delivery.

What a stub does not test

A URLProtocol replaces the entire HTTP layer of URLSession, not just the server. Everything that layer does is therefore absent in a stubbed test. A probe that sent requests through a stub and inspected what arrived and what came back measured the differences on macOS 26:

import Foundation
import Testing

@Suite struct StubFidelity {
    @Test func headersTheSystemWouldAddAreAbsent() async throws {
        let fixture = Fixture { _ in .json("{}") }
        _ = try await fixture.session().data(from: api.appending(path: "probe"))
        let headers = try #require(fixture.requests.first).headers
        #expect(headers["User-Agent"] == nil && headers["Accept-Encoding"] == nil && headers["Accept-Language"] == nil)
    }

    @Test func bodiesArriveAsStreams() async throws {
        let fixture = Fixture { _ in .json("{}") }
        var request = URLRequest(url: api.appending(path: "probe"))
        request.httpMethod = "POST"
        request.httpBody = Data("hello".utf8)
        _ = try await fixture.session().data(for: request)
        #expect(try #require(fixture.requests.first).body == Data("hello".utf8))  // only because StubProtocol read the stream
    }

    @Test func lostConnectionsAreNotRetried() async {
        let fixture = Fixture { _ in .failure(.networkConnectionLost) }
        _ = try? await fixture.session().data(from: api.appending(path: "probe"))
        #expect(fixture.requests.count == 1)   // the real stack tried a GET three times
    }

    @Test func contentEncodingIsNotDecoded() async throws {
        let gzippedHello = Data([0x1f, 0x8b, 0x08, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x03, 0xcb, 0x48, 0xcd, 0xc9,
                                 0xc9, 0x07, 0x00, 0x86, 0xa6, 0x10, 0x36, 0x05, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00])
        let fixture = Fixture { _ in StubResponse(headers: ["Content-Encoding": "gzip"], body: gzippedHello) }
        let (data, _) = try await fixture.session().data(from: api.appending(path: "probe"))
        #expect(data == gzippedHello)          // the real stack would return "hello"
    }

    @Test func redirectResponsesAreNotFollowedAutomatically() async throws {
        let fixture = Fixture { _ in StubResponse(status: 302, headers: ["Location": "/elsewhere"]) }
        let (_, response) = try await fixture.session().data(from: api.appending(path: "probe"))
        #expect((response as? HTTPURLResponse)?.statusCode == 302)   // only wasRedirectedTo makes it redirect
    }
}
Behavior of the real HTTP stack Under a URLProtocol stub (measured)
Adds User-Agent, Accept-Encoding, Accept-Language Absent
httpBody on the request nil; the body is in httpBodyStream
Retries GET up to three times on a lost connection One attempt
Decompresses Content-Encoding: gzip Raw compressed bytes returned
Follows 3xx with Location Only if the protocol calls wasRedirectedTo
Stores Set-Cookie, applies URLCache Not observed in the probe; do not rely on either
Connection reuse, DNS, TLS, HTTP/2, timing Not involved at all

None of this makes stubs less useful. It defines what a stubbed test proves: that the code under test builds the right requests and handles the responses it is given, including ones that are hard to produce for real. It does not prove that the real stack and a real server will produce those responses. That is the job of tests against a controlled server, which Verifying Contracts Against a Controlled Server builds with the same LocalServer used throughout this series, and a stub that emulates redirects, retries, or compression is a second HTTP implementation that can drift from the first.

Summary

  • URLProtocol subclasses registered in a configuration’s protocolClasses answer every request of sessions made from it; avoid global registration.
  • A static, mutable handler is rejected by Swift 6 for good reason: it races under parallel tests. Give each test a fixture, register it under an ID, and route by a header set in httpAdditionalHeaders.
  • Claim every request in canInit for stub sessions, and fail requests without a fixture, so tests never reach the network by accident.
  • Read request bodies from httpBodyStream; httpBody is nil inside a protocol.
  • Measured: request timeouts and cancellation (stopLoading) work with protocol-backed tasks; 50 parallel parameterized tests with separate fixtures never crossed.
  • Measured gaps: no system headers, no retry on lost connections, no decompression, no automatic redirects. Stubs test the client’s logic, not the HTTP stack.

Exercise

Add a StubResponse.chunks option that delivers the body in several didLoad calls with delays between them, and use it to test a function that reads bytes(for:) and reports progress. Then write a test that fails if any test in the suite makes a request without a fixture: record unmatched requests in the registry, and check the record in a test that runs last, or with a custom Swift Testing trait. Finally, try to reproduce the shared-handler race with nonisolated(unsafe) static var and 50 parallel tests, and count how often it fails in 20 runs.

Further reading

  • Apple’s URLProtocol and URLSessionConfiguration.protocolClasses.
  • Meet Swift Testing, WWDC24, on parameterized tests and parallel execution.
  • The concurrency roadmap’s Testing Concurrent Work with Controlled Interleavings.

Previous: Streaming Responses and Incremental Parsing. Next: Testing Status Codes, Invalid Payloads, and Transport Errors.

Return to the Networking roadmap.
entry.summary: A test that talks to a real server is slow, depends on the network and the server’s data, and cannot easily produce the responses that matter most: the 503, the truncated body, the timeout. The standard way to give URLSession canned responses without changing the code under test is URLProtocol, the extension point the URL Loading System uses to decide how to load a request. A test registers a protocol class on a session’s configuration, and every request through that session is answered by the test’s own code. It is an old API with sharp edges, and two of them cut most test suites: a shared static handler that races once tests run in parallel, which Swift Testing does by default, and request bodies that are not where the code expects them. This article builds a fixture protocol that is safe under parallel tests and Swift 6 strict concurrency, uses it to test a small client’s success, failure, redirect, timeout, and cancellation paths, and then measures what a URLProtocol stub does not reproduce from the real HTTP stack, so the tests’ claims stay honest.

entry.title: Streaming Responses and Incremental Parsing
entry.content:
Most responses are read whole: wait for the last byte, then decode. Some responses are worth reading while they arrive. A search that returns results as the server finds them, a log tail, a progress feed for a server-side job, or a language model generating text token by token all have the same shape: the first useful piece exists long before the last one, and a client that waits for the end throws away the head start.

URLSession.bytes(for:) makes the bytes available as an AsyncSequence as soon as they arrive. Turning bytes into values is the hard part, because the network does not respect message boundaries: a JSON record, a UTF-8 character, or an event can be split anywhere. This article covers the three streaming formats an app is most likely to meet: newline-delimited JSON, Server-Sent Events, and a large JSON array parsed element by element. It measures the details that decide whether a streaming client works: when bytes are delivered, what AsyncBytes.lines does with empty lines, what happens when the consumer is slow, and what breaking out of the loop actually stops.

The examples use Swift 6 language mode and were compiled and run with the Swift 6.4 toolchain from Xcode 27.1 on macOS 26. They send requests to LocalServer, the loopback HTTP server from the appendix of the first article; paste that code first, then the blocks below in order, into one main.swift. Consuming Values with AsyncSequence covers the protocol itself.

Delivery: when bytes become available

Two things stand between the server’s write and the client’s loop. One is the server’s own buffering, which is outside the client’s control. The other is URLSession’s content sniffing, measured in Requests and Responses with async and await: for a response with no Content-Type or with text/plain, delivery waits for 512 bytes or the end of the body. Streaming formats have registered media types that are not sniffed, application/x-ndjson and text/event-stream, and a streaming server must send them.

The server below emits five records 100 ms apart, with chunked transfer encoding because the total length is unknown when it starts, which is what makes streaming possible over HTTP/1.1:

import Foundation
import Synchronization
import Darwin

struct Hit: Decodable, Equatable, Sendable {
    let id: Int
    let title: String
}

let server = try await LocalServer.start { request in
    switch request.path {
    case "/search":
        var pieces: [HTTPResponse.Piece] = []
        for index in 1...5 {
            pieces += [.pause(.milliseconds(100)), .bytes(Data((#"{"id":\#(index),"title":"Result \#(index)"}"# + "\n").utf8))]
        }
        return HTTPResponse(status: 200, headers: [("Content-Type", request.query["type"] ?? "application/x-ndjson")],
                            body: pieces, chunked: true)
    default:
        return .text("not found", status: 404)
    }
}

func searchURL(type: String) -> URL {
    var components = URLComponents(url: server.baseURL.appending(path: "search"), resolvingAgainstBaseURL: false)!
    components.queryItems = [URLQueryItem(name: "type", value: type)]
    return components.url!
}

func arrivals(type: String) async throws -> [Duration] {
    let start = ContinuousClock.now
    let (bytes, _) = try await URLSession.shared.bytes(from: searchURL(type: type))
    var times: [Duration] = []
    for try await line in bytes.lines {
        _ = try JSONDecoder().decode(Hit.self, from: Data(line.utf8))
        times.append(ContinuousClock.now - start)
    }
    return times
}

let streamed = try await arrivals(type: "application/x-ndjson")
let sniffed = try await arrivals(type: "text/plain")
print("ndjson:", streamed, "\ntext/plain:", sniffed)
assert(streamed.count == 5 && streamed[0] < .milliseconds(250))   // the first result after ~100 ms
assert(sniffed.count == 5 && sniffed[0] > .milliseconds(450))     // held back until the body ended

With the right type, the first result was decoded about 100 ms after the request started and the rest followed at 100 ms intervals. With text/plain, all five arrived together after half a second, because the five records add up to less than 512 bytes: a “streaming” endpoint that behaves exactly like a normal one, for a reason that is invisible in the client’s code.

Bytes are not characters

The network splits data wherever it likes, including in the middle of a multi-byte UTF-8 character. Code that decodes each received chunk separately, which is easy to write with a data-task delegate that receives Data pieces, turns split characters into replacement characters:

let text = "Café ☕ résumé"
let bytes = Array(text.utf8)
let split = bytes.firstIndex(of: 0xE2)! + 1   // inside the three-byte encoding of ☕
let chunks = [Data(bytes[..<split]), Data(bytes[split...])]

let perChunk = chunks.map { String(decoding: $0, as: UTF8.self) }.joined()
assert(perChunk != text && perChunk.contains("\u{FFFD}"))   // corrupted at the boundary

var assembled = Data()
chunks.forEach { assembled.append($0) }
assert(String(decoding: assembled, as: UTF8.self) == text)   // decode only complete sequences

AsyncBytes delivers one byte at a time, and its .characters, .unicodeScalars, and .lines views decode across chunk boundaries correctly, so this bug cannot happen with them. It reappears whenever code buffers bytes into its own chunks: decode at message boundaries, which for every format below is a newline or a delimiter that is a single ASCII byte, never at arbitrary chunk boundaries.

lines drops empty lines

AsyncBytes.lines is the obvious way to read line-based formats. What it considers a line matters, so it is worth measuring with every kind of line ending and some empty lines:

let lineServer = try await LocalServer.start { _ in
    HTTPResponse(status: 200, headers: [("Content-Type", "text/event-stream")],
                 body: [.bytes(Data("a\n\nb\r\n\r\nc\rd\n\n\ne".utf8))])
}
let (lineBytes, _) = try await URLSession.shared.bytes(from: lineServer.baseURL)
var lines: [String] = []
for try await line in lineBytes.lines { lines.append(line) }
assert(lines == ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"])   // every empty line is gone

It accepts \n, \r\n, and a lone \r as line endings, which is generous and correct. It also skips every empty line. For newline-delimited JSON that is harmless, since empty lines carry nothing. For Server-Sent Events it is fatal: an empty line is the signal that an event is complete, and a parser built on .lines never sees it. The SSE parser below therefore splits lines itself.

Server-Sent Events

Server-Sent Events, specified in the HTML Standard, are a simple, one-way streaming protocol over plain HTTP. The body is text/event-stream, a sequence of lines grouped into events by empty lines:

: comments start with a colon and are ignored
event: availability
id: 41
data: {"book":"b-7","copies":2}

data: first line
data: second line

retry: 5000

Each line is field: value. data lines accumulate, joined with newlines; event sets the event’s type; id sets the last event ID that a reconnecting client sends back in a Last-Event-ID header; retry sets the reconnection delay in milliseconds. An empty line dispatches the event built so far. The rules have a few precise details, such as that a single space after the colon is removed but further spaces are kept, that a line without a colon is a field name with an empty value, and that an event with no data is not dispatched. The parser below follows them, and reads raw bytes so it can see empty lines:

struct ServerSentEvent: Equatable, Sendable {
    var type = "message"
    var data = ""
    var id: String?
}

struct SSEParser {
    private var data: [String] = []
    private var type = ""
    private(set) var lastEventID: String?
    private(set) var retry: Duration?
    private var line: [UInt8] = []
    private var previousWasCR = false

    /// Feeds one byte; returns an event when a blank line completes one.
    mutating func feed(_ byte: UInt8) -> ServerSentEvent? {
        if previousWasCR && byte == 0x0A { previousWasCR = false; return nil }  // the LF of a CRLF
        previousWasCR = byte == 0x0D
        guard byte == 0x0A || byte == 0x0D else { line.append(byte); return nil }
        defer { line.removeAll(keepingCapacity: true) }
        return process(String(decoding: line, as: UTF8.self))
    }

    private mutating func process(_ text: String) -> ServerSentEvent? {
        if text.isEmpty { return dispatch() }
        if text.hasPrefix(":") { return nil }  // comment
        let field: Substring
        var value: Substring
        if let colon = text.firstIndex(of: ":") {
            field = text[..<colon]
            value = text[text.index(after: colon)...]
            if value.hasPrefix(" ") { value = value.dropFirst() }
        } else {
            (field, value) = (text[...], "")
        }
        switch field {
        case "data": data.append(String(value))
        case "event": type = String(value)
        case "id" where !value.contains("\0"): lastEventID = String(value)
        case "retry": if let milliseconds = Int(value) { retry = .milliseconds(milliseconds) }
        default: break
        }
        return nil
    }

    private mutating func dispatch() -> ServerSentEvent? {
        defer { data.removeAll(); type = "" }
        guard !data.isEmpty else { return nil }
        return ServerSentEvent(type: type.isEmpty ? "message" : type, data: data.joined(separator: "\n"), id: lastEventID)
    }
}

func parse(_ text: String) -> (events: [ServerSentEvent], parser: SSEParser) {
    var parser = SSEParser()
    var events: [ServerSentEvent] = []
    for byte in text.utf8 { if let event = parser.feed(byte) { events.append(event) } }
    return (events, parser)
}

let sample = ": keep-alive\r\nevent: availability\r\nid: 41\r\ndata: {\"book\":\"b-7\"}\r\n\r\ndata: first line\ndata:  second line\n\nretry: 5000\n\ndata\n\nevent: ignored\n\n"
let (sampleEvents, sampleParser) = parse(sample)
assert(sampleEvents == [
    ServerSentEvent(type: "availability", data: #"{"book":"b-7"}"#, id: "41"),
    ServerSentEvent(type: "message", data: "first line\n second line", id: "41"),  // one leading space removed
    ServerSentEvent(type: "message", data: "", id: "41"),                          // "data" without a colon
])
assert(sampleParser.retry == .milliseconds(5000) && sampleParser.lastEventID == "41")

The last event in the sample, event: ignored followed by a blank line, produced nothing, because it had no data field. The third event, a bare data line, is dispatched with empty data, which the specification treats as distinct from no data. Running the parser over a live stream is a loop over AsyncBytes:

let sse = try await LocalServer.start { request in
    var pieces: [HTTPResponse.Piece] = [.bytes(Data(": connected\n\n".utf8))]
    let start = Int(request.header("Last-Event-ID") ?? "0") ?? 0
    for id in (start + 1)...(start + 3) {
        pieces += [.pause(.milliseconds(80)),
                   .bytes(Data("event: availability\nid: \(id)\ndata: {\"copies\":\(id)}\n\n".utf8))]
    }
    return HTTPResponse(status: 200, headers: [("Content-Type", "text/event-stream"), ("Cache-Control", "no-store")],
                        body: pieces, chunked: true)
}

func listen(lastEventID: String?) async throws -> (events: [ServerSentEvent], firstAfter: Duration) {
    var request = URLRequest(url: sse.baseURL.appending(path: "events"))
    request.setValue("text/event-stream", forHTTPHeaderField: "Accept")
    if let lastEventID { request.setValue(lastEventID, forHTTPHeaderField: "Last-Event-ID") }
    let start = ContinuousClock.now
    let (bytes, _) = try await URLSession.shared.bytes(for: request)
    var parser = SSEParser()
    var events: [ServerSentEvent] = []
    var firstAfter = Duration.zero
    for try await byte in bytes {
        if let event = parser.feed(byte) {
            if events.isEmpty { firstAfter = ContinuousClock.now - start }
            events.append(event)
        }
    }
    return (events, firstAfter)
}

let firstConnection = try await listen(lastEventID: nil)
assert(firstConnection.events.map(\.id) == ["1", "2", "3"] && firstConnection.firstAfter < .milliseconds(200))
let resumed = try await listen(lastEventID: firstConnection.events.last?.id)
assert(resumed.events.map(\.id) == ["4", "5", "6"])  // the server continued after the last seen event

The Last-Event-ID mechanism is what makes SSE recoverable where a raw WebSocket is not: the client tells the server where it stopped, and the server resumes from there. The reconnecting connection manager in WebSockets: Connection State and Reconnection applies directly to SSE too, with retry from the stream as the backoff floor.

A large JSON array, one element at a time

APIs that were not designed for streaming still often return large arrays: [{...}, {...}, ...], thousands of elements, several megabytes. JSONDecoder needs the whole document. A small scanner can find the boundaries of top-level elements while the bytes arrive, by tracking nesting depth and whether it is inside a string, so each element can be decoded as soon as it is complete:

struct ArrayElementScanner {
    private var depth = 0
    private var inString = false
    private var escaped = false
    private var element: [UInt8] = []

    /// Feeds one byte of a JSON array; returns the bytes of a complete top-level element.
    mutating func feed(_ byte: UInt8) -> Data? {
        if inString {
            element.append(byte)
            if escaped { escaped = false } else if byte == UInt8(ascii: "\\") { escaped = true } else if byte == UInt8(ascii: "\"") { inString = false }
            return nil
        }
        switch byte {
        case UInt8(ascii: "["), UInt8(ascii: "{"):
            depth += 1
            if depth > 1 { element.append(byte) }
        case UInt8(ascii: "]"), UInt8(ascii: "}"):
            depth -= 1
            if depth >= 1 { element.append(byte) }
            if depth == 1 && byte == UInt8(ascii: "}") { return take() }
            if depth == 0 { return element.isEmpty ? nil : take() }
        case UInt8(ascii: ","):
            if depth == 1 { return element.isEmpty ? nil : take() }
            element.append(byte)
        case UInt8(ascii: "\""):
            inString = true
            element.append(byte)
        case 0x20, 0x0A, 0x0D, 0x09:
            if depth > 1 { element.append(byte) }
        default:
            element.append(byte)
        }
        return nil
    }

    private mutating func take() -> Data {
        defer { element.removeAll(keepingCapacity: true) }
        return Data(element)
    }
}

let tricky = #"[ {"id":1,"title":"Braces { and ] in a string"}, {"id":2,"title":"Escaped \" quote"} ,{"id":3,"title":"Ünïcode ☕"} ]"#
var scanner = ArrayElementScanner()
let elements = tricky.utf8.compactMap { scanner.feed($0) }
let decodedHits = try elements.map { try JSONDecoder().decode(Hit.self, from: $0) }
assert(decodedHits.map(\.id) == [1, 2, 3] && decodedHits[0].title == "Braces { and ] in a string")
assert(decodedHits[2].title == "Ünïcode ☕")

The scanner handles braces and brackets inside strings, escaped quotes, and whitespace between elements. It returns an element when its closing } brings the depth back to the array level, and handles scalars such as numbers in an array at the following comma or ]. It does not validate JSON; each element is validated when it is decoded, so a malformed element fails on its own, which is the lossy behavior from Decoding JSON with Codable for free.

Against a server that sends a 2,000-element array in 50 pieces with a short pause between pieces, the first element is available long before the last byte:

let arrayServer = try await LocalServer.start { _ in
    let items = (1...2_000).map { #"{"id":\#($0),"title":"Book number \#($0)"}"# }
    let document = Data(("[" + items.joined(separator: ",") + "]").utf8)
    let pieceSize = document.count / 50 + 1
    var pieces: [HTTPResponse.Piece] = []
    for start in stride(from: 0, to: document.count, by: pieceSize) {
        pieces += [.bytes(document[start..<min(start + pieceSize, document.count)]), .pause(.milliseconds(10))]
    }
    return HTTPResponse(status: 200, headers: [("Content-Type", "application/json")], body: pieces, chunked: true)
}

func streamArray() async throws -> (count: Int, firstAfter: Duration, total: Duration) {
    let start = ContinuousClock.now
    let (bytes, _) = try await URLSession.shared.bytes(from: arrayServer.baseURL)
    var scanner = ArrayElementScanner()
    var count = 0
    var firstAfter = Duration.zero
    for try await byte in bytes {
        guard let element = scanner.feed(byte) else { continue }
        _ = try JSONDecoder().decode(Hit.self, from: element)
        if count == 0 { firstAfter = ContinuousClock.now - start }
        count += 1
    }
    return (count, firstAfter, ContinuousClock.now - start)
}

let streamedArray = try await streamArray()
print("2,000 elements: first after \(streamedArray.firstAfter), all after \(streamedArray.total)")
assert(streamedArray.count == 2_000)
assert(streamedArray.firstAfter * 5 < streamedArray.total)

The first book was ready a few milliseconds into a transfer that lasted more than half a second. A list screen can show its first rows immediately and keep appending, instead of showing a spinner for the full download.

Slow consumers, cancellation, and cost

A streaming client is a pipeline, and three properties of the pipeline need checking: what happens when the consumer cannot keep up, what stops the transfer, and what each byte costs.

Backpressure. When the loop stops pulling bytes, URLSession does not keep reading the socket into memory without limit. With a server ready to send 100 MB and a consumer paused for two seconds after the first byte, the process’s physical footprint grew by about 5 MB in this measurement. Beyond that buffer, TCP flow control pushes back to the server. A slow consumer slows the transfer instead of exhausting memory.

Stopping. Breaking out of the for try await loop does not end the request. The AsyncBytes value still owns a running task, and the transfer continues until that value is released, at the end of the scope that holds it:

let feed = try await LocalServer.start { _ in
    var pieces: [HTTPResponse.Piece] = []
    for index in 0..<50 { pieces += [.bytes(Data((#"{"n":\#(index)}"# + "\n").utf8)), .pause(.milliseconds(100))] }
    return HTTPResponse(status: 200, headers: [("Content-Type", "application/x-ndjson")], body: pieces, chunked: true)
}

func takeThree(cancelling: Bool) async throws -> URLSessionTask.State {
    let (bytes, _) = try await URLSession.shared.bytes(from: feed.baseURL)
    var count = 0
    for try await _ in bytes.lines {
        count += 1
        if count == 3 { break }
    }
    if cancelling { bytes.task.cancel() }
    try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(200))
    return bytes.task.state
}

let afterBreak = try await takeThree(cancelling: false)
let afterCancel = try await takeThree(cancelling: true)
assert(afterBreak == .running)      // the 5-second stream is still open
assert(afterCancel == .completed)

In a function that returns right after the loop, release comes soon. In a long-lived object that keeps the AsyncBytes around, or in a loop that breaks and then does more work, the connection stays open. Cancel bytes.task explicitly when you are done with a stream early; cancelling the enclosing Swift task works too, as Requests and Responses with async and await showed.

Cost per byte. Iterating AsyncBytes one byte at a time is cheap in an optimized build and expensive in a debug build, where each step of the async iterator is a real function call:

50 MB over loopback -O -Onone (debug)
for try await byte in bytes 0.05 s (about 1 ns per byte) 4.15 s (about 83 ns per byte)
data(from:) 0.02 s 0.02 s

For streams of a few hundred kilobytes the difference is invisible. For multi-megabyte streams, a debug build that takes seconds to parse is easy to mistake for a slow server, and a scanner that appends byte by byte into a buffer, like the one above, is where the time goes. Measure parsing performance in a release build, and for large streams consider handling bytes in batches through a data-task delegate, decoding only at the delimiters as described above.

The throughput of a streaming pipeline is the minimum of its stages:

\[\text{throughput} = \min(\text{network}, \text{parser}, \text{consumer})\]

The 83 ns per byte of a debug build caps parsing at about 12 MB/s, below a good Wi-Fi link. The 1 ns of a release build, about 1 GB/s, does not limit any network a phone has.

Summary

  • Stream when the first useful value arrives long before the last byte. Use a non-sniffed media type: measured, five NDJSON records were usable from 100 ms as application/x-ndjson but only after the whole body as text/plain.
  • Decode UTF-8 only at message boundaries; per-chunk decoding corrupts characters split across chunks.
  • AsyncBytes.lines accepts \n, \r\n, and \r, and silently drops empty lines. Fine for NDJSON, wrong for Server-Sent Events.
  • Parse SSE from bytes: accumulate data lines, dispatch on a blank line, track id for Last-Event-ID resumption and retry for backoff.
  • A small scanner that tracks depth and strings can hand out the elements of a large JSON array as they complete.
  • A paused consumer grew the footprint by only about 5 MB with 100 MB pending; breaking out of the loop does not end the transfer until AsyncBytes is released, so cancel bytes.task.
  • Per-byte iteration costs about 1 ns optimized and 83 ns in debug builds; measure parsers in release builds.

Exercise

Write an AsyncSequence adapter, ServerSentEvents<Base: AsyncSequence> where Base.Element == UInt8, that wraps SSEParser, and a reconnecting function that reconnects with the server-provided retry delay and the last id when the stream ends or fails. Test it against a server that closes the stream after three events each time. Assert that ten events arrive in order with no duplicates across four connections, and that the delay between connections matches a retry: 200 sent in the stream.

Further reading

  • The HTML Standard’s Server-sent events section, including the parsing algorithm the parser follows.
  • NDJSON and RFC 7464: JSON Text Sequences, two conventions for streaming JSON values.
  • Apple’s URLSession.AsyncBytes documentation.

Previous: WebSockets: Connection State and Reconnection. Next: Isolating HTTP Fixtures with URLProtocol.
