entry.summary: Most responses are read whole: wait for the last byte, then decode. Some responses are worth reading while they arrive. A search that returns results as the server finds them, a log tail, a progress feed for a server-side job, or a language model generating text token by token all have the same shape: the first useful piece exists long before the last one, and a client that waits for the end throws away the head start. URLSession.bytes(for:) makes the bytes available as an AsyncSequence as soon as they arrive. Turning bytes into values is the hard part, because the network does not respect message boundaries: a JSON record, a UTF-8 character, or an event can be split anywhere. This article covers the three streaming formats an app is most likely to meet: newline-delimited JSON, Server-Sent Events, and a large JSON array parsed element by element. It measures the details that decide whether a streaming client works: when bytes are delivered, what AsyncBytes.lines does with empty lines, what happens when the consumer is slow, and what breaking out of the loop actually stops.

entry.title: WebSockets: Connection State and Reconnection
entry.content:
An HTTP request has a beginning and an end, and the client always knows which of the two it is waiting for. A WebSocket has neither. It is a long-lived, two-way channel that is open until something closes it: the server deliberately, the network accidentally, or nothing at all, when the other end has silently disappeared and the socket looks healthy forever. A live feature built on a WebSocket, such as chat, a shared reading list, or a “books available now” ticker, is only as good as the client’s answer to one question: what state is the connection in right now, and what does it do about it?

This article starts from the protocol: the upgrade handshake that turns an HTTP request into a WebSocket, and the frames that follow. It then measures the three ways a URLSessionWebSocketTask connection ends, against a WebSocket server built with Network framework, including the one that produces no error at all. Finally it builds a connection manager with an explicit state machine, heartbeats that detect dead peers within a bounded time, jittered reconnection, and resubscription after every reconnect.

The examples use Swift 6 language mode and were compiled and run with the Swift 6.4 toolchain from Xcode 27.1 on macOS 26. One section sends a request to LocalServer, the loopback HTTP server from the appendix of the first article; the WebSocket server is built in this article. Paste LocalServer first, then the blocks below in order, into one main.swift.

From HTTP to WebSocket

A WebSocket connection starts as an HTTP/1.1 GET with an Upgrade: websocket header, defined in RFC 6455. If the server agrees, it answers 101 Switching Protocols, and from then on the TCP connection carries WebSocket frames instead of HTTP messages. Pointing a URLSessionWebSocketTask at LocalServer, which speaks only HTTP, shows the request it sends:

import Foundation
import Network
import CryptoKit
import Synchronization

let http = try await LocalServer.start { request in .text("not a WebSocket server", status: 400) }
let probe = URLSession.shared.webSocketTask(with: URL(string: "ws://127.0.0.1:\(http.port)/live")!, protocols: ["library.v1"])
probe.resume()
do {
    _ = try await probe.receive()
    assertionFailure("the handshake cannot succeed against an HTTP-only server")
} catch let error as URLError {
    assert(error.code == .badServerResponse)  // -1011: the server did not answer 101
}
let handshake = http.requests[0]
print(handshake.head)
assert(handshake.header("Upgrade") == "websocket" && handshake.header("Connection") == "Upgrade")
assert(handshake.header("Sec-WebSocket-Version") == "13")
assert(handshake.header("Sec-WebSocket-Protocol") == "library.v1")
assert(probe.maximumMessageSize == 1_048_576)

GET /live HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:50174
Sec-WebSocket-Protocol: library.v1
Sec-WebSocket-Key: g1x9S8H+Burq1v3oY/F9gg==
Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13
Upgrade: websocket
Sec-WebSocket-Extensions: permessage-deflate
Connection: Upgrade

The Sec-WebSocket-Key is 16 random bytes in base64. The server proves it understood the WebSocket handshake, rather than being an HTTP server that happened to echo headers, by returning Sec-WebSocket-Accept: the SHA-1 of the key concatenated with a fixed GUID from the RFC, in base64.

\[\text{Accept} = \operatorname{base64}\big(\operatorname{SHA1}(\text{Key} \,\|\, \texttt{258EAFA5-E914-47DA-95CA-C5AB0DC85B11})\big)\]

The RFC’s own example checks the formula:

func websocketAccept(for key: String) -> String {
    let digest = Insecure.SHA1.hash(data: Data((key + "258EAFA5-E914-47DA-95CA-C5AB0DC85B11").utf8))
    return Data(digest).base64EncodedString()
}
assert(websocketAccept(for: "dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==") == "s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo=")  // RFC 6455 §1.3

SHA-1 is not used for security here; it only makes the response specific to this request. The security of a WebSocket comes from TLS, so production URLs use wss://, which App Transport Security requires anyway. The client also offered permessage-deflate (RFC 7692) compression, and the 1 MiB maximumMessageSize is the largest message receive() accepts before failing.

After the handshake, data flows as frames: text and binary frames carry messages, ping and pong frames check liveness, and a close frame ends the connection with a close code:

Close code Meaning
1000 Normal closure
1001 Going away (server shutting down, page navigating)
1008 Policy violation
1011 Server error
1006 Never sent: reported locally when the connection dropped without a close frame
4000–4999 Reserved for applications, e.g. 4001 “token expired”, 4003 “forbidden” 
sequenceDiagram
    accTitle: The life of a WebSocket connection
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Server
    C->>S: GET /live, Upgrade: websocket, Sec-WebSocket-Key
    S-->>C: 101 Switching Protocols, Sec-WebSocket-Accept
    C->>S: text: subscribe:availability
    S-->>C: text: event 1
    C->>S: ping
    S-->>C: pong
    S-->>C: text: event 2
    S-->>C: close 4001 "token expired"
    C->>S: close 4001

A WebSocket server for tests

Network framework can terminate WebSockets itself: adding NWProtocolWebSocket.Options to a listener’s protocol stack makes it perform the handshake and deliver whole messages. The server below echoes text messages, records subscriptions per connection, and lets a test close or drop every connection. With autoReplyPing turned off, it simulates a peer that has vanished: the socket stays open, but nothing answers.

final class WebSocketServer: Sendable {
    private let listener: NWListener
    private let connections = Mutex<[NWConnection]>([])
    let subscriptions = Mutex<[String]>([])   // "connection#:topic", in arrival order
    private let accepted = Mutex(0)
    let port: Int

    init(answersPings: Bool = true) async throws {
        let websocket = NWProtocolWebSocket.Options()
        websocket.autoReplyPing = answersPings
        let parameters = NWParameters.tcp
        parameters.defaultProtocolStack.applicationProtocols.insert(websocket, at: 0)
        parameters.requiredLocalEndpoint = .hostPort(host: .ipv4(.loopback), port: .any)
        let listener = try NWListener(using: parameters)
        listener.newConnectionHandler = { _ in }
        port = try await withCheckedThrowingContinuation { continuation in
            let resumed = Mutex(false)
            listener.stateUpdateHandler = { state in
                guard case .ready = state, resumed.withLock({ done in defer { done = true }; return !done }) else { return }
                continuation.resume(returning: Int(listener.port!.rawValue))
            }
            listener.start(queue: .global())
        }
        self.listener = listener
        listener.newConnectionHandler = { [self] connection in accept(connection) }
    }

    var connectionCount: Int { accepted.withLock { $0 } }

    private func accept(_ connection: NWConnection) {
        let number = accepted.withLock { count in count += 1; return count }
        connections.withLock { $0.append(connection) }
        connection.start(queue: .global())
        receive(on: connection, number: number)
    }

    private func receive(on connection: NWConnection, number: Int) {
        connection.receiveMessage { [self] data, context, _, error in
            guard error == nil, let data else { return }
            let metadata = context?.protocolMetadata(definition: NWProtocolWebSocket.definition) as? NWProtocolWebSocket.Metadata
            if metadata?.opcode == .text {
                let text = String(decoding: data, as: UTF8.self)
                if text.hasPrefix("subscribe:") {
                    subscriptions.withLock { $0.append("\(number):\(text.dropFirst(10))") }
                }
                send("echo: \(text)", on: connection)
            }
            receive(on: connection, number: number)
        }
    }

    private func send(_ text: String, on connection: NWConnection) {
        let context = NWConnection.ContentContext(identifier: "text", metadata: [NWProtocolWebSocket.Metadata(opcode: .text)])
        connection.send(content: Data(text.utf8), contentContext: context, isComplete: true, completion: .contentProcessed { _ in })
    }

    func broadcast(_ text: String) {
        for connection in connections.withLock({ $0 }) { send(text, on: connection) }
    }

    /// Sends a close frame with the given code, then closes the socket.
    func closeAll(code: NWProtocolWebSocket.CloseCode) {
        for connection in connections.withLock({ $0 }) {
            let metadata = NWProtocolWebSocket.Metadata(opcode: .close)
            metadata.closeCode = code
            let context = NWConnection.ContentContext(identifier: "close", metadata: [metadata])
            connection.send(content: nil, contentContext: context, isComplete: true,
                            completion: .contentProcessed { _ in connection.cancel() })
        }
        connections.withLock { $0.removeAll() }
    }

    /// Resets every connection without a close frame, like a network failure.
    func dropAll() {
        for connection in connections.withLock({ $0 }) { connection.forceCancel() }
        connections.withLock { $0.removeAll() }
    }
}

Three ways a connection ends

With the server in place, each ending can be produced and observed:

let server = try await WebSocketServer()
let liveURL = URL(string: "ws://127.0.0.1:\(server.port)/live")!

// 1. A deliberate close frame with an application code.
let closing = URLSession.shared.webSocketTask(with: liveURL)
closing.resume()
try await closing.send(.string("hello"))
guard case .string(let echo) = try await closing.receive() else { fatalError() }
assert(echo == "echo: hello")
server.closeAll(code: .applicationCode(4001))
var closeError: (any Error)?
do { _ = try await closing.receive() } catch { closeError = error }
assert((closeError as NSError?)?.domain == NSPOSIXErrorDomain && (closeError as NSError?)?.code == 57)  // ENOTCONN
assert(closing.closeCode.rawValue == 4001)

// 2. An abrupt reset, as when a network path disappears.
let resetting = URLSession.shared.webSocketTask(with: liveURL)
resetting.resume()
try await resetting.send(.string("x"))
_ = try await resetting.receive()
server.dropAll()
var resetError: (any Error)?
do { _ = try await resetting.receive() } catch { resetError = error }
assert((resetError as NSError?)?.code == 54)            // ECONNRESET
assert(resetting.closeCode == .invalid)                  // no close frame was received

// 3. A peer that is gone but whose socket is still open.
let silentServer = try await WebSocketServer(answersPings: false)
let silent = URLSession.shared.webSocketTask(with: URL(string: "ws://127.0.0.1:\(silentServer.port)/live")!)
silent.resume()
try await silent.send(.string("y"))
_ = try await silent.receive()
let pongArrived = Mutex(false)
silent.sendPing { _ in pongArrived.withLock { $0 = true } }
try await Task.sleep(for: .seconds(2))
assert(!pongArrived.withLock { $0 })   // nothing happened, and nothing will
silent.cancel(with: .goingAway, reason: nil)
How the connection ended What the client observed (macOS 26)
Server sent close frame 4001 receive() threw POSIX 57, “Socket is not connected”; closeCode was 4001
Connection reset, no close frame receive() threw POSIX 54, “Connection reset by peer”; closeCode was .invalid
Peer silent, socket open No error, no event; the ping’s pong handler was never called

Two details matter for code that handles these. The errors are NSErrors in the POSIX domain, not URLErrors, so an error handler written for HTTP requests, which matches on URLError.Code, does not recognize them. The reliable signal for a deliberate close is closeCode and closeReason on the task, read after receive() throws.

The third row is the dangerous one. A phone that walks out of Wi-Fi range, a NAT gateway that silently forgets an idle mapping, or a server process that froze all produce a socket that neither delivers data nor reports an error. Without a heartbeat, the app shows “Live” over a connection that died minutes ago.

Detecting a dead peer: heartbeats

A heartbeat sends a ping every \(P\) seconds and treats a missing pong after \(T\) seconds as a dead connection. If the peer dies at a random moment, the next ping goes out within \(P\) seconds and its timeout fires \(T\) seconds later, so the time to detection \(D\) is bounded and, on average, about half an interval plus the timeout:

\[D \le P + T, \qquad \mathbb{E}[D] \approx \tfrac{P}{2} + T\]

The interval is a trade between detection time and cost. Each ping wakes the radio, and on cellular networks a radio that wakes every few seconds drains the battery noticeably. NAT and carrier-grade NAT gateways commonly drop idle mappings after somewhere between 30 seconds and a few minutes, so an interval under that limit also keeps the connection alive. For an app in the foreground, \(P = 25\) s and \(T = 10\) s gives detection within 35 seconds at about 144 pings per hour. The tests below use \(P = 0.5\) s and \(T = 0.5\) s so they run quickly.

sendPing takes a completion handler, which is never called if no pong arrives. The heartbeat wraps it in a continuation and races it against a timeout. When the timeout wins, it cancels the WebSocket task, which is what makes the pending pong handler finally run, with an error, so the continuation is resumed exactly once. Cancelling the task also makes any pending receive() fail, and that error can reach the caller before HeartbeatMissed does, so the heartbeat sets a flag first; the flag, not the error type, says why the connection ended:

struct HeartbeatMissed: Error {}

/// Records that a heartbeat failed, so the reason survives whichever child task reports its error first.
final class HeartbeatFlag: Sendable {
    private let missed = Mutex(false)
    func set() { missed.withLock { $0 = true } }
    var isSet: Bool { missed.withLock { $0 } }
}

func ping(_ task: URLSessionWebSocketTask, timeout: Duration, flag: HeartbeatFlag) async throws {
    try await withThrowingTaskGroup(of: Void.self) { group in
        group.addTask {
            try await withCheckedThrowingContinuation { (continuation: CheckedContinuation<Void, any Error>) in
                task.sendPing { error in
                    if let error { continuation.resume(throwing: error) } else { continuation.resume() }
                }
            }
        }
        group.addTask {
            try await Task.sleep(for: timeout)
            flag.set()
            task.cancel(with: .goingAway, reason: nil)  // unblocks the pending pong handler
            throw HeartbeatMissed()
        }
        defer { group.cancelAll() }
        _ = try await group.next()
    }
}

A connection manager with explicit states

Everything a live feature needs fits in one actor with a small state machine. The states are what the UI shows; the transitions are what the network does:

stateDiagram-v2
    accTitle: The states of a reconnecting WebSocket connection
    [*] --> Connecting
    Connecting --> Open: handshake done, subscriptions sent
    Open --> Waiting: error, close, or missed heartbeat
    Connecting --> Waiting: handshake failed
    Waiting --> Connecting: backoff elapsed
    Open --> Stopped: stop(), or close code that forbids reconnecting
    Waiting --> Stopped: stop()
    Stopped --> [*]

The manager publishes events through an AsyncStream. Each connection runs two child tasks, a receive loop and a heartbeat loop, in a task group: whichever fails first ends the connection, and the group cancels the other. Between connections it waits with the full-jitter backoff from Retry Policies, Backoff, and Idempotency, and the attempt counter resets after a connection succeeds, so a connection that worked for an hour reconnects quickly after a blip:

actor LiveConnection {
    enum Event: Sendable, Equatable {
        case open(attempt: Int)
        case message(String)
        case waiting(reason: String, retryIn: Duration)
        case stopped(reason: String)
    }

    let url: URL
    let topics: [String]
    let pingInterval: Duration
    let pingTimeout: Duration
    let backoffBase: Duration = .milliseconds(100)
    let backoffCap: Duration = .seconds(2)
    /// Close codes after which reconnecting cannot help without user action.
    let terminalCloseCodes: Set<Int> = [1008, 4003]

    private var runner: Task<Void, Never>?
    private var current: URLSessionWebSocketTask?

    init(url: URL, topics: [String], pingInterval: Duration, pingTimeout: Duration) {
        (self.url, self.topics, self.pingInterval, self.pingTimeout) = (url, topics, pingInterval, pingTimeout)
    }

    func start() -> AsyncStream<Event> {
        let (stream, continuation) = AsyncStream.makeStream(of: Event.self)
        runner = Task { await run(continuation) }
        return stream
    }

    func stop() {
        runner?.cancel()
        current?.cancel(with: .normalClosure, reason: nil)
    }

    func send(_ text: String) async throws {
        guard let current else { throw URLError(.networkConnectionLost) }
        try await current.send(.string(text))
    }

    private func run(_ events: AsyncStream<Event>.Continuation) async {
        var failures = 0
        while !Task.isCancelled {
            let task = URLSession.shared.webSocketTask(with: url)
            let heartbeat = HeartbeatFlag()
            current = task
            task.resume()
            var reason = "cancelled"
            do {
                for topic in topics { try await task.send(.string("subscribe:\(topic)")) }  // resubscribe every time
                events.yield(.open(attempt: failures + 1))
                failures = 0
                try await withThrowingTaskGroup(of: Void.self) { [pingInterval, pingTimeout] group in
                    group.addTask {
                        while true {
                            if case .string(let text) = try await task.receive() { events.yield(.message(text)) }
                        }
                    }
                    group.addTask {
                        while true {
                            try await Task.sleep(for: pingInterval)
                            try await ping(task, timeout: pingTimeout, flag: heartbeat)
                        }
                    }
                    defer { group.cancelAll() }
                    _ = try await group.next()
                }
            } catch {
                let code = task.closeCode.rawValue
                if heartbeat.isSet {
                    reason = "heartbeat missed"
                } else {
                    reason = code != 0 ? "closed \(code)" : "error \((error as NSError).domain) \((error as NSError).code)"
                }
            }
            task.cancel(with: .goingAway, reason: nil)
            current = nil
            if Task.isCancelled { break }
            if terminalCloseCodes.contains(task.closeCode.rawValue) {
                events.yield(.stopped(reason: reason))
                events.finish()
                return
            }
            failures += 1
            let ceiling = min(backoffCap, backoffBase * (1 << min(failures - 1, 16)))
            let milliseconds = Int(ceiling.components.seconds * 1000 + ceiling.components.attoseconds / 1_000_000_000_000_000)
            let delay = Duration.milliseconds(Int.random(in: 0...milliseconds))
            events.yield(.waiting(reason: reason, retryIn: delay))
            try? await Task.sleep(for: delay)
        }
        events.yield(.stopped(reason: "stopped"))
        events.finish()
    }
}

The decisions in that code, each of which is a common bug when missing:

  • Resubscribe on every connection. Subscriptions are server-side state attached to a connection, and a new connection starts with none. A client that subscribes once at startup receives nothing after its first reconnect.
  • Distinguish terminal closes. A close code that means “forbidden” or “policy violation” will be repeated on every attempt; reconnecting in a loop only hammers the server. Code 4001, “token expired” in this example’s protocol, is not terminal: the right response is to refresh the token, as in Refreshing Credentials Without Duplicate Requests, and reconnect.
  • Report the reason. The waiting event carries why the connection ended, which is what makes “Reconnecting… (connection reset)” possible in the UI and in logs.

Reconnection, measured

The first test resets the server’s connections twice while a client is subscribed to two topics. The client must reconnect each time and resubscribe on each new connection:

/// Collects a connection's events and waits for particular ones.
actor EventRecorder {
    private var iterator: AsyncStream<LiveConnection.Event>.Iterator
    private(set) var log: [LiveConnection.Event] = []
    init(_ stream: AsyncStream<LiveConnection.Event>) { iterator = stream.makeAsyncIterator() }

    func next(where matches: @Sendable (LiveConnection.Event) -> Bool) async -> LiveConnection.Event {
        var events = iterator  // a mutating async call cannot be made on actor-isolated storage directly
        defer { iterator = events }
        while let event = await events.next(isolation: self) {
            log.append(event)
            if matches(event) { return event }
        }
        fatalError("stream ended")
    }
}

@Sendable func isOpen(_ event: LiveConnection.Event) -> Bool { if case .open = event { true } else { false } }

let feed = try await WebSocketServer()
let connection = LiveConnection(url: URL(string: "ws://127.0.0.1:\(feed.port)/live")!,
                                topics: ["availability", "loans"],
                                pingInterval: .milliseconds(500), pingTimeout: .milliseconds(500))
let recorder = EventRecorder(await connection.start())

_ = await recorder.next(where: isOpen)
feed.broadcast("event:1")
_ = await recorder.next { $0 == .message("event:1") }

for _ in 0..<2 {
    feed.dropAll()
    _ = await recorder.next(where: isOpen)
}
try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(100))
feed.broadcast("event:2")
_ = await recorder.next { $0 == .message("event:2") }

assert(feed.connectionCount == 3)
assert(feed.subscriptions.withLock { $0 } == ["1:availability", "1:loans", "2:availability", "2:loans", "3:availability", "3:loans"])
let waits = await recorder.log.compactMap { event -> String? in if case .waiting(let reason, _) = event { reason } else { nil } }
assert(waits == ["error NSPOSIXErrorDomain 54", "error NSPOSIXErrorDomain 54"])

Three connections, each with both subscriptions, and the second broadcast arrived after two resets. The two waiting events name the reset that caused them, POSIX error 54, as in the table above.

The second test points a client at a server that stops answering pings after the handshake. The heartbeat must detect it within \(P + T\), one second here:

let frozen = try await WebSocketServer(answersPings: false)
let frozenConnection = LiveConnection(url: URL(string: "ws://127.0.0.1:\(frozen.port)/live")!, topics: ["availability"],
                                      pingInterval: .milliseconds(500), pingTimeout: .milliseconds(500))
let frozenRecorder = EventRecorder(await frozenConnection.start())
_ = await frozenRecorder.next(where: isOpen)
let openedAt = ContinuousClock.now
guard case .waiting(let reason, _) = await frozenRecorder.next(where: { if case .waiting = $0 { true } else { false } }) else {
    fatalError()
}
let detection = ContinuousClock.now - openedAt
print("dead peer detected after \(detection): \(reason)")
assert(reason == "heartbeat missed")
assert(detection < .milliseconds(1_300))   // within P + T, plus scheduling
await frozenConnection.stop()

The dead peer was detected about one second after the connection opened: a 500 ms interval to the first ping, then 500 ms without a pong. Without the heartbeat the client would have stayed “open” indefinitely.

The last test closes the connection with code 4003, which the manager treats as terminal:

feed.closeAll(code: .applicationCode(4003))
let final = await recorder.next { if case .stopped = $0 { true } else { false } }
assert(final == .stopped(reason: "closed 4003"))
assert(feed.connectionCount == 3)   // no reconnection attempt

What reconnection does not fix

A reconnected socket is a new conversation. Messages the server sent while the client was disconnected are gone, unless the protocol says otherwise. Two designs handle the gap:

  • Resume from a position. Every server message carries a sequence number or event ID, the client sends the last one it processed when it resubscribes, and the server replays what it missed. Server-Sent Events build this in with Last-Event-ID; WebSocket protocols have to add it themselves.
  • Refetch the state. After reconnecting, the client fetches the current state of what it displays over plain HTTP, and applies live messages on top. Combined with the version-based merge from Coalescing Duplicate Requests and Rejecting Stale Results, late or duplicate messages cannot move the state backwards.

Outgoing messages need the same thought. send(_:) above throws when there is no connection, which is honest. Queueing them for later is right only for messages that are still meaningful later, and then they need the idempotency and outbox treatment of Offline Behavior and Reachability Assumptions.

Finally, on iOS a WebSocket does not survive the app being suspended. Close it when the app moves to the background, and reconnect, then refetch, when it returns. For updates while the app is not running, push notifications are the mechanism, not a socket.

Summary

  • A WebSocket begins as an HTTP GET with Upgrade: websocket; the server answers 101 with Sec-WebSocket-Accept, \(\operatorname{base64}(\operatorname{SHA1}(\text{key} \| \text{GUID}))\). A non-101 answer fails with badServerResponse.
  • Measured endings: a close frame gives POSIX 57 from receive() and the code in closeCode; a reset gives POSIX 54 and closeCode == .invalid; a silent peer gives nothing at all. These are not URLErrors.
  • Heartbeats bound detection of dead peers: \(D \le P + T\). Cancel the task on timeout, so the pending pong handler runs and the continuation resumes once. Measured: detection in about one second with \(P = T = 0.5\) s.
  • Model the connection as explicit states, reconnect with full-jitter backoff that resets after success, resubscribe on every connection, and stop on terminal close codes.
  • Reconnection loses messages: resume from a sequence number or refetch state over HTTP, and merge by version.

Exercise

Add sequence numbers to WebSocketServer.broadcast and a resume:<n> message that makes the server replay every broadcast after n from an in-memory log. Extend LiveConnection to remember the last sequence number it delivered and send resume: after resubscribing. Test it by broadcasting ten events, dropping the connection after the fourth, broadcasting the rest while the client waits to reconnect, and asserting that the client delivers all ten exactly once and in order.

Further reading

  • RFC 6455: The WebSocket Protocol and RFC 8441, which carries WebSockets over HTTP/2.
  • Apple’s URLSessionWebSocketTask and NWProtocolWebSocket documentation.
  • Advances in Networking, Part 1, WWDC19, which introduced URLSessionWebSocketTask.

It is a long-lived, two-way channel that is open until something closes it: the server deliberately, the network accidentally, or nothing at all, when the other end has silently disappeared and the socket looks healthy forever. A live feature built on a WebSocket, such as chat, a shared reading list, or a “books available now” ticker, is only as good as the client’s answer to one question: what state is the connection in right now, and what does it do about it? This article starts from the protocol: the upgrade handshake that turns an HTTP request into a WebSocket, and the frames that follow. It then measures the three ways a URLSessionWebSocketTask connection ends, against a WebSocket server built with Network framework, including the one that produces no error at all. Finally it builds a connection manager with an explicit state machine, heartbeats that detect dead peers within a bounded time, jittered reconnection, and resubscription after every reconnect.

entry.title: Background Transfers and App Relaunch
entry.content:
An iOS app gets a few seconds of execution after the user leaves it, and then it is suspended. A 600 MB podcast download or a batch of photo uploads does not fit in a few seconds. For that, URLSession offers background sessions: the app hands transfers to a system daemon, nsurlsessiond, which performs them whether the app is running, suspended, or terminated, and wakes the app when they finish.

The price is a different programming model. A background session accepts only some kinds of tasks, reports results only through a delegate, outlives the process that created it, and delivers events to a process that may not have existed when the transfer started. This article measures those rules on macOS, where a command-line tool can use background sessions too, including a transfer that keeps going after its process exits and is picked up by a new one. It then covers the app side on iOS: relaunch, the completion handler, mapping tasks back to app state, and the scheduling decisions the system makes on the user’s behalf.

The examples use Swift 6 language mode and were compiled with the Swift 6.4 toolchain from Xcode 27.1. The in-process examples ran on macOS 26 against LocalServer, the loopback HTTP server from the appendix of the first article; paste that code first, then the unmarked blocks below in order, into one main.swift. The relaunch experiment uses two processes and is run from the shell as shown. The iOS app code was compiled against the iOS 26 SDK.

Who owns a background transfer

In an ordinary session, the app’s process performs the transfer: its sockets, its memory, its lifetime. In a background session, the app’s process only describes the transfer. The daemon performs it and keeps the results until the app collects them:

sequenceDiagram
    accTitle: A background download that completes while the app is suspended, followed by relaunch
    participant App
    participant Daemon as nsurlsessiond
    participant Server
    App->>Daemon: downloadTask(with:).resume() on background session "downloads"
    App->>App: user leaves, app suspended, later terminated
    Daemon->>Server: GET /episodes/412.mp3
    Server-->>Daemon: 200, body (minutes)
    Daemon->>App: relaunch in background
    App->>App: application(_:handleEventsForBackgroundURLSession:completionHandler:) stores handler
    App->>Daemon: URLSession(configuration: .background("downloads"), delegate:)
    Daemon-->>App: didFinishDownloadingTo, didCompleteWithError
    Daemon-->>App: urlSessionDidFinishEvents(forBackgroundURLSession:)
    App->>App: call stored completion handler: system may suspend the app again

Everything in the model follows from that split. The daemon cannot call a closure in a process that no longer exists, so results go to a delegate that the next process provides. It cannot read a Data value that lived in the app’s memory, so uploads must come from files. And the session is identified by a string the app chooses, because that string is the only thing a relaunched process can use to say “I am the owner of those transfers.”

What a background session accepts

Background sessions are available to command-line tools on macOS, which makes their rules easy to measure. A session is created with an identifier and a delegate. A download from the local server completes through the delegate, and its temporary file is in the daemon’s directory, not the process’s:

import Foundation
import Synchronization

final class BackgroundDelegate: NSObject, URLSessionDownloadDelegate, URLSessionDataDelegate, Sendable {
    let events = Mutex<[String]>([])
    let finished = Mutex<CheckedContinuation<Void, Never>?>(nil)
    let completedTasks = Mutex(0)
    let expectedTasks: Int

    init(expecting count: Int) { expectedTasks = count }

    func urlSession(_ session: URLSession, downloadTask: URLSessionDownloadTask, didFinishDownloadingTo location: URL) {
        let size = (try? FileManager.default.attributesOfItem(atPath: location.path)[.size] as? Int) ?? -1
        events.withLock { $0.append("downloaded \(downloadTask.taskDescription ?? "?") \(size) bytes at \(location.path)") }
    }

    func urlSession(_ session: URLSession, dataTask: URLSessionDataTask, didReceive data: Data) {
        events.withLock { $0.append("received \(dataTask.taskDescription ?? "?") \(data.count) bytes") }
    }

    func urlSession(_ session: URLSession, task: URLSessionTask, didCompleteWithError error: (any Error)?) {
        events.withLock { $0.append("completed \(task.taskDescription ?? "?") \(error.map { "\($0)" } ?? "ok")") }
        let done = completedTasks.withLock { count in count += 1; return count == expectedTasks }
        if done { finished.withLock { $0?.resume(); $0 = nil } }
    }
}

let server = try await LocalServer.start { request in
    .text("\(request.method) \(request.path) \(request.body.count) bytes")
}

let configuration = URLSessionConfiguration.background(withIdentifier: "com.example.library.transfers")
configuration.sessionSendsLaunchEvents = true
let delegate = BackgroundDelegate(expecting: 3)
let background = URLSession(configuration: configuration, delegate: delegate, delegateQueue: nil)

let uploadFile = FileManager.default.temporaryDirectory.appending(path: "upload-\(UUID().uuidString).bin")
try Data(repeating: 1, count: 1_000).write(to: uploadFile)
var uploadRequest = URLRequest(url: server.baseURL.appending(path: "uploads"))
uploadRequest.httpMethod = "POST"

await withCheckedContinuation { continuation in
    delegate.finished.withLock { $0 = continuation }
    let download = background.downloadTask(with: server.baseURL.appending(path: "episodes/412"))
    download.taskDescription = "episode-412"
    download.resume()
    let upload = background.uploadTask(with: uploadRequest, fromFile: uploadFile)
    upload.taskDescription = "photo-upload-7"
    upload.resume()
    let data = background.dataTask(with: server.baseURL.appending(path: "status"))
    data.taskDescription = "status-check"
    data.resume()
}

let events = delegate.events.withLock { $0 }
events.forEach { print($0) }
assert(events.contains { $0.hasPrefix("downloaded episode-412") && $0.contains("com.apple.nsurlsessiond/Downloads") })
assert(events.contains("received photo-upload-7 24 bytes") && events.contains("completed photo-upload-7 ok"))  // "POST /uploads 1000 bytes"
assert(events.contains("completed status-check ok"))
assert(server.requests.contains { $0.method == "POST" && $0.body.count == 1_000 })
try FileManager.default.removeItem(at: uploadFile)

The download’s temporary file was in ~/Library/Caches/com.apple.nsurlsessiond/Downloads/<process name>/, owned by the daemon. The upload from a file and the data task both completed while the process was running. Two other calls, which work on ordinary sessions, are not allowed. Each terminates the process with an Objective-C exception that Swift cannot catch, so they are shown here rather than run:

// Each of these crashed the test process on macOS 26 with NSGenericException:

_ = try await background.download(from: url)
// "Completion handler blocks are not supported in background sessions. Use a delegate instead."

background.uploadTask(with: request, from: Data(repeating: 1, count: 1_000)).resume()
// "Upload tasks from NSData are not supported in background sessions."
On a background session Allowed Notes
downloadTask(with:), downloadTask(withResumeData:) Yes Continue while the app is suspended or terminated
uploadTask(with:fromFile:) Yes The daemon reads the file; it must stay in place until the upload completes
uploadTask(with:from: Data), stream bodies Crash The daemon cannot read the app’s memory
dataTask(with:) Only while the app runs Not continued while the app is suspended
Any async method, or completion-handler task Crash Results are delivered only to the session delegate

The async restriction is the one most likely to surprise a Swift 6 codebase, where every other networking call is an await. The delegate is not optional plumbing here: it is the only channel through which results can reach a process that did not exist when the transfer started.

A transfer that outlives its process

The decisive property is that the transfer continues when the process that started it is gone. The tool below takes a mode argument. In start mode it begins a download of a 2 MB file, from a server that sends 50 KB every 250 ms, waits two seconds, and exits. In resume mode, run afterwards as a new process, it creates a session with the same identifier, lists the tasks the daemon still holds for it, and waits for their events:

// bgtool.swift — compile with: swiftc -swift-version 6 bgtool.swift -o bgtool
import Foundation
import Synchronization

final class Relaunched: NSObject, URLSessionDownloadDelegate, Sendable {
    let done = Mutex<CheckedContinuation<Void, Never>?>(nil)
    func urlSession(_ session: URLSession, downloadTask: URLSessionDownloadTask, didFinishDownloadingTo location: URL) {
        let size = (try? FileManager.default.attributesOfItem(atPath: location.path)[.size] as? Int) ?? -1
        print("finished", downloadTask.taskIdentifier, downloadTask.taskDescription ?? "-", size)
    }
    func urlSession(_ session: URLSession, task: URLSessionTask, didCompleteWithError error: (any Error)?) {
        print("complete", task.taskIdentifier, error.map { "\($0)" } ?? "nil")
        done.withLock { $0?.resume(); $0 = nil }
    }
}

let configuration = URLSessionConfiguration.background(withIdentifier: "com.example.library.relaunch")
let delegate = Relaunched()
let session = URLSession(configuration: configuration, delegate: delegate, delegateQueue: nil)

if CommandLine.arguments[1] == "start" {
    let task = session.downloadTask(with: URL(string: "http://127.0.0.1:8765/audiobook")!)
    task.taskDescription = "audiobook-42"
    task.resume()
    try await Task.sleep(for: .seconds(2))
    print("start process exiting")
    exit(0)
} else {
    let tasks = await session.allTasks
    print("relaunch sees:", tasks.map { "\($0.taskIdentifier) \($0.taskDescription ?? "-") received=\($0.countOfBytesReceived)" })
    await withCheckedContinuation { continuation in delegate.done.withLock { $0 = continuation } }
}

The server is a slow Python script on port 8765, so that it outlives both Swift processes. Running the two modes one after the other:

$ ./bgtool start
start process exiting
$ ./bgtool resume
relaunch sees: ["1 audiobook-42 received=650000"]
finished 1 audiobook-42 2000000
complete 1 nil

The first process exited after receiving about 400 KB. When the second one connected a second later, the daemon had kept downloading and held 650 KB; the task kept its identifier and its taskDescription. The second process then received the finished 2 MB file through its own delegate, and the server’s log showed a single request with no Range header: the transfer was never interrupted, only its owner was replaced.

On iOS the same thing happens without anyone running the second process: the system launches the app in the background when the daemon has events for it.

The app side on iOS

When a background session’s tasks finish while the app is not running, and the configuration’s sessionSendsLaunchEvents is true (the default), the system launches the app in the background and calls the app delegate with the session’s identifier and a completion handler. The app must recreate the session with that identifier, let the delegate process the events, and call the completion handler when they are done, which tells the system it may suspend the app again and update its snapshot. A SwiftUI app receives the same event through the backgroundTask(.urlSession(_:)) scene modifier.

The pieces, compiled against the iOS 26 SDK:

import SwiftUI
import UIKit

final class TransferService: NSObject, URLSessionDownloadDelegate, @unchecked Sendable {
    static let shared = TransferService()
    static let identifier = "com.example.library.downloads"

    // Set by the app delegate when the system relaunches the app for this session.
    @MainActor var pendingCompletionHandler: (() -> Void)?

    // Created eagerly at launch, so events for tasks started in a previous process are delivered.
    lazy var session: URLSession = {
        let configuration = URLSessionConfiguration.background(withIdentifier: Self.identifier)
        configuration.isDiscretionary = false            // user-initiated: start as soon as possible
        configuration.sessionSendsLaunchEvents = true
        return URLSession(configuration: configuration, delegate: self, delegateQueue: nil)
    }()

    func download(episode: Int, from url: URL) {
        let task = session.downloadTask(with: url)
        task.taskDescription = "episode-\(episode)"      // the key back into the app's own records
        task.countOfBytesClientExpectsToReceive = 600_000_000
        task.resume()
    }

    func urlSession(_ session: URLSession, downloadTask: URLSessionDownloadTask, didFinishDownloadingTo location: URL) {
        guard let episode = downloadTask.taskDescription,
              (downloadTask.response as? HTTPURLResponse)?.statusCode == 200 else { return }
        let destination = URL.applicationSupportDirectory.appending(path: "\(episode).mp3")
        try? FileManager.default.removeItem(at: destination)
        try? FileManager.default.moveItem(at: location, to: destination)  // before returning
        // Record completion in the app's database, keyed by `episode`.
    }

    func urlSession(_ session: URLSession, task: URLSessionTask, didCompleteWithError error: (any Error)?) {
        if let error = error as? URLError, let resumeData = error.downloadTaskResumeData {
            // Persist resumeData with the episode record, and retry later with downloadTask(withResumeData:).
            _ = resumeData
        }
    }

    func urlSessionDidFinishEvents(forBackgroundURLSession session: URLSession) {
        Task { @MainActor in
            pendingCompletionHandler?()
            pendingCompletionHandler = nil
        }
    }
}

final class AppDelegate: NSObject, UIApplicationDelegate {
    func application(_ application: UIApplication, didFinishLaunchingWithOptions launchOptions: [UIApplication.LaunchOptionsKey: Any]? = nil) -> Bool {
        _ = TransferService.shared.session   // reconnect to the daemon on every launch
        return true
    }

    func application(_ application: UIApplication, handleEventsForBackgroundURLSession identifier: String,
                     completionHandler: @escaping () -> Void) {
        guard identifier == TransferService.identifier else { return completionHandler() }
        TransferService.shared.pendingCompletionHandler = completionHandler
        _ = TransferService.shared.session
    }
}

@main
struct LibraryApp: App {
    @UIApplicationDelegateAdaptor(AppDelegate.self) var appDelegate
    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup { Text("Library") }
    }
}

The rules embedded in that code, in the order they matter:

  1. Recreate the session at every launch, not only in the relaunch callback. A user who opens the app while transfers are pending needs the delegate connected, or the events wait.
  2. One session object per identifier per process. Creating a second session with an identifier that is already in use is an error that the system logs and that leaves the second session unable to receive events. A singleton owning the session is the simplest way to guarantee it.
  3. Map tasks back to app state through stable data. taskDescription survived the process change in the measurement above, and so did taskIdentifier, but the identifier is meaningful only within that session. A string such as episode-412, or a UUID stored in the app’s database, connects a delegate callback to the record it belongs to.
  4. Move the file before didFinishDownloadingTo returns, exactly as in Download Progress, Resuming, and Temporary Files. In a background relaunch, the app has only a short time to do so.
  5. Call the completion handler on the main thread after urlSessionDidFinishEvents(forBackgroundURLSession:). Not calling it costs the app background execution time, and the system takes that into account the next time.

The system decides when

Background transfers are scheduled by the system with the battery, the network, and the user’s habits in mind. The app influences that scheduling but does not control it:

Setting Effect
isDiscretionary = true The system may wait for Wi-Fi and power. Transfers started while the app is in the background are treated as discretionary regardless.
earliestBeginDate on a task The transfer will not start before this date, useful for scheduled prefetching.
countOfBytesClientExpectsToSend / ToReceive Size estimates the scheduler uses to pick a good moment.
allowsExpensiveNetworkAccess, allowsConstrainedNetworkAccess As for ordinary sessions; respect Low Data Mode for optional content.
timeoutIntervalForResource How long the system keeps trying; the default is one week.

Two consequences shape the product. First, a background download is not a fast download: it is a reliable one. A user waiting for an episode to start playing should get an ordinary session, or isDiscretionary = false with the transfer started while the app is in the foreground. Second, the system throttles how often an app is relaunched for background session events, so an app that queues hundreds of small transfers, each producing its own completion event, will see them delayed. Batch small items into fewer, larger transfers.

And one rule overrides everything: if the user force-quits the app from the app switcher, the system cancels its background transfers and does not relaunch it for them. The next time the app starts, those tasks complete with an error, which is another reason to keep resume data and the app’s own record of what was in progress.

Testing background transfers

Background behavior is hard to exercise from unit tests, but each part can be checked:

  • Delegate logic runs the same in an ordinary session. Test it with LocalServer or a URLProtocol stub (Isolating HTTP Fixtures with URLProtocol); note that custom protocol classes are not supported in background sessions, so the stub must use an ordinary configuration.
  • The process boundary can be tested on macOS exactly as the bgtool experiment does: start, exit, reattach.
  • Relaunch on iOS is tested on a device: start a transfer, background the app, and stop it from Xcode’s debugger with “Debug › Detach”, or terminate it with a memory warning simulation rather than a force-quit, which would cancel the transfer. Xcode can then attach to the app when the system relaunches it.

Summary

  • Background sessions hand transfers to nsurlsessiond, which continues them while the app is suspended or terminated and relaunches the app with the results.
  • Measured on macOS 26: downloads, file uploads, and (while running) data tasks work; async methods and uploads from Data crash with uncatchable exceptions. Use a delegate and files.
  • Measured: a download continued after its process exited, and a new process with the same session identifier saw the task, its taskDescription, and 650 KB already received, then received the complete file.
  • On iOS, recreate the session at every launch, store the completion handler from handleEventsForBackgroundURLSession, and call it after urlSessionDidFinishEvents.
  • Map tasks to app records with taskDescription, move files before the delegate method returns, and keep resume data for failures.
  • The system schedules background transfers for reliability, not speed, throttles relaunches, and cancels everything on force-quit.

Exercise

Extend bgtool with an upload mode that uploads a 5 MB file to the Python server, and a status mode that prints countOfBytesSent for every pending task. Start an upload, exit, run status twice a second apart, and confirm the counter advances while no process of yours is running. Then delete the source file while the upload is in progress and record what error the next process receives, and decide how an app should present that to a user who removed the photo they were uploading.

Further reading

  • Apple’s Downloading files in the background and application(_:handleEventsForBackgroundURLSession:completionHandler:).
  • Advances in App Background Execution, WWDC19, on how the system schedules background work, including background URL sessions.
  • Build robust and resumable file transfers, WWDC23.

Previous: Download Progress, Resuming, and Temporary Files. Next: WebSockets: Connection State and Reconnection.
