entry.title: Download Progress, Resuming, and Temporary Files

link.title: Download Progress, Resuming, and Temporary Files

entry.content:
A large download has three needs that a small request does not. The user wants to see it progress. It must survive interruption, because a 400 MB audiobook over cellular will lose its connection at some point, and starting again from zero each time means it may never finish. And its result is a file, which lives somewhere with rules about how long it stays there.

HTTP makes resuming possible with range requests: a client that has the first 300 MB asks for the rest, and a server that still has the same version of the file sends only the rest. URLSession wraps this in resume data. This article implements range support on the test server, measures exactly when URLSession can produce resume data and what it sends when it resumes, including two behaviors of the async download API that decide which API to use, and ends with progress reporting and an ETA estimate that does not jump around.

The examples use Swift 6 language mode and were compiled and run with the Swift 6.4 toolchain from Xcode 27.1 on macOS 26. They send requests to LocalServer, the loopback HTTP server from the appendix of the first article; paste that code first, then the blocks below in order, into one main.swift.

Range requests

RFC 9110 §14 defines the mechanism. A client sends Range: bytes=500000- to ask for everything from byte 500,000. A server that supports it answers 206 Partial Content with a Content-Range header saying which bytes the body contains. A server that does not, or that chooses not to, answers 200 with the whole representation, which the client must then use from the start.

Resuming safely needs one more piece: the client must know the bytes it already has belong to the same version of the file. Otherwise it would splice the first half of version 1 onto the second half of version 2. The If-Range header carries a validator, an ETag or a Last-Modified date, and means “send me the range if the representation still matches this; otherwise send me the whole new one”:

sequenceDiagram
    accTitle: Resuming a download with a range request guarded by If-Range
    participant C as URLSession
    participant S as Server
    C->>S: GET /audiobook
    S-->>C: 200, ETag "v1", Content-Length 2000000 (connection lost at 500000)
    C->>S: GET /audiobook, Range: bytes=500000-, If-Range: "v1"
    alt ETag still "v1"
        S-->>C: 206, Content-Range: bytes 500000-1999999/2000000
    else file changed to "v2"
        S-->>C: 200, ETag "v2", full body (client discards the partial file)
    end

The test server implements exactly that. It serves 2 MB in 100 KB pieces with a 20 ms pause between them, so a download takes about 400 ms and can be interrupted. A flag makes it cut the connection at a chosen byte, and query parameters remove its validator or its range support:

import Foundation
import Synchronization

let content = Data((0..<2_000_000).map { UInt8(truncatingIfNeeded: $0 &* 13) })
let currentETag = Mutex(#""v1""#)
let cutAt = Mutex<Int?>(nil)

let server = try await LocalServer.start { request in
    let etag = currentETag.withLock { $0 }
    let sendsValidator = request.query["novalidator"] == nil
    var start = 0
    var status = 200
    if let range = request.header("Range"), range.hasPrefix("bytes="), request.query["norange"] == nil {
        let ifRange = request.header("If-Range")
        if ifRange == nil || ifRange == etag {           // If-Range mismatch: send the whole new version
            start = Int(range.dropFirst(6).split(separator: "-").first ?? "0") ?? 0
            status = 206
        }
    }
    var headers: [(name: String, value: String)] = [("Content-Type", "application/octet-stream"),
                                                    ("Content-Length", "\(content.count - start)")]
    if sendsValidator { headers.append(("ETag", etag)) }
    if status == 206 { headers.append(("Content-Range", "bytes \(start)-\(content.count - 1)/\(content.count)")) }

    var pieces: [HTTPResponse.Piece] = []
    let limit = cutAt.withLock { cut in defer { cut = nil }; return cut }
    var offset = start
    while offset < content.count {
        let end = min(offset + 100_000, content.count)
        if let limit, end > limit {
            pieces += [.bytes(content[offset..<limit]), .close]   // the connection dies mid-body
            break
        }
        pieces += [.bytes(content[offset..<end]), .pause(.milliseconds(20))]
        offset = end
    }
    return HTTPResponse(status: status, headers: headers, body: pieces)
}

A delegate-based downloader

URLSession has an async download API, and it is the right choice for small files. For large ones, the measurements later in this article show it lacks two things: it delivers no progress to a per-task delegate, and cancelling it produces no resume data. The full feature set is on URLSessionDownloadTask with a session delegate. The downloader below wraps one download at a time in async methods, so the rest of the code can still await it:

final class Downloader: NSObject, URLSessionDownloadDelegate, Sendable {
    struct Progress: Sendable { let written: Int64; let expected: Int64; let at: ContinuousClock.Instant }

    private let state = Mutex<(continuation: CheckedContinuation<URL, any Error>?, task: URLSessionDownloadTask?)>((nil, nil))
    let progress = Mutex<[Progress]>([])
    let resumedAt = Mutex<[Int64]>([])
    let lastTemporaryLocation = Mutex<URL?>(nil)
    let destinationDirectory: URL
    nonisolated(unsafe) private(set) var session: URLSession!  // assigned once, in init

    init(destination: URL) {
        destinationDirectory = destination
        super.init()
        session = URLSession(configuration: .ephemeral, delegate: self, delegateQueue: nil)
    }

    func download(_ url: URL) async throws -> URL { try await run(session.downloadTask(with: url)) }
    func resume(from data: Data) async throws -> URL { try await run(session.downloadTask(withResumeData: data)) }

    /// Cancels the current download and returns resume data if the server allows resuming.
    func pause() async -> Data? {
        guard let task = state.withLock({ $0.task }) else { return nil }
        return await task.cancelByProducingResumeData()
    }

    private func run(_ task: URLSessionDownloadTask) async throws -> URL {
        try await withCheckedThrowingContinuation { continuation in
            state.withLock { $0 = (continuation, task) }
            task.resume()
        }
    }

    private func finish(_ result: Result<URL, any Error>) {
        state.withLock { state in
            state.continuation?.resume(with: result)
            state = (nil, nil)
        }
    }

    // MARK: URLSessionDownloadDelegate

    func urlSession(_ session: URLSession, downloadTask: URLSessionDownloadTask, didFinishDownloadingTo location: URL) {
        lastTemporaryLocation.withLock { $0 = location }
        let status = (downloadTask.response as? HTTPURLResponse)?.statusCode ?? 0
        guard (200..<300).contains(status) else { return finish(.failure(URLError(.badServerResponse))) }
        do {
            let destination = destinationDirectory.appending(path: UUID().uuidString)
            try FileManager.default.moveItem(at: location, to: destination)  // must happen before returning
            finish(.success(destination))
        } catch {
            finish(.failure(error))
        }
    }

    func urlSession(_ session: URLSession, downloadTask: URLSessionDownloadTask, didWriteData bytesWritten: Int64,
                    totalBytesWritten: Int64, totalBytesExpectedToWrite: Int64) {
        progress.withLock { $0.append(Progress(written: totalBytesWritten, expected: totalBytesExpectedToWrite, at: .now)) }
    }

    func urlSession(_ session: URLSession, downloadTask: URLSessionDownloadTask, didResumeAtOffset fileOffset: Int64,
                    expectedTotalBytes: Int64) {
        resumedAt.withLock { $0.append(fileOffset) }
    }

    func urlSession(_ session: URLSession, task: URLSessionTask, didCompleteWithError error: (any Error)?) {
        if let error { finish(.failure(error)) }
    }
}

The move in didFinishDownloadingTo is the most important line. The documentation says the file at location is removed when that delegate method returns, so the file must be moved, or opened, before then. The test below checks that it really is gone afterwards.

Pausing and resuming

The first test downloads for 150 ms, pauses with cancelByProducingResumeData(), and resumes. The server records what the resumed request asked for:

let downloads = FileManager.default.temporaryDirectory.appending(path: "downloads-\(UUID().uuidString)")
try FileManager.default.createDirectory(at: downloads, withIntermediateDirectories: true)
let downloader = Downloader(destination: downloads)
let fileURL = server.baseURL.appending(path: "audiobook")

async let firstAttempt = downloader.download(fileURL)
try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(150))
let resumeData = await downloader.pause()
do {
    _ = try await firstAttempt
    assertionFailure("the download was paused")
} catch let error as URLError {
    assert(error.code == .cancelled)
}
assert(resumeData != nil)
print("resume data: \(resumeData!.count) bytes")

let beforeResume = server.requests.count
let completed = try await downloader.resume(from: resumeData!)
let resumeRequest = server.requests[beforeResume]
assert(resumeRequest.header("Range")?.hasPrefix("bytes=") == true && resumeRequest.header("Range") != "bytes=0-")
assert(resumeRequest.header("If-Range") == #""v1""#)
assert((try? Data(contentsOf: completed)) == content)
let offsets = downloader.resumedAt.withLock { $0 }
assert(offsets.count == 1 && offsets[0] > 0 && offsets[0] < 2_000_000)
print("resumed with \(resumeRequest.header("Range")!) at offset \(offsets[0])")

let temporary = downloader.lastTemporaryLocation.withLock { $0 }!
assert(!FileManager.default.fileExists(atPath: temporary.path))  // moved away before the method returned

In this run the resume data was 7,325 bytes, and the resumed request carried Range: bytes=581660- and If-Range: "v1": the session had received 581,660 bytes before the pause, kept them in its temporary file, and asked only for the remaining 1.4 MB. The offset is not a multiple of the server’s 100 KB pieces, because TCP delivers bytes in whatever segments the network produces. The delegate’s didResumeAtOffset reported the same offset, and the assembled file matched the original byte for byte.

Resume data is an opaque blob. It is a property list that records, among other things, the URL, the validator, the byte count, and the path of the partial temporary file, but its format is private and has changed between OS versions. Store it as Data, do not parse it, and be prepared for it to stop working: if the system has purged the temporary file, resuming fails and the download must start again.

When resume data exists

Resume data is a promise that the session can continue safely, so it is produced only when continuing can be made safe. Varying the server’s behavior shows which conditions matter:

func pausedResumeData(_ url: URL) async -> Data? {
    async let attempt = downloader.download(url)
    try? await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(150))
    let data = await downloader.pause()
    _ = try? await attempt
    return data
}

let withoutValidator = await pausedResumeData(URL(string: fileURL.absoluteString + "?novalidator=1")!)
assert(withoutValidator == nil)          // no ETag or Last-Modified: nothing to check a resume against

cutAt.withLock { $0 = 700_000 }
var droppedResumeData: Data?
do {
    _ = try await downloader.download(fileURL)
    assertionFailure("the connection was cut")
} catch let error as URLError {
    assert(error.code == .networkConnectionLost)
    droppedResumeData = error.downloadTaskResumeData   // resume data arrives inside the error
}
assert(droppedResumeData != nil)
Situation Resume data Resumed request
Paused with cancelByProducingResumeData(), ETag present Yes, about 7 KB Range: bytes=N-, If-Range with the ETag
Paused, no ETag or Last-Modified nil (must restart)
Paused, server does not send Accept-Ranges Yes Same as the first row; Accept-Ranges is not required
Connection lost mid-body In URLError.downloadTaskResumeData Same as the first row
Plain cancel() None (must restart)

The validator is the requirement. Without one, the session cannot ask the server whether its partial bytes are still the right ones, so it refuses to offer a resume. That puts the decision on the server: any endpoint that serves large files should send an ETag, which costs nothing and enables both resuming and caching. Note that Accept-Ranges is advisory: the session resumes optimistically and falls back to the full body if the server answers 200.

The file changed in between

If the file is replaced on the server between the interruption and the resume, If-Range no longer matches, and the server sends the whole new version. The session notices the 200, discards its partial file, and starts at zero:

currentETag.withLock { $0 = #""v2""# }     // the server now has a new version
downloader.resumedAt.withLock { $0.removeAll() }
let beforeChanged = server.requests.count
let restarted = try await downloader.resume(from: droppedResumeData!)
assert(server.requests[beforeChanged].header("If-Range") == #""v1""#)   // asked for the old version's range
assert(downloader.resumedAt.withLock { $0 } == [0])                      // and started over
assert((try? Data(contentsOf: restarted)) == content)

didResumeAtOffset reported 0, which is how an app can tell a real resume from a restart, for example to reset an ETA estimate.

The async API: simpler, with two gaps

session.download(from:) returns the downloaded file’s URL and is the simplest way to fetch a file. Two measurements show what it gives up:

final class ProgressProbe: NSObject, URLSessionDownloadDelegate, Sendable {
    let calls = Mutex(0)
    func urlSession(_ session: URLSession, downloadTask: URLSessionDownloadTask, didFinishDownloadingTo location: URL) {
        calls.withLock { $0 += 1 }
    }
    func urlSession(_ session: URLSession, downloadTask: URLSessionDownloadTask, didWriteData bytesWritten: Int64,
                    totalBytesWritten: Int64, totalBytesExpectedToWrite: Int64) {
        calls.withLock { $0 += 1 }
    }
}

let probe = ProgressProbe()
let (asyncFile, _) = try await URLSession.shared.download(from: fileURL, delegate: probe)
assert(probe.calls.withLock { $0 } == 0)                    // no download delegate callbacks at all
assert(FileManager.default.fileExists(atPath: asyncFile.path))

let asyncTask = Task { try await URLSession.shared.download(from: fileURL) }
try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(150))
asyncTask.cancel()
do {
    _ = try await asyncTask.value
} catch let error as URLError {
    assert(error.code == .cancelled && error.downloadTaskResumeData == nil)  // cancelling discards progress
}

cutAt.withLock { $0 = 700_000 }
do {
    _ = try await URLSession.shared.download(from: fileURL)
} catch let error as URLError {
    guard let data = error.downloadTaskResumeData else { fatalError("a lost connection should yield resume data") }
    let (resumedFile, response) = try await URLSession.shared.download(resumeFrom: data)
    assert((response as! HTTPURLResponse).statusCode == 206)
    assert((try? Data(contentsOf: resumedFile)) == content)
}
async download API Measured
Per-task delegate: with URLSessionDownloadDelegate methods No didWriteData, no didFinishDownloadingTo
Cancelling the Swift task URLError.cancelled, no resume data
Connection lost Resume data in the error; download(resumeFrom:) continues with 206
The returned file Not deleted on return; move it promptly anyway

The async API is therefore good for files that download in a few seconds, and fine for resuming after network failures. For a pause button or a progress bar, use the delegate-based task.

Progress you can show

The downloader recorded every didWriteData call. Download progress behaves differently from the upload progress measured in Uploading Files and Multipart Form Data, which arrived at most every 110 ms. Here the 2 MB download produced 20 callbacks in 0.53 seconds, one for each 100 KB piece the server sent, so the callbacks track the data as it arrives:

downloader.progress.withLock { $0.removeAll() }
let progressStart = ContinuousClock.now
_ = try await downloader.download(fileURL)
let samples = downloader.progress.withLock { $0 }
print("\(samples.count) progress callbacks in \(ContinuousClock.now - progressStart)")
assert(!samples.isEmpty && samples.last?.written == 2_000_000 && samples.allSatisfy { $0.expected == 2_000_000 })
assert(zip(samples, samples.dropFirst()).allSatisfy { $0.written <= $1.written })

The fraction complete is simply written / expected. The estimated time remaining is harder, because the instantaneous rate between two callbacks is noisy: one burst of 300 KB in 50 ms suggests 6 MB/s, the next stall suggests zero, and an ETA computed from either jumps between “2 seconds” and “an hour.” The standard remedy is an exponentially weighted moving average of the rate. Because callbacks arrive at irregular intervals, the weight of each new sample should depend on how much time it covers. With a time constant \(\tau\):

\[\alpha_i = 1 - e^{-\Delta t_i / \tau}, \qquad \hat r_i = \alpha_i\, r_i + (1 - \alpha_i)\, \hat r_{i-1}, \qquad \text{ETA} = \frac{\text{expected} - \text{written}}{\hat r_i}\]

A sample covering a long interval moves the estimate a lot, a sample covering a short one moves it a little, and \(\tau\) sets how quickly the estimate forgets: a few seconds is typical. The estimator below applies it to a synthetic sequence with a stall in the middle:

struct RateEstimator {
    let timeConstant: Double
    private(set) var rate: Double?   // bytes per second

    mutating func add(bytes: Double, over seconds: Double) {
        guard seconds > 0 else { return }
        let sample = bytes / seconds
        guard let previous = rate else { rate = sample; return }
        let alpha = 1 - exp(-seconds / timeConstant)
        rate = alpha * sample + (1 - alpha) * previous
    }

    func eta(remaining: Double) -> Double? { rate.flatMap { $0 > 0 ? remaining / $0 : nil } }
}

var estimator = RateEstimator(timeConstant: 3)
var naiveETAs: [Double] = []
var smoothETAs: [Double] = []
var remaining = 40_000_000.0
// 1 MB/s steady, then one second with no data, then 1 MB/s again; a sample every 250 ms.
let chunks = Array(repeating: 250_000.0, count: 12) + [0, 0, 0, 0] + Array(repeating: 250_000.0, count: 12)
for bytes in chunks {
    remaining -= bytes
    estimator.add(bytes: bytes, over: 0.25)
    smoothETAs.append(estimator.eta(remaining: remaining) ?? .infinity)
    naiveETAs.append(bytes > 0 ? remaining / (bytes / 0.25) : .infinity)
}
assert(naiveETAs.contains(.infinity))                   // the naive estimate jumped to "forever" during the stall
assert(smoothETAs.allSatisfy { $0.isFinite && $0 < 60 }) // the smoothed one stayed finite
let duringStall = smoothETAs[15]
print("smoothed ETA before stall \(smoothETAs[11]), at the end of the stall \(duringStall)")
assert(duringStall > smoothETAs[11] && duringStall < 2.5 * smoothETAs[11])  // it rose, but did not explode

During the one-second stall the naive estimate became infinite four times in a row. The smoothed one rose from 37 to 52 seconds, a factor of 1.4, and recovered as data resumed, which is what a person watching it expects. Reset the estimator when didResumeAtOffset reports a restart.

Where the file should go

didFinishDownloadingTo hands over a file in a temporary location; the app decides where it lives next. On iOS the choice determines whether it is backed up and whether the system may delete it:

Directory Backed up May be purged by the system Use for
tmp No Yes, any time the app is not running Files needed only briefly
Library/Caches No Yes, when storage is low Re-downloadable content: covers, previews
Application Support Yes, unless excluded No Content the user chose to keep offline
Documents Yes No User-visible documents

Downloaded content that can be fetched again, such as an audiobook the user can re-download, belongs in Application Support with isExcludedFromBackup set, so it neither fills the user’s iCloud backup nor disappears when the device runs low on space. Resume data, which is small, should be stored alongside the record of the download, together with the time it was produced, since it is only useful while its partial file survives.

try FileManager.default.removeItem(at: downloads)

Summary

  • Range requests resume a download: Range: bytes=N- gets 206 Partial Content; If-Range with the ETag makes the server send the whole new version instead if the file changed.
  • Measured: pausing with cancelByProducingResumeData() gave about 7 KB of resume data, and resuming sent Range: bytes=581660-, exactly the bytes already received, with If-Range: "v1". A changed ETag restarted the download at offset 0.
  • Resume data requires a validator (ETag or Last-Modified), not Accept-Ranges. A lost connection delivers it in URLError.downloadTaskResumeData.
  • The async download API sends no download delegate callbacks and produces no resume data on cancellation. Use a delegate-based URLSessionDownloadTask for progress and pause.
  • The temporary file is deleted when didFinishDownloadingTo returns; move it first, and check the status code before keeping it.
  • Smooth the transfer rate with a time-weighted EWMA, \(\alpha = 1 - e^{-\Delta t/\tau}\), for an ETA that survives stalls.
  • Keep re-downloadable files in Application Support excluded from backup, or in Caches if losing them is fine.

Exercise

Add a DownloadManager actor that keeps several Downloader-style tasks keyed by URL, persists each one’s resume data and destination to a JSON file when paused or interrupted, and on launch offers to resume each one. Test it against the server by interrupting three downloads at different offsets with cutAt, recreating the manager from its file, resuming all three concurrently, and asserting that every file matches content and that each resumed request’s Range header matches the bytes that were already received.

Further reading

  • RFC 9110 §14: Range Requests and §13.1.5 on If-Range.
  • Apple’s Pausing and resuming downloads and urlSession(_:downloadTask:didFinishDownloadingTo:).
  • Build robust and resumable file transfers, WWDC23.

Previous: Uploading Files and Multipart Form Data. Next: Background Transfers and App Relaunch.

Return to the Networking roadmap.
entry.summary: A large download has three needs that a small request does not. The user wants to see it progress. It must survive interruption, because a 400 MB audiobook over cellular will lose its connection at some point, and starting again from zero each time means it may never finish. And its result is a file, which lives somewhere with rules about how long it stays there. HTTP makes resuming possible with range requests: a client that has the first 300 MB asks for the rest, and a server that still has the same version of the file sends only the rest. URLSession wraps this in resume data. This article implements range support on the test server, measures exactly when URLSession can produce resume data and what it sends when it resumes, including two behaviors of the async download API that decide which API to use, and ends with progress reporting and an ETA estimate that does not jump around.

entry.title: Uploading Files and Multipart Form Data

link.title: Uploading Files and Multipart Form Data

entry.content:
Uploading a file looks like a request with a large body, and for small files that is all it is. The details start to matter as files grow and as servers ask for more than a file. A profile photo upload usually needs the image, its file name, and a caption in one request, which is what multipart/form-data is for. A video from the camera roll is hundreds of megabytes, and loading it into a Data value before sending it can get an app terminated for memory use. And a user who watches a progress bar expects it to move.

This article builds a multipart body by hand, following RFC 7578, and verifies it with a parser on the server side. It measures the memory cost of building a 100 MB body in memory against streaming it through a file, including a trap in the streaming version that makes it as expensive as the in-memory one. It reports progress from the session delegate, and it ends with when not to use multipart at all.

The examples use Swift 6 language mode and were compiled and run with the Swift 6.4 toolchain from Xcode 27.1 on macOS 26. They send requests to LocalServer, the loopback HTTP server from the appendix of the first article; paste that code first, then the blocks below in order, into one main.swift.

The shape of a multipart body

A multipart/form-data body is a sequence of parts, each with its own small header section and content, separated by a boundary string that the client chooses and announces in the request’s Content-Type:

POST /uploads HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=Boundary-5C1A...
Content-Length: 1843

--Boundary-5C1A...
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="caption"

Reading on the train
--Boundary-5C1A...
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="photo"; filename="cover.jpg"
Content-Type: image/jpeg

<binary bytes of the file>
--Boundary-5C1A...--

The rules are few and strict, and each one is a bug in a hand-written encoder somewhere:

  • Every line break in the framing is CRLF, \r\n, never a bare \n.
  • Each part starts with -- followed by the boundary, then CRLF.
  • A part’s headers end with an empty line. Content-Disposition: form-data; name="..." is required; filename marks a file; Content-Type defaults to text/plain if omitted.
  • The CRLF before each boundary line belongs to the delimiter, not to the preceding content. A file that ends without a newline must not gain one.
  • The body ends with -- boundary --.
flowchart LR
    accTitle: The structure of a multipart/form-data body
    D1["--boundary CRLF"] --> H1["Content-Disposition: form-data; name=caption CRLF CRLF"]
    H1 --> C1["Reading on the train"]
    C1 --> D2["CRLF --boundary CRLF"]
    D2 --> H2["Content-Disposition ... filename=cover.jpg CRLF<br/>Content-Type: image/jpeg CRLF CRLF"]
    H2 --> C2["file bytes"]
    C2 --> E["CRLF --boundary-- CRLF"]

Choosing a boundary

The boundary must not occur inside any part’s content, because the receiver would take that occurrence as the end of the part. Scanning every file for the boundary would require reading it twice, so encoders instead choose a boundary long and random enough that a collision is not a practical concern. With a boundary containing \(k\) random bits, the chance that it appears at any given position of arbitrary content is at most \(2^{-k}\), so over a body of \(n\) bytes:

\[P(\text{collision}) \;\le\; n \cdot 2^{-k}\]

A UUID has 122 random bits. For a terabyte of uploads, \(n = 10^{12}\), the bound is \(10^{12} \times 2^{-122} \approx 2 \times 10^{-25}\). Random boundaries are safe; fixed ones such as "----boundary" are not, because they can appear in content the app does not control, including a previous multipart body uploaded as a file.

An encoder

The encoder writes to any destination that accepts bytes, so the same code builds a body in memory or streams it into a file:

import Foundation
import CryptoKit
import Synchronization

struct MultipartForm {
    enum Part {
        case field(name: String, value: String)
        case file(name: String, filename: String, contentType: String, source: URL)
    }

    let boundary = "Boundary-\(UUID().uuidString)"
    var parts: [Part] = []

    var contentType: String { "multipart/form-data; boundary=\(boundary)" }

    /// RFC 7578 §4.2 and the HTML standard: quote names and escape ", CR and LF by percent-encoding.
    static func quoted(_ value: String) -> String {
        let escaped = value.replacing("\"", with: "%22").replacing("\r", with: "%0D").replacing("\n", with: "%0A")
        return "\"\(escaped)\""
    }

    func write(to sink: (Data) throws -> Void) throws {
        let crlf = Data("\r\n".utf8)
        for part in parts {
            try sink(Data("--\(boundary)\r\n".utf8))
            switch part {
            case .field(let name, let value):
                try sink(Data("Content-Disposition: form-data; name=\(Self.quoted(name))\r\n\r\n".utf8))
                try sink(Data(value.utf8))
            case .file(let name, let filename, let contentType, let source):
                try sink(Data(("Content-Disposition: form-data; name=\(Self.quoted(name)); filename=\(Self.quoted(filename))\r\n"
                               + "Content-Type: \(contentType)\r\n\r\n").utf8))
                let reader = try FileHandle(forReadingFrom: source)
                defer { try? reader.close() }
                while try autoreleasepool(invoking: {
                    guard let chunk = try reader.read(upToCount: 1 << 20), !chunk.isEmpty else { return false }
                    try sink(chunk)
                    return true
                }) {}
            }
            try sink(crlf)
        }
        try sink(Data("--\(boundary)--\r\n".utf8))
    }

    func data() throws -> Data {
        var body = Data()
        try write { body.append($0) }
        return body
    }

    func writeFile() throws -> URL {
        let url = FileManager.default.temporaryDirectory.appending(path: "upload-\(UUID().uuidString).multipart")
        FileManager.default.createFile(atPath: url.path, contents: nil)
        let writer = try FileHandle(forWritingTo: url)
        defer { try? writer.close() }
        try write { try writer.write(contentsOf: $0) }
        return url
    }
}

File names are UTF-8 inside the quotes. RFC 7578 explicitly says the filename* syntax from other headers is not used in multipart/form-data, and servers that accept form uploads from browsers expect what browsers send: raw UTF-8, with ", CR, and LF percent-encoded. The autoreleasepool around each chunk read is not decoration; the measurement below shows what happens without it.

A server that checks the bytes

A parser on the server side splits the body at the boundary and reports each part’s headers and the SHA-256 of its content, so the test can compare exact bytes, not just sizes:

struct ReceivedPart: Equatable {
    var disposition: String
    var contentType: String?
    var sha256: String
    var text: String?
}

func parseMultipart(_ body: Data, contentType: String?) -> [ReceivedPart]? {
    guard let contentType, let range = contentType.range(of: "boundary=") else { return nil }
    let boundary = String(contentType[range.upperBound...])
    let delimiter = Data("\r\n--\(boundary)".utf8)
    let framed = Data("\r\n".utf8) + body                      // the first delimiter has no leading CRLF
    var parts: [ReceivedPart] = []
    var cursor = framed.startIndex
    guard let first = framed.range(of: delimiter, in: cursor..<framed.endIndex) else { return nil }
    cursor = first.upperBound
    while true {
        if framed[cursor...].starts(with: Data("--".utf8)) { return parts }   // closing delimiter
        guard framed[cursor...].starts(with: Data("\r\n".utf8)) else { return nil }
        cursor += 2
        guard let headerEnd = framed.range(of: Data("\r\n\r\n".utf8), in: cursor..<framed.endIndex),
              let next = framed.range(of: delimiter, in: headerEnd.upperBound..<framed.endIndex) else { return nil }
        let headers = String(decoding: framed[cursor..<headerEnd.lowerBound], as: UTF8.self).components(separatedBy: "\r\n")
        let content = framed[headerEnd.upperBound..<next.lowerBound]
        let disposition = headers.first { $0.lowercased().hasPrefix("content-disposition:") } ?? ""
        let type = headers.first { $0.lowercased().hasPrefix("content-type:") }.map { String($0.dropFirst(13)).trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespaces) }
        parts.append(ReceivedPart(disposition: String(disposition.dropFirst(20)).trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespaces),
                                  contentType: type,
                                  sha256: SHA256.hash(data: content).map { String(format: "%02x", $0) }.joined(),
                                  text: content.count < 200 ? String(data: content, encoding: .utf8) : nil))
        cursor = next.upperBound
    }
}

let received = Mutex<[ReceivedPart]>([])
let server = try await LocalServer.start { request in
    guard request.path == "/uploads", let parts = parseMultipart(request.body, contentType: request.header("Content-Type")) else {
        return .text("malformed multipart body", status: 400)
    }
    received.withLock { $0 = parts }
    return .json(#"{"parts":\#(parts.count),"bytes":\#(request.body.count)}"#, status: 201)
}

Sending a small upload

A caption and a small file with a non-ASCII name that contains quotes. The test file deliberately ends without a newline, to catch an encoder that adds one:

let workspace = FileManager.default.temporaryDirectory.appending(path: "uploads-\(UUID().uuidString)")
try FileManager.default.createDirectory(at: workspace, withIntermediateDirectories: true)
let coverFile = workspace.appending(path: "cover.jpg")
let coverBytes = Data((0..<5_000).map { UInt8(truncatingIfNeeded: $0 &* 7) }) + Data("--Boundary-".utf8)
try coverBytes.write(to: coverFile)

var form = MultipartForm()
form.parts = [
    .field(name: "caption", value: "Reading on the train ☕"),
    .file(name: "photo", filename: #"résumé "final".jpg"#, contentType: "image/jpeg", source: coverFile),
]

var request = URLRequest(url: server.baseURL.appending(path: "uploads"))
request.httpMethod = "POST"
request.setValue(form.contentType, forHTTPHeaderField: "Content-Type")
let (_, response) = try await URLSession.shared.upload(for: request, from: try form.data())
assert((response as! HTTPURLResponse).statusCode == 201)

let parts = received.withLock { $0 }
assert(parts.count == 2)
assert(parts[0].disposition == #"form-data; name="caption""# && parts[0].text == "Reading on the train ☕")
assert(parts[1].disposition == #"form-data; name="photo"; filename="résumé %22final%22.jpg""#)
assert(parts[1].contentType == "image/jpeg")
assert(parts[1].sha256 == SHA256.hash(data: coverBytes).map { String(format: "%02x", $0) }.joined())

The file’s hash matches byte for byte, including its last bytes, which look like the start of a boundary on purpose. Content that resembles the delimiter is harmless as long as it does not contain the whole delimiter, CRLF followed by -- and the exact boundary, which a random boundary guarantees in practice.

Large files: memory is the constraint

upload(for:from:) takes a Data, so the whole body is in memory, and building it with Data(contentsOf:) and append holds the file twice for a moment. For a 100 MB video that is the difference between a smooth upload and the system terminating an app extension, whose memory limits are far lower than an app’s. upload(for:fromFile:) streams the body from disk instead. The cost of each approach, measured with the process’s physical footprint, the number the system uses for memory limits:

func physicalFootprint() -> Int {
    var info = task_vm_info_data_t()
    var count = mach_msg_type_number_t(MemoryLayout<task_vm_info_data_t>.size / MemoryLayout<natural_t>.size)
    let result = withUnsafeMutablePointer(to: &info) {
        $0.withMemoryRebound(to: integer_t.self, capacity: Int(count)) {
            task_info(mach_task_self_, task_flavor_t(TASK_VM_INFO), $0, &count)
        }
    }
    precondition(result == KERN_SUCCESS)
    return Int(info.phys_footprint)
}

let videoFile = workspace.appending(path: "video.mov")
FileManager.default.createFile(atPath: videoFile.path, contents: nil)
let videoWriter = try FileHandle(forWritingTo: videoFile)
let megabyte = Data((0..<1_048_576).map { UInt8(truncatingIfNeeded: $0 &* 31) })
for _ in 0..<100 { try autoreleasepool { try videoWriter.write(contentsOf: megabyte) } }
try videoWriter.close()

var videoForm = MultipartForm()
videoForm.parts = [.file(name: "video", filename: "video.mov", contentType: "video/quicktime", source: videoFile)]

let beforeInMemory = physicalFootprint()
var inMemoryBody: Data? = try videoForm.data()
let inMemoryCost = physicalFootprint() - beforeInMemory
inMemoryBody = nil

let beforeStreaming = physicalFootprint()
let bodyFile = try videoForm.writeFile()
let streamingCost = physicalFootprint() - beforeStreaming

print("in memory: +\(inMemoryCost / 1_000_000) MB, streamed to a file: +\(streamingCost / 1_000_000) MB")
assert(inMemoryCost > 100_000_000)
assert(streamingCost < 10_000_000)
Building a 100 MB multipart body Footprint increase (measured)
Data(contentsOf:) for the file, then append into a body Data 209 MB
The encoder above writing into a Data (videoForm.data()) 108 MB
Streamed to a file, chunked reads without autoreleasepool 105 MB
Streamed to a file, chunked reads inside autoreleasepool (videoForm.writeFile()) under 1 MB

The first row holds the file twice for a moment: once as read, once as copied into the body. The second holds the body once, which is the minimum for any Data-based upload. The third is the trap.

Reading the file in 1 MB chunks looks like streaming, but each chunk returned by FileHandle.read(upToCount:) is released only when the enclosing autorelease pool drains. In a loop on one thread, that happens only after the loop, so every chunk stays alive and the “streaming” version holds the whole file in memory anyway. On the main thread of an app the pool drains once per run-loop pass, which does not help a loop that runs within one pass. Wrapping each iteration in autoreleasepool releases each chunk before the next is read.

The body file is then sent with upload(for:fromFile:), which also streams, and sets Content-Length from the file’s size. The server’s hash of the received part confirms the 100 MB arrived intact:

var videoRequest = URLRequest(url: server.baseURL.appending(path: "uploads"))
videoRequest.httpMethod = "POST"
videoRequest.setValue(videoForm.contentType, forHTTPHeaderField: "Content-Type")
let (_, videoResponse) = try await URLSession.shared.upload(for: videoRequest, fromFile: bodyFile)
assert((videoResponse as! HTTPURLResponse).statusCode == 201)

let videoPart = received.withLock { $0 }.first
let expectedVideoHash = try autoreleasepool { SHA256.hash(data: try Data(contentsOf: videoFile)) }
assert(videoPart?.sha256 == expectedVideoHash.map { String(format: "%02x", $0) }.joined())
try FileManager.default.removeItem(at: bodyFile)

Reporting progress

The session delegate’s urlSession(_:task:didSendBodyData:totalBytesSent:totalBytesExpectedToSend:) reports upload progress. Measured against LocalServer, it was called exactly once for the 100 MB upload, with the full size: over the loopback interface the whole body was accepted in a fraction of a second, and progress callbacks are delivered at a limited rate. To see what a user on a real network sees, the server below reads at a fixed rate, 256 KB every 10 ms, about 25 MB/s, and records how much it has received:

import Network

final class ByteCounter: Sendable {
    let value = Mutex(0)
}

final class SlowSink: Sendable {
    let received = ByteCounter()
    private let listener: NWListener
    var port: Int { Int(listener.port!.rawValue) }

    init(bytesPerTick: Int, tick: Duration) async throws {
        let parameters = NWParameters.tcp
        parameters.requiredLocalEndpoint = .hostPort(host: .ipv4(.loopback), port: .any)
        listener = try NWListener(using: parameters)
        let received = self.received
        listener.newConnectionHandler = { connection in
            connection.start(queue: .global())
            Task {
                do {
                    var buffer = Data()
                    while buffer.range(of: Data("\r\n\r\n".utf8)) == nil {
                        guard let more = try await connection.receiveSome() else { return }
                        buffer += more
                    }
                    let headEnd = buffer.range(of: Data("\r\n\r\n".utf8))!
                    let head = String(decoding: buffer[..<headEnd.lowerBound], as: UTF8.self).lowercased()
                    let length = head.split(separator: "\r\n").first { $0.hasPrefix("content-length:") }
                        .flatMap { Int($0.dropFirst(15).trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespaces)) } ?? 0
                    received.value.withLock { $0 = buffer.count - headEnd.upperBound }
                    while received.value.withLock({ $0 }) < length {
                        try await Task.sleep(for: tick)
                        let chunk: Data? = try await withCheckedThrowingContinuation { continuation in
                            connection.receive(minimumIncompleteLength: 1, maximumLength: bytesPerTick) { data, _, _, error in
                                if let error { continuation.resume(throwing: error) } else { continuation.resume(returning: data) }
                            }
                        }
                        received.value.withLock { $0 += chunk?.count ?? 0 }
                    }
                    try await connection.sendAll(Data("HTTP/1.1 201 \r\nContent-Length: 0\r\n\r\n".utf8))
                } catch {
                    connection.cancel()
                }
            }
        }
        try await withCheckedThrowingContinuation { (continuation: CheckedContinuation<Void, any Error>) in
            let resumed = Mutex(false)
            listener.stateUpdateHandler = { state in
                if case .ready = state, resumed.withLock({ done in defer { done = true }; return !done }) {
                    continuation.resume()
                }
            }
            listener.start(queue: .global())
        }
    }
}

final class UploadProgress: NSObject, URLSessionTaskDelegate, Sendable {
    let events = Mutex<[(sent: Int64, expected: Int64, serverHad: Int, at: ContinuousClock.Instant)]>([])
    let sink: SlowSink
    init(sink: SlowSink) { self.sink = sink }

    func urlSession(_ session: URLSession, task: URLSessionTask, didSendBodyData bytesSent: Int64,
                    totalBytesSent: Int64, totalBytesExpectedToSend: Int64) {
        let serverHad = sink.received.value.withLock { $0 }
        events.withLock { $0.append((totalBytesSent, totalBytesExpectedToSend, serverHad, .now)) }
    }
}

let slowSink = try await SlowSink(bytesPerTick: 256 * 1024, tick: .milliseconds(10))
let twentyMegabytes = FileManager.default.temporaryDirectory.appending(path: "progress-\(UUID().uuidString).bin")
try Data(repeating: 7, count: 20_000_000).write(to: twentyMegabytes)
var progressRequest = URLRequest(url: URL(string: "http://127.0.0.1:\(slowSink.port)/uploads")!)
progressRequest.httpMethod = "POST"

let progress = UploadProgress(sink: slowSink)
let progressStart = ContinuousClock.now
let (_, progressResponse) = try await URLSession.shared.upload(for: progressRequest, fromFile: twentyMegabytes, delegate: progress)
assert((progressResponse as! HTTPURLResponse).statusCode == 201)

let events = progress.events.withLock { $0 }
let gaps = zip(events, events.dropFirst()).map { $1.at - $0.at }
print("\(events.count) events in \(ContinuousClock.now - progressStart); first: sent \(events[0].sent), server had \(events[0].serverHad)")
assert(events.count >= 4 && events.count <= 20)
assert(events.last?.sent == 20_000_000 && events.allSatisfy { $0.expected == 20_000_000 })
assert(zip(events, events.dropFirst()).allSatisfy { $0.sent <= $1.sent })   // monotonic
assert(gaps.allSatisfy { $0 > .milliseconds(80) })                         // rate-limited callbacks
assert(events[0].sent > Int64(events[0].serverHad))                          // sent runs ahead of received
try FileManager.default.removeItem(at: twentyMegabytes)
try FileManager.default.removeItem(at: workspace)

The 20 MB upload took about 1.1 seconds and produced seven progress events, never closer together than about 110 ms; the median gap was 150 ms. The first event reported 5,242,880 bytes sent 0.16 seconds in, when the server had read only 2 MB in this run: the difference was sitting in socket buffers on the way. Two consequences for a progress bar:

  • It should animate between events rather than jump, because events arrive a few times per second at most, and on a fast network there may be only one.
  • It runs ahead of the server and reaches 100% before the server has finished receiving, let alone processing. Keep the bar at “Processing…” until the response arrives.

When the body length is unknown, as with a stream body, totalBytesExpectedToSend is NSURLSessionTransferSizeUnknown (-1), and the bar can only be indeterminate.

When not to use multipart

Multipart exists for browser forms, where one submission mixes text fields and files. An API designed for an app often has better options:

Approach When it fits Why
PUT or POST the raw file, Content-Type: image/jpeg One file, metadata in headers or the URL No framing, no boundary, the body is the file
Upload to a pre-signed URL, then POST metadata as JSON Large files to object storage (S3, GCS) The file never passes through the API servers
Resumable upload protocols, such as tus or the IETF’s resumable uploads draft Very large files on unreliable networks An interrupted upload continues from where it stopped
multipart/form-data Server already accepts browser forms, or several files plus fields in one request Compatibility

Resumability is the strongest argument against a single large request. A 500 MB upload that fails at 90% over cellular has to start again unless the protocol can resume it. Since iOS 17, URLSession supports the IETF resumable upload draft for servers that implement it, which Background Transfers and App Relaunch touches on, and downloads have resumed for much longer, as Download Progress, Resuming, and Temporary Files shows.

Summary

  • A multipart body is parts separated by CRLF--boundary, each with Content-Disposition and optional Content-Type, ending with --boundary--. The CRLF before a boundary belongs to the delimiter.
  • Use a random boundary; a UUID’s 122 random bits make collisions negligible, \(n \cdot 2^{-122}\).
  • Quote names, keep file names as UTF-8, and percent-encode ", CR, and LF; filename* is not used in form data.
  • Measured for a 100 MB file: building the body in memory cost 209 MB; streaming it to a file cost 105 MB without autoreleasepool and 1 MB with it. Send it with upload(for:fromFile:).
  • Measured: didSendBodyData fired once for a 100 MB loopback upload and seven times, at least 110 ms apart, for 20 MB at 25 MB/s. It reports bytes handed to the network, ahead of what the server has read; the response, not 100%, means done.
  • Prefer a raw-body upload, a pre-signed URL, or a resumable protocol when the API allows.

entry.summary: Uploading a file looks like a request with a large body, and for small files that is all it is. The details start to matter as files grow and as servers ask for more than a file. A profile photo upload usually needs the image, its file name, and a caption in one request, which is what multipart/form-data is for. A video from the camera roll is hundreds of megabytes, and loading it into a Data value before sending it can get an app terminated for memory use. And a user who watches a progress bar expects it to move. This article builds a multipart body by hand, following RFC 7578, and verifies it with a parser on the server side. It measures the memory cost of building a 100 MB body in memory against streaming it through a file, including a trap in the streaming version that makes it as expensive as the in-memory one. It reports progress from the session delegate, and it ends with when not to use multipart at all.
